items.title: Migrations
items.body:
## Migrations: evolving the schema safely
Your data model will *change*, you will add fields, new tables, new relationships, as the app grows, and changing a database that holds *real data* must be done carefully. **Migrations** are versioned, ordered changes to your database structure, and Prisma generates them from your schema:
```bash
# you change schema.prisma (add a field), then:
npx prisma migrate dev --name add_user_phone
# Prisma generates the SQL migration and applies it
```
A migration is a recorded SQL script that transforms the database from one structure to the next (e.g. "add a `phone` column to `users`"), and migrations are *versioned and applied in order*, so the database's structure has a *history* and can be brought to the current schema by running the migrations in sequence. You change the schema (the source of truth), Prisma generates the migration to match, and the migration is applied to update the actual database.

## Why migrations matter: changing data without losing it
The reason migrations are essential, rather than just editing the database directly, is that production databases hold *real data you cannot lose*, and migrations are how you evolve the structure *safely and reproducibly* around that data. Consider the alternatives' problems: editing the production database by hand is error-prone, unrecorded, and not reproducible (you cannot recreate the change in another environment or undo it cleanly); and you cannot just "recreate" the database with the new structure because that would *destroy* the existing data. Migrations solve this by being *scripted, ordered, version-controlled* changes that transform the schema *while preserving the data*: adding a column keeps the existing rows (with the new column defaulted or null), and the migration script can include data transformations (backfilling the new column) where needed. Because migrations are versioned and committed to git, they give you the same benefits version control gives code: the database's structural history is recorded (you can see when and why each change happened), the *same* migrations run in every environment (so local, staging, and production databases all reach the identical structure reproducibly), and changes go through review. This is the database equivalent of the reproducibility and version-everything discipline from the ML infrastructure work, applied to schema: your database structure is defined by versioned migrations, so it is reproducible, auditable, and evolves safely without data loss. Migrations are how a real application's data layer changes over months and years without losing data or drifting out of sync across environments.

## The discipline of safe migrations
Migrations also teach the *care* required when changing live data, which is a real production skill, because a careless migration can lose data or break the app. Key disciplines:
- **Migrations are forward-moving and ordered:** each is applied once, in sequence, and the history is preserved, never edit an already-applied migration; create a new one to make further changes.
- **Consider the existing data:** when you change the structure, think about what happens to the *current* rows, adding a `NOT NULL` column to a table with existing rows needs a default or a backfill, or it fails; renaming or dropping a column can lose data. The migration must account for the data already there.
- **Test migrations before production:** run them on a copy/staging first, because a migration that fails or corrupts data in production is a serious incident.
- **Backwards-compatible changes for zero-downtime:** in production, you often need the old and new code to both work during a deploy, so risky changes (dropping a column) are done in careful stages.
You do not need to master every advanced migration technique now, but internalising that **changing a database with real data requires deliberate, scripted, tested, versioned changes that preserve the data**, never casual hand-edits, is the foundational discipline. Migrations give you the *mechanism* (versioned, reproducible schema changes); the *discipline* (account for existing data, test first, never lose data) is what makes evolving your data layer safe. This is a core part of "data you won't regret": not just designing the schema well initially, but being able to *evolve* it safely as needs change, which migrations make possible.

## Where this fits
You understand migrations: versioned, ordered, scripted schema changes (generated by Prisma from your schema) that evolve the database *while preserving existing data*, giving a reproducible, auditable, version-controlled structural history across environments, applied with the discipline of accounting for existing data and testing before production. Tomorrow you handle a production database concern: connection pooling.

items.title: Connection pooling
items.body:
## Connection pooling: a production necessity
A subtle but critical production concern: databases handle a *limited* number of simultaneous **connections**, and opening a database connection is relatively *expensive* (slow to establish). If your server opened a new connection for every request, two problems hit fast: the overhead of constantly opening/closing connections slows everything, and under load you would *exhaust* the database's connection limit (Postgres has a max, often ~100), crashing or blocking. **Connection pooling** solves this: a *pool* of database connections is opened once and *reused* across requests, so a request *borrows* a ready connection from the pool, uses it, and returns it, rather than opening its own:
```text
without pooling:  each request -> open connection (slow) -> query -> close. Exhausts limits under load.
with pooling:     a pool of N connections is kept open and reused -> requests borrow & return them
```
The pool keeps a manageable number of connections alive and shares them efficiently among many requests.

## Why pooling is essential at scale (and the serverless wrinkle)
Connection pooling matters because it is the difference between a database layer that *survives real traffic* and one that falls over, and understanding *why* connects to the runtime model. A web server handles many concurrent requests (Node's whole strength, W9), and if each needed its own database connection, the number of connections would balloon with traffic and quickly exceed the database's limit, at which point new requests *cannot get a connection* and the app fails, exactly when you need it most (under load). Pooling caps the connections at a sustainable number and *reuses* them, so the server can handle far more concurrent requests than there are connections (most requests use a connection only briefly, so a pool of, say, 20 connections serves hundreds of concurrent requests as they take turns), and the expensive connection-opening happens once (at startup) rather than per request. This is essential for any production database-backed app. There is a modern wrinkle especially relevant to your stack: **serverless** environments (like Vercel/Next.js serverless functions) spin up many short-lived function instances, *each* of which might open its own connections, which can exhaust the database limit fast, so serverless setups need special pooling (a dedicated connection pooler like PgBouncer, or the database provider's pooled connection, e.g. Neon's pooled endpoint that FORGE itself uses). This is a real, common production gotcha, "too many connections" errors under load in a serverless app, and the fix is proper pooling. Knowing that databases have connection limits, that opening connections is expensive, and that pooling (reuse a fixed set) is how you serve many requests within those limits, is essential production knowledge.

## Lean on the tools, but understand the concept
The practical guidance, consistent with the track, is that you usually *configure* pooling rather than build it, Prisma manages a connection pool for you, hosting platforms and managed databases provide pooling, and serverless setups use a provided pooler (like Neon's pooled connection or PgBouncer), so the implementation is handled by the tools. But *understanding the concept* is what lets you configure it correctly and debug the problems when they arise. The classic symptom is an app that works fine in development (low traffic, few connections) and then throws "too many connections" or slows dramatically *in production under load*, and without understanding pooling, this is a baffling, hard-to-diagnose failure; *with* the understanding, you immediately recognise it as a connection-exhaustion problem and apply the fix (proper pooling configuration, a pooled connection string, especially in serverless). This is exactly the kind of production concern that does not show up until real traffic hits, which is why knowing about it *in advance* is so valuable, you build pooling in correctly from the start rather than discovering the problem during an outage. It connects to the broader theme that production has concerns invisible in development (the same lesson as cold starts, drift, and other "works locally, breaks in production" issues across the tracks), and connection pooling is a foundational one for any database-backed app, particularly in the serverless deployments common to modern web apps (and to FORGE specifically). Understand pooling, configure it correctly for your environment (especially serverless), and you avoid one of the most common production database failures.

## Where this fits
You understand connection pooling: reusing a fixed set of database connections across many requests because connections are limited and expensive, essential to surviving production traffic within the database's connection limit, with the serverless wrinkle (many function instances can exhaust connections, needing a dedicated pooler) that affects modern stacks like FORGE's. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship the Postgres + Prisma data layer.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a robust data layer
You assemble the week into a production-grade data layer for a real backend (a URL shortener, or Bean Forge's data, or any app), demonstrating data done right:
- **PostgreSQL** as the database, with a **thoughtfully-designed schema** (well-modelled entities, relationships, constraints enforcing integrity).
- **Prisma** for type-safe queries (schema as the single source of truth, compile-time-checked data access), with **indexes** on the columns your queries use.
- **migrations** evolving the schema safely (versioned, data-preserving) and **connection pooling** configured for your environment.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Data layer: PostgreSQL + Prisma, modelled schema, indexes, migrations, pooling"
git push
```

## The deliverable is a data layer you won't regret
What makes this project demonstrate real backend competence is that the data layer is *well-designed, fast, type-safe, and able to evolve*, the "data you won't regret" the week is named for. The strongest version shows a schema that *models the domain correctly* (proper entities, relationships, and constraints so invalid data is impossible), queried *type-safely* through Prisma (data bugs caught at compile time), with *indexes* making the real queries fast, *migrations* providing a versioned, data-preserving history of how the schema evolved, and *pooling* configured so it survives production load. The proof is that the foundation is *robust*: the database enforces integrity (you cannot create orphaned or duplicate data), queries are fast (indexed) and reliable (type-safe), the schema can change safely (migrations) without data loss, and it scales (pooling). Demonstrating that you can *design and build a data layer thoughtfully*, modelling, integrity, performance, type safety, safe evolution, rather than just dumping data into tables, is the deliverable, and it is one of the most valuable and lasting backend skills, because the data layer is the foundation everything else depends on and the hardest part to fix later.

## What the data layer established
Step back: you have built the data foundation of a real backend, and learned the most consequential and lasting part of backend design. You can model data correctly in a relational database (entities, relationships, constraints, with the database enforcing integrity), work with it type-safely and conveniently through Prisma (schema as truth, compile-time-checked queries), make it fast with indexes (measured, query-driven), evolve it safely with migrations (versioned, data-preserving), and scale it with connection pooling (surviving production load). The throughline is *data you won't regret*: deliberate, correct, fast, evolvable data design, because a good data foundation supports an application for years while a bad one is a constant, costly burden. This is FORGE's own stack (Postgres + Prisma), so it is directly the real-world skill set. Combined with the server (W9), you now have a backend that can store and manage data robustly, the foundation that the APIs (next week) and auth (W12) build on.

## Where this fits
You shipped a robust PostgreSQL + Prisma data layer with a well-modelled schema, indexes, migrations, and pooling, the lasting foundation of a real backend, and FORGE's own stack. With a server (W9) and data (W10) in place, next week you design how clients *access* this functionality well: **REST API design**, building endpoints that are intuitive, consistent, and standard (proper resource URLs, HTTP methods and status codes, pagination, filtering), the "endpoints people don't hate" that make your backend a pleasure to consume.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You add a userId field to your Url model but mark it as optional (userId Int?). Later you decide every URL must have a user and change it to required (userId Int). Why can you not just change the schema and run a migration without extra steps? The migration would add a NOT NULL constraint to a column that already has NULL values (existing URLs created before auth was added). PostgreSQL rejects NOT NULL constraints on columns with existing NULL values. You must first fill in the NULL values, either by adding a default value (userId Int @default(1)), writing a migration that updates existing rows with a placeholder user ID, or accepting a two-step migration: add a temporary default, apply the constraint, remove the default. Database migrations on production data require careful planning.

weeks.title: REST API Design, Endpoints People Don't Hate
weeks.context:
REST is not a technology, it is a set of constraints on how you use HTTP. The word "RESTful" is widely abused. What it actually means in practice: your API uses nouns (resources) not verbs in URLs, HTTP methods carry the semantic meaning of the operation, and responses use standard HTTP status codes so clients do not have to parse error messages to know what happened.

URL design: use plural nouns for collections (/users, /orders, /products). Use the pattern /resource/:id for individual items. Nest sub-resources when the relationship is ownership: /users/:id/orders means the orders that belong to a specific user. Do not nest more than two levels deep, it becomes unwieldy. Avoid verbs in URLs: /users/:id/delete is wrong; DELETE /users/:id is correct. The method IS the verb.

HTTP methods and their contracts. GET is safe (reading does not change state) and idempotent (calling it twice has the same effect as calling it once). PUT replaces an entire resource, sending PUT /users/1 with a partial body should fail or overwrite missing fields with null. PATCH updates specific fields only. POST creates a new resource or triggers an action; it is neither safe nor idempotent. DELETE is idempotent, deleting a resource that does not exist should return 404 or 204, but a second DELETE should not crash.

Status codes. 200 OK, 201 Created (after a successful POST), 204 No Content (success with no response body, common for DELETE). 400 Bad Request (malformed request body), 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict (duplicate email on registration), 422 Unprocessable Entity (valid JSON but failed validation). 500 Internal Server Error (something broke on the server). Never return 200 with an error message in the body, that makes your API a lie.

This week you design and build the full REST API for Bean Forge: CRUD endpoints for menu items, orders, and customers. You write an OpenAPI spec for it. You use zod for request validation so bad input never reaches your database.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## REST: constraints that make APIs predictable
You have built endpoints (Next.js route handlers, Express routes); this week you learn to design them *well*. **REST** is not a technology, it is a set of *constraints* on how you use HTTP, and the word "RESTful" is widely abused, so it is worth stating what it actually means in practice. A well-designed REST API has three properties: URLs are **nouns** (resources), not verbs; **HTTP methods** carry the meaning of the operation (GET reads, POST creates, DELETE removes); and responses use standard **HTTP status codes** so clients know what happened without parsing error messages. The result is an API that is *predictable and consistent*, the title's "endpoints people don't hate", because once you know the conventions, you can guess how any well-designed REST API works. This week you learn to design such APIs, a skill every backend developer needs and many do poorly.

## The core idea: resources and methods
The heart of REST is separating *what* you are acting on (the **resource**, a noun, in the URL) from *how* you are acting on it (the **HTTP method**, the verb):
```text
GET    /products          -> read the list of products
GET    /products/42       -> read product 42
POST   /products          -> create a new product
PUT    /products/42       -> replace/update product 42
DELETE /products/42       -> delete product 42
```
Notice the URL is *always a noun* (`/products`, `/products/42`), and the *method* is the verb (GET, POST, DELETE). You do *not* put the action in the URL: `/products/42/delete` is *wrong*; `DELETE /products/42` is *right*, the method **is** the verb. This is the single most important REST convention, and it makes the API systematic: one set of resource URLs, and the standard HTTP methods acting on them, rather than a sprawl of ad-hoc verb-named endpoints (`/getProduct`, `/createProduct`, `/deleteProduct`) that every API would name differently.

## Why convention is the whole value
The deeper reason to follow REST conventions is that **an API's value is in its predictability**, and conventions are what make it predictable to the developers (including future-you) who consume it. An API is a *contract* used by other code (your own frontend, a mobile app, third parties), and a *consistent, conventional* API is one a developer can learn once and then *guess*, if `/products` and `/products/42` work the standard way, then `/orders`, `/users`, and every other resource work the same way, so the consumer does not have to learn each endpoint from scratch. An *inconsistent* API (verbs in URLs, random naming, non-standard status codes) forces the consumer to read documentation for every single endpoint and handle each one's quirks, which is exactly the "API people hate." So REST's conventions, noun URLs, methods as verbs, standard status codes, are not arbitrary rules but a *shared language* that makes APIs intuitive and consistent, dramatically reducing the effort to use them. This is the same value as semantic HTML or consistent design systems, following established conventions so that things are predictable, now for API design, where the stakes are high because the API is the interface other software depends on. Designing APIs that follow the conventions, that other developers find intuitive and can guess, is a real skill and a mark of a thoughtful backend engineer.

## Where this fits
This week is API design in the Backend phase: REST conventions (resources, methods, status codes, pagination, filtering, documentation) that make endpoints predictable and pleasant to consume. It builds on the endpoints you can already create (W6, W9) and the data layer (W10), now designed *well*, and connects to the API consumption you did on the frontend (TanStack Query consumes APIs, W8). Today's orientation: REST is constraints on using HTTP, noun URLs, methods as verbs, standard status codes, that make APIs predictable and consistent, which is the whole value because an API is a contract other code depends on. Tomorrow you go deeper on resource modelling.

items.title: Resource modelling
items.body:
## Resource modelling: designing your URLs
The foundation of a REST API is identifying your **resources** (the nouns, your domain's entities, users, products, orders) and designing clean URLs for them. The conventions are specific and worth following exactly:
```text
/users                    plural noun for a COLLECTION
/users/:id                /resource/:id for an INDIVIDUAL item
/users/:id/orders         NEST a sub-resource when the relationship is OWNERSHIP
                          (the orders that belong to a specific user)
```
The rules: use **plural nouns** for collections (`/users`, `/orders`, `/products`); use `/resource/:id` for an individual item (`/users/42`); **nest** sub-resources when there is an ownership relationship (`/users/42/orders` = the orders belonging to user 42); but **do not nest more than two levels deep** (`/users/42/orders/7/items/3/...` becomes unwieldy, so flatten beyond two levels). And, again, **no verbs in URLs**, the resource is a noun, the method is the verb.

## Why these conventions, concretely
Each resource-modelling convention solves a real design question consistently, which is why following them produces a clean, guessable API:
- **Plural nouns for collections** (`/users` not `/user`) reads naturally (`GET /users` = "get the users") and is consistent, so every collection follows the same pattern and the consumer never wonders "is it singular or plural here?"
- **`/resource/:id` for items** gives a clear, uniform way to address any individual thing, and it composes (`GET /users/42`, `DELETE /users/42`, all the methods on one resource URL).
- **Nesting for ownership** (`/users/42/orders`) expresses the relationship in the URL, intuitively conveying "orders that belong to this user", which is more meaningful than a flat `/orders?userId=42` for genuinely-owned sub-resources.
- **The two-level limit** keeps URLs readable, deep nesting (`/a/1/b/2/c/3`) is long, rigid, and awkward, so beyond two levels you flatten (reference by id or use query params), keeping the API clean.
These choices together produce URLs that *read like the domain* and follow one consistent pattern, so a developer who learns `/users` and `/users/:id/orders` immediately understands `/products` and `/organizations/:id/members`. Resource modelling is essentially *naming and structuring your API's nouns well*, and doing it conventionally is what makes the whole API coherent.

## Modelling resources is modelling the domain
The deeper skill in resource modelling is that it forces you to *think clearly about your domain's entities and their relationships*, which is closely related to the data modelling from W10 and is the intellectual core of API design. To design good resource URLs, you must identify *what the resources are* (the meaningful nouns of your domain), *how they relate* (which resources own which, where nesting expresses a real ownership), and *what operations* make sense on each. This is largely the same entity-and-relationship thinking as designing the database schema (often your API resources map closely to your data models), so good data modelling and good API modelling reinforce each other. The judgement involved, what is a top-level resource versus a nested sub-resource, when nesting expresses a real relationship versus when to keep things flat, how to name things clearly and consistently, is genuine design work that shapes how pleasant and logical the API is to use. A well-modelled API has resources that correspond to the real concepts of the domain, clean and consistent URLs, and relationships expressed sensibly, so it *feels* like a faithful, navigable representation of the domain, which is exactly what makes it intuitive. Resource modelling done well, clear nouns, consistent URL patterns, sensible nesting, is the foundation of an API people can understand and predict, and it rests on thinking clearly about the domain, the same deliberate, model-the-domain discipline as the data layer.

## Where this fits
You can model resources well: plural-noun collections (`/users`), `/resource/:id` for items, ownership nesting (`/users/:id/orders`) kept to two levels, no verbs in URLs, producing clean, consistent, guessable URLs that read like the domain, which rests on thinking clearly about your domain's entities and relationships. Tomorrow you handle how the API communicates outcomes: status codes.

items.title: Status codes
items.body:
## Status codes: the API's standard language of outcomes
When a client calls your API, it needs to know *what happened*, did it succeed, fail, was the input bad, does the resource exist? REST uses **HTTP status codes** to communicate this in a standard way, so the client knows the outcome from the *code* alone, without parsing the response body or guessing. The codes are grouped by their first digit, and knowing the common ones is essential:
```text
2xx SUCCESS:     200 OK (general success), 201 Created (POST made a new resource),
                 204 No Content (success, nothing to return, e.g. a DELETE)
4xx CLIENT ERROR (the caller's fault):
                 400 Bad Request (invalid input), 401 Unauthorized (not logged in),
                 403 Forbidden (logged in but not allowed), 404 Not Found,
                 409 Conflict (e.g. duplicate), 422 Unprocessable (validation failed)
5xx SERVER ERROR (your fault):  500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable
```
You return the *right* code for each outcome, so the client can react correctly based on the code.

## Why correct status codes matter so much
Using the *correct, specific* status code is one of the most important and most-botched parts of API design, and understanding why shows the payoff. The status code is a *standard, machine-readable* signal of the outcome, so when your API returns the right code, the client can handle each case *programmatically and correctly*: a `401` tells the client "you need to log in" (so it redirects to login), a `404` tells it "this does not exist" (so it shows a not-found state), a `400`/`422` tells it "your input was invalid" (so it shows the validation error), a `403` tells it "you are not allowed" (different from 401, you *are* identified but lack permission), a `201` confirms a creation, a `500` signals a server problem (so the client can retry or show a generic error). The client handles all of these *from the code*, with no need to parse error strings or guess. The common failures, returning `200 OK` for everything (even errors) and putting the real status in the body, or using `500` for what is really a client input error (`400`), break this entirely: the client cannot tell success from failure by the code, so it must parse the body in ad-hoc ways, and worse, returning `200` for an error means generic clients, caches, and monitoring all *think* the request succeeded. Correct status codes are what make the API's outcomes *legible to the machine consuming it*, which is the whole point. The crucial distinctions to get right include `401` (not authenticated) vs `403` (authenticated but not authorised), `400`/`422` (bad input, client's fault) vs `500` (server error, your fault), and `200` vs `201`/`204` for the kind of success, each tells the client something specific and actionable.

## Status codes and consistent, helpful errors
Beyond the codes, well-designed APIs return *helpful, consistent error responses* alongside the right status code, because while the code tells the client the *category* of outcome, a good error body tells it the *specifics*. A `400`/`422` should come with a body explaining *what* was invalid (which field, what rule), so the client (and the developer) can fix it, "email is required" or "price must be positive", not just a bare 400. And the error format should be *consistent* across the whole API (the same shape for every error: a code, a message, maybe field-level details), so the consumer handles errors uniformly rather than dealing with a different error format per endpoint. This combination, the correct standard status code (machine-readable category) plus a consistent, descriptive error body (human- and developer-readable specifics), is what makes an API's errors genuinely usable: the client knows from the code how to react, and from the body what specifically went wrong. This is the API-design version of the "feedback is part of the feature" and "handle the unhappy path" lessons from earlier, errors are a first-class part of the API contract, not an afterthought, and designing them well (right codes, consistent helpful bodies) is exactly what separates an API people can build against confidently from one that is a frustrating guessing game. Getting status codes and error responses right is a large part of "endpoints people don't hate."

## Where this fits
You understand status codes: the standard, machine-readable signals of outcome (2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error) with the crucial distinctions (401 vs 403, 400 vs 500, 200 vs 201/204), returned correctly so clients handle each case programmatically, plus consistent, descriptive error bodies for the specifics. Tomorrow you handle returning large collections sensibly: pagination.

items.title: Pagination
items.body:
## Pagination: not returning everything at once
When a collection is large, returning *all* of it in one response is a problem, imagine `GET /products` returning 100,000 products, that is a huge, slow response that strains the server, the network, and the client. **Pagination** returns results in manageable *pages* instead, with the client requesting one page at a time:
```text
GET /products?page=2&limit=20        -> page 2, 20 items per page (offset pagination)
GET /products?cursor=abc&limit=20    -> the 20 items after cursor 'abc' (cursor pagination)
```
The response includes the page of items *plus* metadata so the client knows how to get more (the total count, or a cursor/link to the next page). Pagination is essential for any collection that can grow, which is most of them, so it is a standard, expected part of API design, not an optional extra.

## The two approaches, and their trade-off
There are two main pagination styles, and knowing the trade-off lets you choose appropriately:
- **Offset/page pagination** (`?page=2&limit=20` or `?offset=40&limit=20`): the client asks for a page number or an offset. It is *simple* and lets the client jump to any page ("go to page 5"), which is great for page-numbered UIs. Its weaknesses: it gets *slow* on very large datasets (the database must skip `offset` rows, which is costly deep into a huge table), and it can *skip or duplicate* items if the data changes between requests (a new item inserted shifts everything, so page 2 might repeat or miss a row).
- **Cursor pagination** (`?cursor=abc`): the client passes a *cursor* (a pointer to the last item it saw, often an id or timestamp), and the server returns the items *after* it. It is *fast and stable* even on huge, changing datasets (no offset-skipping, no shifting), which makes it ideal for large feeds and infinite-scroll. Its trade-off: you cannot jump to an arbitrary page (only "next"/"previous"), so it suits feeds more than page-numbered navigation.
The rule of thumb: offset pagination for modest datasets and page-number UIs (simple, allows jumping); cursor pagination for large or rapidly-changing datasets and infinite-scroll (fast, stable). Choosing the right one is a real design decision based on the data size and the UI's needs.

## Why pagination is non-negotiable, and consistent
The deeper point is that pagination is a *required* part of designing collection endpoints that scale, and forgetting it is a classic mistake that works in development and fails in production, exactly the "works locally, breaks at scale" pattern seen across the tracks. In development, `GET /products` returns your 50 test products fine; in production with 100,000 products, the same endpoint returns a massive response that is slow, memory-heavy, and a poor experience, and may even crash under the load. So you design pagination *in from the start* for any collection that can grow, treating "return everything" as a bug for non-trivial collections. Beyond performance, pagination should be *consistent across your API*, the same pagination style and parameters (`page`/`limit` or `cursor`/`limit`) and the same response metadata format for *every* paginated collection, so a consumer learns your pagination once and it works everywhere, the consistency-is-the-value principle again. The response metadata matters too: including the total count (for offset) or a next-cursor/next-link (for cursor) tells the client how to navigate, so it can show page numbers or load the next page. Pagination, done right, consistently, with the appropriate style, with navigation metadata, is what makes collection endpoints scale gracefully and stay pleasant to consume as the data grows, and it is a standard expectation of any well-designed API. An API whose list endpoints have no pagination is one that will fall over (or frustrate) the moment its data grows, so building it in is part of designing endpoints people don't hate.

## Where this fits
You understand pagination: returning large collections in manageable pages (offset/page pagination for simple page-jumping, cursor pagination for large/changing data and infinite-scroll), with navigation metadata, designed in from the start for any growable collection and kept consistent across the API. Tomorrow you give consumers control over the data they get: filtering, sorting, and sparse fieldsets.

items.title: Filtering, sorting, sparse fieldsets
items.body:
## Letting clients shape the response: filtering, sorting, sparse fieldsets
Beyond paginating, a good API lets clients *shape* what they get back, asking for a subset of items, in a particular order, with only the fields they need. These are expressed via *query parameters*:
```text
GET /products?category=coffee&inStock=true   -> FILTERING (only matching items)
GET /products?sort=-price                     -> SORTING (by price, descending)
GET /products?fields=id,name,price            -> SPARSE FIELDSETS (only these fields)
```
- **Filtering:** query params narrow the collection to matching items (`?category=coffee` returns only coffee products), so clients fetch exactly the subset they need rather than getting everything and filtering client-side.
- **Sorting:** a `sort` param orders the results (`?sort=-price` for price descending, `?sort=name` ascending), so the client gets data in the order it wants.
- **Sparse fieldsets:** a `fields` param returns only the requested fields (`?fields=id,name`), so a client that needs just names does not download every field of every item.

## Why this serves both the client and the server
These response-shaping features matter because they make the API *efficient and flexible* for diverse clients, and understanding the payoff shows why they are worth designing:
- **Less data transferred:** filtering (fewer items) and sparse fieldsets (fewer fields) mean the client downloads only what it needs, which is faster (smaller responses) and cheaper (less bandwidth), important on mobile and at scale. A list view that needs only names and prices should not download every product's full description and metadata.
- **Server-side work where it belongs:** filtering and sorting *on the server* (via the database, using the indexes from W10) is far more efficient than sending everything and having the client filter/sort, the database is built for this, and it keeps the heavy lifting close to the data. (This connects to W10's indexes: the columns clients filter and sort by are exactly the columns to index, so these features and good indexing go together.)
- **One endpoint serves many needs:** different clients (a mobile list, a desktop detail view, a report) have different needs, and filtering/sorting/sparse-fields let *one* well-designed endpoint serve all of them flexibly, rather than building a separate endpoint per use case.
So these features push the right work to the right place (filtering/sorting on the server/database) and let clients get precisely the data they need, which is both efficient and flexible, a hallmark of a well-designed, consumer-friendly API.

## Design these consistently, and guard them
The discipline, as with pagination, is *consistency and care*. Consistency: use the same conventions for filtering (query params named after the fields), sorting (a standard `sort` param with a clear ascending/descending convention), and field selection (a `fields` param) across the *whole* API, so a consumer learns the pattern once. Care (a real one): filtering and sorting parameters become *database queries*, so you must handle them *safely and efficiently*, validate the parameters (only allow filtering/sorting on intended fields, not arbitrary ones, both for security and to avoid unindexed slow queries), build the queries safely (Prisma's typed queries protect against SQL injection here, never concatenate user input into raw SQL), and ensure the filtered/sorted columns are indexed (W10) so the queries are fast. This guarding matters because these features expose query power to the client, and unguarded, they are a performance and security risk (a client filtering/sorting on an unindexed field triggers a slow full scan; naive query-building from user input is an injection vector). Designed well, consistent conventions, validated and safe parameters, indexed columns, filtering, sorting, and sparse fieldsets make an API genuinely pleasant and efficient to consume, letting clients get exactly what they need while the server does the work where it is most efficient. Together with pagination, these features turn a basic "return the list" endpoint into a flexible, scalable, consumer-friendly one, a big part of "endpoints people don't hate."

## Where this fits
You can let clients shape responses with filtering, sorting, and sparse fieldsets (via consistent query parameters), making the API efficient (less data, server-side work on indexed columns) and flexible (one endpoint serves many clients), designed consistently and guarded carefully (validated, safe, indexed). Tomorrow you handle documenting the API so others can use it: OpenAPI.

items.title: OpenAPI 3.x
items.body:
## Documenting the contract: OpenAPI
An API is a *contract* that other developers (and code) consume, and they need to know how to use it, what endpoints exist, what they accept, what they return, without reading your source code. **OpenAPI** (formerly Swagger) is the standard, machine-readable way to *describe* a REST API: a specification (in YAML/JSON) that documents every endpoint, its parameters, request and response shapes, and status codes:
```text
OpenAPI spec describes:
  - every endpoint (GET /products, POST /products, ...)
  - parameters and request body shapes
  - response shapes and status codes for each
  - data models (the shape of a Product, a User, ...)
```
From this single spec, you get a lot: *interactive documentation* (tools render the spec as browsable, try-it-out API docs), *client code generation* (tools generate typed client libraries from the spec, so consumers do not hand-write request code), and a *shared source of truth* for the API's contract that both providers and consumers rely on.

## Why a standard, machine-readable spec matters
The value of OpenAPI over informal documentation (a README, hand-written docs) is that it is *standard and machine-readable*, which unlocks tooling and keeps the documentation honest. Because the spec is a structured, standard format, tools can *do things with it*: generate beautiful interactive docs automatically (so consumers explore and test the API in a browser), generate typed client code in many languages (so a consumer gets a ready-made, type-safe client instead of hand-coding HTTP calls), validate that requests/responses match the spec, and even drive automated testing. Informal docs do none of this, and worse, they *drift* out of date (the docs say one thing, the API does another, a constant and infuriating problem), whereas an OpenAPI spec can be tied closely to the implementation (generated from it, or validated against it) so it stays accurate. This matters because *out-of-date or absent API documentation is one of the biggest pain points* for developers consuming an API, an undocumented or wrongly-documented API forces consumers to reverse-engineer it from trial and error, which is slow and error-prone, exactly the "API people hate." A current, standard, machine-readable spec, by contrast, lets consumers understand and integrate with the API quickly and reliably, with tooling support. So OpenAPI is how you make your API's contract *explicit, accurate, tool-supported, and easy to consume*, which is a major part of building APIs people actually enjoy using.

## Documentation as a first-class part of API design
The deeper lesson is that **documentation is a first-class part of an API, not an afterthought**, because the API's entire purpose is to be *consumed by others*, and an undocumented API is barely usable no matter how well-designed the endpoints are. This connects to the documentation discipline from across the track (the README habit from week 1, the "a stranger can use it" standard): an API specifically *exists* to serve other developers and systems, so its documentation is part of the product, not optional polish. The ideal is to treat the API spec as central, some teams write the OpenAPI spec *first* (design-first: agree the contract, then implement to it, the API equivalent of README-first design), others generate it from the implementation, but either way the spec is a maintained, accurate description of the contract. For your own work, even a simple, accurate OpenAPI spec (or auto-generated docs) dramatically improves how usable your API is, and demonstrates the professionalism of treating the API as a consumable product with a documented contract. The combination of *well-designed endpoints* (the week's resource modelling, status codes, pagination, filtering) *and a clear, accurate, standard specification documenting them* is what makes an API genuinely pleasant to build against, the consumer can both predict how it works (good design) and look up the specifics reliably (good docs). Documenting the API with OpenAPI is the final piece of "endpoints people don't hate": not just designing the contract well, but communicating it clearly and accurately so others can use it.

## Where this fits
You understand OpenAPI: a standard, machine-readable specification of your API's contract (endpoints, parameters, request/response shapes, status codes) that unlocks interactive docs, client generation, and validation, and stays accurate where informal docs drift, treating documentation as a first-class part of the API, which exists to be consumed. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship a well-designed, documented REST API.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a REST API people don't hate
You assemble the week into a well-designed, documented REST API for a real backend (Bean Forge's data, or any app), demonstrating API design done right:
- **resources** modelled with clean, consistent, conventional URLs (plural nouns, `/resource/:id`, sensible ownership nesting, no verbs).
- correct **HTTP methods** and **status codes** (the right code for each outcome, with consistent, helpful error bodies).
- **pagination** on collections (appropriate style), plus **filtering, sorting, and sparse fieldsets** (consistent, safe, indexed).
- an **OpenAPI** specification documenting the contract accurately.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "REST API: conventional resources, status codes, pagination, filtering, OpenAPI docs"
git push
```

## The deliverable is an API a stranger can use confidently
What makes this project demonstrate real API-design competence is that a developer who has never seen your API can *understand and use it confidently and quickly*, which is the entire point of good API design. The strongest version is *predictable* (conventional resource URLs and methods, so once you know one resource you can guess the rest), *clear about outcomes* (correct status codes and helpful errors, so the client knows exactly what happened and why), *scalable* (pagination so collections do not blow up), *flexible* (filtering/sorting/fields so clients get exactly what they need), and *documented* (an accurate OpenAPI spec so the specifics are looked up, not reverse-engineered). The proof is the *consumer experience*: someone can read your OpenAPI docs, understand the API's shape immediately because it follows conventions, and integrate with it without frustration, the opposite of the inconsistent, undocumented, status-code-mangling APIs that developers dread. Demonstrating that you can design an API that is *intuitive, consistent, standard, scalable, and documented*, an API people *don't hate*, is the deliverable, and it is a skill that makes you valuable on any team, because the API is the contract that the frontend, mobile apps, and integrations all depend on, and a well-designed one saves every consumer enormous effort.

## What REST API design established
Step back: you have learned to design the *interface* to your backend well, which is as important as the backend itself because it is what everything else consumes. You understand REST as conventions that make APIs predictable (resources as noun URLs, methods as verbs, standard status codes), resource modelling (clean, consistent, domain-faithful URLs), correct status codes and helpful errors (legible outcomes), pagination (scalable collections), filtering/sorting/sparse-fields (flexible, efficient access), and OpenAPI documentation (an accurate, consumable contract). The throughline is that *an API's value is in its predictability and clarity to the developers who consume it*, so following conventions and documenting well is not pedantry but the core of good API design. This completes the picture of building a real backend: you have the server (W9), the data layer (W10), and now well-designed APIs (W11) that expose the backend's functionality cleanly. One piece remains: controlling *who* can access it, which is authentication and authorisation.

## Where this fits
You shipped a well-designed, documented REST API, conventional, clear, scalable, flexible, and OpenAPI-documented, "endpoints people don't hate", the clean interface to your backend. With the server, data, and API in place, next week handles the critical security dimension: **authentication and authorisation, done right**, who a user *is* (authentication) and what they are *allowed to do* (authorisation), with the trade-offs (sessions vs JWTs, OAuth, auth providers, RBAC) that you must get right, because getting auth wrong is how security breaches happen.

weeks.title: Authentication and Authorization, Done Right
weeks.context:
Authentication is about identity: who are you? Authorisation is about permission: what are you allowed to do? These are different systems and conflating them causes security holes. This week you build both correctly for Bean Forge, and you understand the tradeoffs between the two main approaches: sessions and JWTs.

Sessions: when a user logs in, you create a server-side session record (stored in a database or Redis) and set a session ID in an HttpOnly cookie. On every subsequent request, the browser sends the cookie, you look up the session, and you know who the user is. Sessions are easy to invalidate: delete the record. The cookie is HttpOnly so JavaScript cannot read it, preventing XSS token theft. The downside: every request hits the database. For most apps, this is fine.

JWTs (JSON Web Tokens): you sign a payload (user ID, roles, expiry) with a secret key and send the token to the client. The client stores it and sends it with every request. You verify the signature without hitting the database, stateless. The downside: you cannot invalidate a JWT until it expires. If a user's permissions change or their account is compromised, the old token keeps working until expiry. Workarounds exist (blocklist, short expiry + refresh tokens) but they add complexity. Use sessions unless you have a specific reason for JWTs (microservices, third-party clients).

Password storage: hash with bcrypt or argon2. Never store plain text. Never use MD5 or SHA-1 for passwords, these are fast hashing algorithms and can be brute-forced. Bcrypt is deliberately slow. The cost factor (work factor) controls how slow, a cost factor of 12 means 2^12 iterations. Always hash on the server, never trust a hash sent from the client.

OAuth 2.0: the protocol that powers "Sign in with Google." The user is redirected to Google, they grant permission, Google redirects back with an authorization code, your server exchanges the code for tokens using a back-channel request. The key security feature: the client secret never leaves your server. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) prevents code interception attacks when the redirect target is a public client (like a mobile app or SPA) that cannot keep a client secret.

This week: add email/password auth to Bean Forge with sessions. Add "Sign in with Google" using NextAuth or a manual OAuth implementation. Protect routes with middleware that checks for a valid session.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Two different questions: who are you, and what can you do
This week handles the security foundation of any real app: **authentication** and **authorisation**, and the first thing to get straight is that they are *two different things* that are constantly conflated, and conflating them causes security holes. **Authentication** is about *identity*: who are you? (Verifying a user is who they claim, via login.) **Authorisation** is about *permission*: what are you allowed to do? (Checking whether an identified user may perform an action or access a resource.) These are *separate systems*, you first establish *who* someone is (authentication), then separately decide *what* that person may do (authorisation), and treating them as one thing, or skipping the second, is how breaches happen. This week you build both correctly for Bean Forge, and you learn the real trade-offs (sessions vs JWTs, OAuth, auth providers, RBAC), because getting auth right is critical and getting it wrong is catastrophic.

## Authentication vs authorisation, concretely
The distinction is worth making concrete because it governs how you structure security:
```text
AUTHENTICATION (identity): "Who are you?"
  - the user logs in (proves identity with credentials)
  - result: the system knows WHO the request is from (this is user #42)

AUTHORISATION (permission): "What are you allowed to do?"
  - given a known user, check if they MAY do this action / access this resource
  - result: allow or deny (user #42 can edit their own post, but not someone else's;
            an admin can delete any post; a regular user cannot)
```
Every protected operation involves *both*: first authenticate (establish identity), then authorise (check permission for *this specific action*). A logged-in user is *authenticated*, but that does not mean they are *authorised* to do everything, a normal user is authenticated but not authorised to access the admin panel or edit other users' data. Recall the status codes from last week: **401 Unauthorized** is actually an *authentication* failure (you are not logged in), while **403 Forbidden** is an *authorisation* failure (you are logged in but not allowed), the two codes exist precisely because these are two different checks.

## Why conflating them is dangerous
The reason the distinction matters so much, beyond tidiness, is that *conflating authentication with authorisation is a classic source of serious security vulnerabilities*. The dangerous mistake is assuming that *authenticated* means *authorised*, "the user is logged in, so let them do it", which skips the permission check. This leads directly to vulnerabilities like *broken access control* (the most common serious web vulnerability): a logged-in user accesses or modifies data they should not be able to (another user's account, an admin-only function) because the code checked *that* they were logged in but not *whether they were allowed to do this specific thing*. For example, if `GET /users/42/orders` only checks that the requester is authenticated (logged in) but not that they *are* user 42 (or an admin), then any logged-in user can read *anyone's* orders by changing the id, a real, severe, and extremely common breach. The fix is to *always do both checks separately*: authenticate (who is this?), then authorise (is *this user* allowed to access *this specific resource/action*?). Internalising that *authentication is necessary but not sufficient*, that establishing identity is only the first step and you must *separately* enforce what that identity is permitted to do, is the foundational security mindset of the week, and it is what prevents the broken-access-control vulnerabilities that plague real applications. Auth done right means both systems, each enforced, never assuming one implies the other.

## Where this fits
This week completes the Backend phase with authentication and authorisation, done right: verifying identity and enforcing permissions, with the trade-offs (sessions vs JWTs, OAuth, auth providers, login methods, RBAC) that secure a real app. It protects the server, data, and APIs you built (W9-11), and it is FORGE's concern too (NextAuth, role-based access). Today's orientation: authentication (who you are) and authorisation (what you may do) are *separate* systems, both must be enforced, and conflating them, assuming authenticated means authorised, causes the broken-access-control breaches that are among the most common serious vulnerabilities. Tomorrow you handle how authentication state is maintained: sessions vs JWTs.

items.title: Sessions vs JWTs
items.body:
## Maintaining login: sessions vs JWTs
Once a user logs in (proves their identity), the server must *remember* they are logged in across their subsequent requests, because HTTP is stateless (each request is independent), so something must carry the "I am logged in as user 42" information on every request. There are two main approaches, and understanding their trade-off is fundamental:
- **Sessions:** when a user logs in, the server creates a *session record* (stored server-side, in a database or Redis) and sends the browser a *session ID* in an **HttpOnly cookie**. On each later request, the browser sends the cookie, the server looks up the session record, and knows who the user is.
- **JWTs (JSON Web Tokens):** the server *signs* a token containing the user's info (id, roles) and sends it to the client; on each request the client sends the token back, and the server *verifies the signature* to trust the contents, *without* looking anything up server-side. The token itself carries the identity, cryptographically signed so it cannot be forged.

## The core trade-off: server-side state vs stateless tokens
The essential difference is *where the state lives*, and it drives every trade-off between them:
- **Sessions are stateful (server-side):** the session record lives on the server, so the token (the session ID) is just an opaque key. The big advantages: sessions are *easy to invalidate* (delete the record, and the user is instantly logged out, crucial for "log out everywhere" or revoking a compromised session), and the cookie is *HttpOnly* (JavaScript cannot read it, which prevents an XSS attack from stealing the session token). The downside: *every request hits the session store* (a database/Redis lookup) to validate, which is a small cost, "for most apps, this is fine," but it is a per-request lookup and requires the shared session store.
- **JWTs are stateless (self-contained):** the token carries the identity and is verified by signature alone, *no server lookup needed*, which scales beautifully (any server can verify the token without a shared session store) and avoids the per-request database hit. The downside is the mirror image: JWTs are *hard to invalidate* (the token is valid until it expires, since the server does not track it, so you cannot easily "log out" a token before expiry or revoke a compromised one), which is why JWTs use short expiry times plus refresh tokens, adding complexity.
So the trade-off is **easy revocation but per-request lookups (sessions)** vs **stateless scalability but hard revocation (JWTs)**.

## Choosing, and the security considerations
The practical guidance, cutting through a lot of dogma, is that **for most applications, sessions are the simpler and safer default**, and JWTs are for specific needs. Sessions' easy invalidation is a *real security advantage* (you can revoke access immediately, which matters when a session is compromised or a user logs out), and the per-request lookup cost is negligible for most apps, so the common advice is to *default to sessions* unless you have a specific reason for JWTs. JWTs shine when you need *statelessness at scale* (many services verifying tokens without a shared session store) or *cross-service/API authentication* (a token that multiple independent services can verify), but they bring real complexity (short expiry, refresh-token rotation, the inability to easily revoke) that is easy to get wrong, and a poorly-implemented JWT system (long-lived tokens with no revocation strategy) is a security liability. Crucial security points either way: store the token/session-id in an **HttpOnly cookie** (so JavaScript, and thus an XSS attack, cannot steal it, storing tokens in `localStorage`, which JS *can* read, is a common and dangerous mistake), use HTTPS, and set secure cookie flags. The deeper lesson is that this is a *trade-off to understand*, not a fashion to follow (JWTs are often reached for reflexively when sessions would be simpler and safer), and the right choice depends on your needs: sessions for the typical app (simple, revocable, secure), JWTs when stateless scale genuinely requires it (accepting the revocation complexity). Understanding *where the state lives* and what that implies for invalidation, scale, and security is what lets you choose correctly rather than cargo-culting.

## Where this fits
You understand sessions vs JWTs: the core trade-off of server-side state (sessions: easy revocation, per-request lookup, the simpler safer default for most apps) vs stateless tokens (JWTs: scalable, lookup-free, but hard to revoke, for specific scale/cross-service needs), with the shared security disciplines (HttpOnly cookies, never localStorage for tokens, HTTPS). Tomorrow you handle logging in via other providers: OAuth 2.0.

items.title: OAuth 2.0 fundamentals
items.body:
## OAuth 2.0: logging in with another service
Users increasingly log in with "Sign in with Google/GitHub/Apple" rather than creating yet another password, and **OAuth 2.0** is the protocol that makes this work. OAuth lets a user grant your app limited access to their account on *another* service (Google, GitHub) *without* sharing their password with you, the other service handles the authentication and tells your app "yes, this is a verified user, here is their basic info":
```text
1. user clicks "Sign in with Google" on your app
2. your app redirects them to Google
3. user logs in to GOOGLE (not your app) and approves your app's access
4. Google redirects back to your app with an authorisation code
5. your app exchanges the code (server-side) for tokens + the user's info
6. your app now knows the verified user (and never saw their Google password)
```
The crucial property: the user authenticates *with the trusted provider*, and your app receives a verified identity (and possibly permission to access certain data) *without ever handling the user's password for that service*.

## Why OAuth exists and what it solves
Understanding *what problem OAuth solves* clarifies why it is everywhere:
- **No password sharing:** the user never gives your app their Google/GitHub password, the whole point. They authenticate directly with the provider they already trust, and your app gets only a verified identity and whatever limited access the user approved. This is far safer than the user creating (and you storing) yet another password, and it means a breach of your app does not expose their Google credentials.
- **Delegated, scoped access:** OAuth grants *specific, limited* permissions (scopes), "this app may see your email and name," not "this app has full access to your account", so the user controls exactly what your app can do, and your app gets only what it needs.
- **Convenience and trust:** users avoid creating and remembering another password (better UX, higher sign-up rates), and they trust the big provider's security and login (with its own protections like 2FA) rather than your app's.
So OAuth solves the problem of "let users prove their identity (and optionally grant limited access to their data) via a service they already use, without password-sharing and with scoped permissions." It is an *authorisation* protocol (granting scoped access) commonly used *for authentication* (proving identity via the provider), and the flow, redirect to the provider, user approves, your app gets a code, exchange it server-side for tokens/identity, is the standard "social login" mechanism.

## Use OAuth correctly, and don't roll your own
The vital practical guidance is that OAuth is *security-critical and subtle*, so you should **use well-established libraries and providers, not implement the protocol from scratch**, because the flow has many security-sensitive details (validating the state parameter to prevent CSRF, exchanging the code *server-side* so secrets are not exposed, validating tokens correctly, handling the redirect securely) that are easy to get wrong, and getting OAuth wrong creates serious vulnerabilities. This is the broader and most important security lesson of the whole week, applied here: **do not roll your own auth.** Authentication (and OAuth specifically) is a domain where subtle mistakes have severe consequences, and the security community has built robust, well-tested libraries and services that handle the protocol's details correctly, so the right move is to *use* them (a library like the providers' SDKs, or an auth service, tomorrow's topic) rather than hand-implementing the flow and inevitably missing a security-critical step. This is not laziness, it is *responsible engineering*: auth is too important and too subtle to reinvent, and the established solutions encode hard-won security knowledge you would otherwise have to (and likely fail to) reproduce. Understanding *how OAuth works* (the flow, the no-password-sharing principle, scopes) is valuable so you use it correctly and debug it, but *implementing* it means standing on proven libraries. The combination, understand the protocol, use trusted implementations, is exactly how you get the benefits of OAuth (safe, convenient, scoped social login) without the risks of doing security-critical cryptographic protocol work yourself.

## Where this fits
You understand OAuth 2.0: letting users authenticate via a trusted provider (Google, GitHub) without password-sharing, granting scoped access through a redirect-and-code-exchange flow, which solves social login safely, and the crucial discipline of using established libraries/providers rather than implementing the subtle, security-critical protocol yourself, *don't roll your own auth*. Tomorrow you handle the services that provide auth as managed infrastructure.

items.title: Auth provider services
items.body:
## Auth provider services: managed auth
Given that auth is security-critical and subtle (don't roll your own), a whole category of **auth provider services** exists to handle it for you, Auth0, Clerk, Supabase Auth, Firebase Auth, NextAuth/Auth.js (FORGE's choice), and others. These services provide authentication (and often authorisation) as managed infrastructure: they handle the password storage, session/token management, OAuth/social login flows, email verification, password reset, multi-factor authentication, and the security best practices, so you integrate their solution rather than building auth from scratch:
```text
auth provider handles:  secure password storage (hashing), login/logout, sessions/tokens,
                        OAuth social logins, email verification, password reset, MFA,
                        security best practices (rate limiting, secure cookies, etc.)
you handle:             integrating it and defining your authorisation rules
```
You get a robust, secure, full-featured auth system quickly, and you focus on *your* app's specific authorisation logic (what each user may do) rather than reimplementing the universal authentication machinery.

## Why using an auth service is usually the right call
The reasoning for reaching for an auth service is the strongest version of the "don't roll your own auth" principle, and it is worth being clear about because auth is exactly where the build-vs-buy judgement should usually favour buy. Auth is:
- **Security-critical:** mistakes are catastrophic (account takeover, data breaches), and there are *many* security-sensitive details (correct password hashing, secure session/token handling, protection against a long list of attacks, secure password reset, etc.) that are individually easy to get wrong.
- **Largely universal:** the authentication machinery (login, logout, password reset, social login, MFA) is essentially the *same* for every app, so building it yourself means re-solving a solved problem, badly, for no differentiation, your app's value is not in its login system.
- **A huge surface to maintain:** auth needs ongoing security maintenance (responding to new threats, keeping up with best practices), which a dedicated provider does far better than you can on the side.
Given all this, an auth service that has *specialised* in getting auth right, with security expertise, audits, and constant maintenance, almost always provides *more secure and more complete* auth than you would build yourself, in a fraction of the time. This is the clearest case in the whole track for buying over building: the thing is critical, hard, universal, and not your differentiator, so you use the specialist solution and spend your effort on *your* app. (FORGE itself uses NextAuth/Auth.js for exactly this reason.) The result is that you ship a secure, full-featured auth system fast, and you do not carry the enormous risk and maintenance burden of hand-rolled security.

## What you still own: authorisation and integration
Using an auth provider does *not* mean auth is entirely off your plate, an important nuance, because the provider mainly handles *authentication* (and some authorisation tooling), while *your app's specific authorisation rules* remain yours to define and enforce. The provider verifies *who* a user is (and gives you their identity and perhaps roles); *you* still implement *what each user is allowed to do* in your app's context (this user can edit their own posts, an admin can manage all users, a user can only access their own data), the authorisation checks that are specific to your domain (and that the W12-D1 lesson stressed you must always enforce, separately from authentication, to avoid broken access control). So the division is: the auth *service* handles the universal, security-critical *authentication* machinery (and provides identity/roles), and *you* handle *integrating* it and enforcing your app's *authorisation* logic (the permission checks, including the role-based access control of D6). You also still own using it *correctly* (configuring it securely, protecting the right routes, handling the identity it gives you properly). This means understanding auth concepts (this whole week) remains valuable even when using a service, you need to integrate it correctly, enforce authorisation yourself, and debug issues, all of which require understanding what is happening. The mature stance is: use a trusted auth provider for the authentication machinery (the right build-vs-buy call for security-critical universal work), and own the authorisation logic and correct integration that are specific to your app. That combination gives you secure, fast-to-build authentication *and* the app-specific permission enforcement that only you can define.

## Where this fits
You understand auth provider services (Auth0, Clerk, NextAuth/Auth.js, and others) as managed authentication infrastructure that handles the security-critical, universal machinery (passwords, sessions, social login, MFA, best practices), the right build-vs-buy call for auth, while you still own integrating it and enforcing your app's specific *authorisation* rules. Tomorrow you compare the login methods themselves: magic link vs password vs social.

items.title: Magic link vs password vs social login
items.body:
## Choosing login methods: magic link, password, social
Beyond *how* auth state is maintained, there is the question of *how users actually log in*, and the main methods each have trade-offs worth understanding so you choose well for your app:
- **Password:** the traditional username/email + password. Familiar to everyone and fully under your (or your auth provider's) control, but it puts a *secret to manage* on both sides, users reuse and forget passwords, and you must store them securely (hashed, never plaintext) and handle reset flows. The weakest link is often the user's password habits (reuse, weak passwords).
- **Magic link:** the user enters their email, you send them a one-time login link, they click it and are logged in, *no password at all*. It is simple for users (nothing to remember) and removes password-storage risk entirely (there is no password), but it depends on email (delivery, the user having access to their inbox) and each login requires the email round-trip.
- **Social login (OAuth):** "Sign in with Google/GitHub" (W12-D3). Very convenient (no new password, fast sign-up), leverages the provider's security (including their MFA), but ties the user to a third-party provider and requires OAuth integration.

## The trade-offs: security, UX, and control
Choosing a login method (or which to offer) balances several factors, and understanding them is the real skill:
- **Security:** passwords are only as strong as the user's habits (and your storage), and are the most attacked method (credential stuffing, phishing); magic links remove password risk but shift trust to email security (whoever controls the inbox can log in); social login leverages the provider's (usually strong) security including their MFA. Generally, social login and magic links avoid the password-specific risks, while passwords require careful handling (hashing, rate limiting, encouraging strong passwords, offering MFA) to be safe.
- **User experience:** social login is usually the smoothest (one click, no new account); magic links are easy (no password to remember) but add the email round-trip; passwords are familiar but create friction (remembering, resetting). UX strongly affects sign-up and login completion rates.
- **Control and dependencies:** passwords keep you fully independent; magic links depend on email; social login depends on (and ties users to) a third-party provider (and a user without that provider account cannot use it).
There is no single best method, the right choice depends on your users and context, and many apps *offer several* (social login *and* email/password or magic link) so users choose what suits them. The judgement is to weigh security, UX, and control for *your* situation, a consumer app might lead with social login for frictionless sign-up, a security-sensitive app might require strong passwords plus MFA, a simple app might use magic links to avoid passwords entirely.

## The deeper point: auth is a product and security decision together
The broader lesson is that choosing login methods is where *security and user experience meet*, and the best choice optimises *both* rather than trading one off entirely, which is a nuanced product-and-security judgement. A method that is maximally secure but so cumbersome that users avoid the app (or, worse, work around the security) is a failure, and a method that is maximally convenient but insecure is also a failure, so you seek the methods that are *both* reasonably secure *and* low-friction for your users. This is why social login and magic links have grown popular, they often improve *both* security (no weak reused passwords for you to protect) *and* UX (less friction) at once, a genuine win, while passwords, though familiar, increasingly require extra measures (MFA, strong-password enforcement) to be secure, adding friction. The mature approach considers the *whole* picture: who your users are, what level of security the app's data warrants, what friction they will tolerate, and offers the method(s) that best serve both security and experience for that context. It also connects to the responsibility theme: respecting users means giving them secure *and* usable authentication, not forcing a painful or insecure choice. Understanding the login methods and their security/UX/control trade-offs lets you make this decision deliberately, designing an auth experience that protects users *and* serves them well, rather than defaulting to passwords (and their risks) or chasing convenience at security's expense. The right login design is part of building an app that is both safe and pleasant to use.

## Where this fits
You can choose login methods deliberately, password (familiar, but password-handling risk), magic link (no password, email-dependent), social/OAuth (convenient, leverages provider security, third-party dependency), by weighing security, UX, and control for your context, often offering several, recognising that the best choice serves *both* security and user experience. Tomorrow you handle authorisation at scale: role-based access control.
