items.title: Role-based access control
items.body:
## Authorisation at scale: role-based access control
Authentication establishes *who* a user is; now you systematically handle *what they can do*, authorisation, and the standard pattern for managing permissions at scale is **role-based access control (RBAC)**. Instead of assigning permissions to each user individually (unmanageable as users and permissions grow), you define **roles** (admin, editor, member, viewer), attach *permissions* to roles, and assign *users* to roles:
```text
roles -> permissions:        admin   = can do everything
                             editor  = can create/edit content, not manage users
                             member  = can read, and edit their OWN content
                             viewer  = can read only
users -> roles:              user #42 is a "member", user #7 is an "admin"
check:                       does this user's ROLE permit this action? (allow/deny)
```
A user's permissions come from their role(s), so to authorise an action you check whether the user's *role* permits it, and managing access becomes managing roles (change what "editor" can do once, and every editor is updated) rather than juggling per-user permissions.

## Why RBAC, and enforcing it correctly
RBAC is the standard because it makes authorisation *manageable and consistent* as an app grows, and understanding why shows how to use it well:
- **Manageable:** with potentially thousands of users and many possible actions, assigning permissions per user is hopeless to maintain; grouping permissions into a few roles and assigning users to roles is tractable, you reason about a handful of roles, not thousands of users. Changing a role's permissions updates everyone with that role at once.
- **Consistent and auditable:** roles make the permission structure *explicit and reviewable* ("here are our roles and what each can do"), so you can reason about and audit who can do what, which is important for security and often for compliance.
- **The crucial discipline, enforce on the server, on every protected action:** authorisation checks must happen on the *server* (the backend, where the data and the real security boundary are), *never only on the client*. Hiding an admin button in the UI is *not* security, a user can still call the API directly, so the *server* must check the user's role/permission on *every* protected endpoint and action. This is the broken-access-control lesson (D1) made concrete: every protected operation must verify, server-side, that the authenticated user's role actually permits it. Client-side checks are for UX (don't show buttons they can't use); server-side checks are the *actual* security.

## Authorisation as a first-class, always-enforced concern
The deeper lesson, closing the week, is that **authorisation must be enforced rigorously, on every protected action, server-side, because it is where the most common serious web vulnerabilities live.** Broken access control, failing to properly check that a user is *authorised* for a specific action or resource, is consistently among the top web security vulnerabilities, and it happens because authorisation is easy to *forget* or do incompletely: developers authenticate the user (check they are logged in) but then fail to check, on *each* operation, that *this* user may do *this* thing. RBAC gives you the *structure* (roles and permissions) to reason about access clearly, but the *enforcement* is the critical part, you must actually check the user's permission on *every* protected endpoint and for *every* protected resource (including ownership: a "member" can edit *their own* content, so you check both the role *and* that the resource belongs to them, the `/users/42/orders` example from D1). The mindset to internalise is *deny by default and explicitly authorise*: assume an action is *not* permitted unless you have verified the user's role/ownership allows it, rather than assuming permitted unless explicitly forbidden (which leaks access when you forget a check). Combined with the week's other principles, separate authentication from authorisation, use trusted auth providers, secure your tokens/cookies, choose login methods well, RBAC enforced server-side on every protected action is how you build access control that actually protects your users' data. Authorisation is not a feature you add once; it is a discipline you apply to *every* protected operation, and getting it right, with RBAC for structure and rigorous server-side enforcement, is what makes the difference between a secure app and one with the broken-access-control holes that breach so many real systems. This is the heart of "auth done right."

## Where this fits
You understand role-based access control: structuring permissions into roles assigned to users, which makes authorisation manageable, consistent, and auditable at scale, *enforced rigorously server-side on every protected action* (and ownership check), with a deny-by-default mindset, because broken access control is among the most common serious vulnerabilities. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship secure auth.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: authentication and authorisation done right
You assemble the week into correct, secure auth for a real app (Bean Forge, or your project), demonstrating auth done right:
- **authentication** that verifies identity securely (via a trusted auth provider / library, not hand-rolled), with a deliberate choice of session vs JWT and login method(s), and secure token handling (HttpOnly cookies, HTTPS).
- **authorisation** via **RBAC**, enforced *server-side on every protected action* (and resource ownership), separate from authentication, deny-by-default.
- the two kept distinct (correct 401 vs 403), with no broken-access-control holes.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Auth done right: secure authentication + server-enforced RBAC authorisation"
git push
```

## The deliverable is security you can defend
What makes this project demonstrate real competence is that the auth is *actually secure*, which you can reason about and defend, not just "there's a login." The strongest version shows the two systems correctly separated and both enforced: authentication that does not roll its own crypto (uses a trusted provider/library), tokens stored safely (HttpOnly cookies, never localStorage), and, critically, *authorisation enforced on the server for every protected operation* so that no logged-in user can access or modify data or actions they should not, no broken access control. The proof is in *trying to break it*: can a logged-in non-admin call an admin endpoint directly (bypassing the hidden UI button)? Can user A access user B's data by changing an id? In a correct implementation, the server *denies* these because it checks authorisation (role and ownership) on every request, regardless of the UI. Demonstrating that you understand auth deeply enough to build it *securely*, the authentication/authorisation distinction, server-side enforcement, secure token handling, using trusted providers, and that you can articulate *why* it is secure (and where naive implementations fail), is the deliverable, and it is one of the most valuable backend skills because auth is where security breaches concentrate and getting it right protects real users' data.

## What auth, and the Backend phase, established
Step back: you have learned to secure an application correctly, which is non-negotiable for any real app. You understand the fundamental distinction (authentication = identity, authorisation = permission, separate systems both enforced), how login state is maintained (sessions vs JWTs and their trade-offs), social login (OAuth, without password-sharing), the strong case for using trusted auth providers rather than rolling your own (auth is too critical and subtle to reinvent), login-method trade-offs (security vs UX vs control), and authorisation at scale (RBAC, enforced server-side on every protected action, deny-by-default), all anchored by the core lesson that *broken access control comes from failing to enforce authorisation*, so you enforce it rigorously. And this *completes the Backend phase*: you can now build a secure, real backend end to end, the server (W9, Node/Express), the data layer (W10, Postgres/Prisma), well-designed APIs (W11, REST), and correct auth (W12), the full server side that your frontends consume. Combined with the frontend phases, you are now a complete *full-stack* developer who can build both sides securely, which is exactly FORGE's own stack and concerns.

## Where this fits
You shipped secure authentication and authorisation (trusted provider, session/JWT and login-method choices, RBAC enforced server-side, no broken access control), completing the Backend phase and making you a full-stack developer who can build secure applications end to end. Next comes the **Real-World Features phase** (W13-16), the features real products need beyond CRUD: **payments** (Stripe), **email** (transactional and marketing), **file uploads** (object storage and CDNs), and **real-time** (WebSockets), the capabilities that turn a working app into a real product.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A user logs in and you create a session. Two hours later, the user's account is suspended by an admin. The user still has their session cookie. What happens on their next request, and how do you handle it? The session lookup finds the session record in the database. But before trusting it, you must re-fetch the user from the database to check their current status. If you only store the user object in the session at login time, you will not see the suspension until the session expires. The correct approach: store only the userId in the session, fetch the user on every request (or cache with short TTL), and check the active/suspended status.

weeks.title: Payments with Stripe, The Easy Way to Lose All Your Money
weeks.context:
Stripe is the standard for online payments because it handles the hard parts: PCI compliance, fraud detection, 3D Secure, global payment methods, tax calculation. Your job is to integrate it correctly, and "correctly" means understanding that webhooks, not API responses, are the source of truth.

Stripe primitives. A Customer is a Stripe object that represents a paying user, attach your user's database ID to the Stripe customer for lookups. A Product is what you sell (a SaaS plan, a physical item). A Price is how you sell it, attached to a Product, can be recurring (subscription) or one-time. A PaymentIntent represents an attempt to collect payment, it has a status lifecycle (requires_payment_method, requires_confirmation, processing, succeeded, canceled). A Subscription links a Customer to a Price with a billing cycle.

Checkout vs Elements. Stripe Checkout is a hosted payment page, Stripe renders the UI, handles card number entry, validation, and 3D Secure. Use Checkout for most apps: it is the fastest path to PCI compliance because card numbers never touch your server. Stripe Elements is a set of embeddable UI components, you control the layout, Stripe handles the secure input fields. Use Elements when you need a custom checkout experience (your design team will not accept the Stripe-hosted page).

Webhooks are the source of truth. When a user completes payment, Stripe fires a webhook to your server. You must handle these events and update your database accordingly, do not update the database based on the API response from your server-side checkout creation call, because the user might close the browser before the success page loads. The events you care about: checkout.session.completed, customer.subscription.created, customer.subscription.updated, customer.subscription.deleted, invoice.payment_succeeded, invoice.payment_failed. Verify webhook signatures using Stripe's library, reject any request that does not have a valid signature.

This week you add a subscription to Bean Forge. Users can subscribe to "Bean Forge Pro" for a monthly fee. You create the Stripe checkout session, handle the success/cancel redirects, and process webhooks to grant/revoke Pro status in your database.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Payments: high stakes, get it right
This week you handle money, and the title, "the easy way to lose all your money", is a warning: payment integration is where small mistakes have *expensive* consequences (failed charges, double charges, granting paid access for free, losing revenue), so correctness matters more here than almost anywhere. **Stripe** is the standard for online payments because it handles the genuinely *hard* parts for you, and your job is to integrate it *correctly*, where "correctly" has a specific, crucial meaning you will learn: **webhooks, not API responses, are the source of truth.** This week you integrate Stripe properly, building the payment flow, subscriptions, refunds, and the testing discipline that money demands.

## What Stripe handles, and why you don't build payments yourself
The first thing to understand is *why* you use Stripe (or a similar processor) and never build payments yourself, which is the strongest build-vs-buy case in the whole track. Payment processing involves a huge amount of hard, security-critical, regulated machinery that Stripe handles:
- **PCI compliance:** strict legal/security requirements for handling card data, building compliant card handling yourself is enormously costly and risky, and Stripe's design means you *never touch raw card numbers* (they go directly to Stripe), keeping you out of most PCI scope.
- **Fraud detection, 3D Secure, global payment methods, tax calculation:** Stripe provides fraud screening, the bank-authentication flows (3D Secure) required in many regions, support for many payment methods and currencies worldwide, and tax handling, each a major undertaking on its own.
Building any of this yourself would be reckless (handling card data wrong is a catastrophic liability) and pointless (your app's value is not its payment plumbing). So you *use* Stripe, which has specialised in getting all of this right, and your job is the *integration*, connecting Stripe's machinery to your app correctly and securely. This is the same "use the specialist for critical, hard, universal infrastructure" judgement as auth, taken to its strongest form, because payments combine money, security, and regulation, the highest-stakes combination.

## The central lesson: webhooks are the source of truth
The single most important concept for integrating Stripe *correctly* is that **webhooks, not API responses, are the source of truth** for what actually happened with a payment. When a payment flow completes in the browser, you might *think* "the API call succeeded, so the payment worked, grant access", but this is the classic, dangerous mistake. Payment events happen *asynchronously* and partly *outside* your direct request (the customer's bank, Stripe's processing, 3D Secure challenges), so the *authoritative* confirmation that a payment truly succeeded (or failed, or a subscription renewed, or a refund processed) comes from Stripe *telling your server* via a **webhook** (a server-to-server notification Stripe sends when an event occurs), not from the response to your own API call or anything in the browser. So the correct pattern is: your server listens for Stripe's webhooks, and *those events* drive your app's state (grant access when the `payment succeeded` webhook arrives, not when the frontend thinks it did). Getting this right, treating Stripe's webhooks as the truth and *not* trusting client-side or premature signals, is what separates a correct, reliable payment integration from a buggy one that grants access for unpaid orders or misses successful payments. This principle drives the whole week, and internalising it now is the key to handling money correctly.

## Where this fits
This opens the **Real-World Features phase** (W13-16), the features real products need beyond CRUD: payments (this week), email, file uploads, and real-time. It builds on your backend (server, data, APIs, auth) to add the capability that turns an app into a *business*. Today's orientation: payments are high-stakes (mistakes cost money), Stripe handles the hard regulated/security parts so you integrate rather than build, and the central rule for correctness is that *webhooks, not API responses, are the source of truth* for what actually happened. Tomorrow you learn Stripe's primitives.

items.title: Stripe primitives
items.body:
## Stripe's building blocks
To integrate Stripe you model your billing with its **primitives**, a small set of objects that represent customers, what you sell, and payment attempts:
- **Customer:** a Stripe object representing a paying user. You *attach your app's user ID* to the Stripe customer (in metadata), so you can map between your users and Stripe's, the link between your database and Stripe.
- **Product:** *what* you sell (a SaaS plan, a physical item) at a conceptual level ("Pro Plan").
- **Price:** *how* you sell a product, attached to a Product, can be **recurring** (a subscription, e.g. $20/month) or **one-time**. A product can have multiple prices (monthly vs annual).
- **PaymentIntent:** represents a *single attempt to collect a payment*, with a status *lifecycle* (`requires_payment_method` -> `requires_confirmation` -> `processing` -> `succeeded` or `canceled`). It tracks one payment from start to finish.
- **Subscription:** links a Customer to a recurring Price with a billing cycle, managing ongoing recurring payments (and its own lifecycle, D4).

## How the primitives fit together
Understanding how these objects relate is what lets you model your billing correctly:
```text
Customer (your user #42)  --subscribes to-->  Price ($20/mo, recurring)  --of a-->  Product (Pro Plan)
                                                 |
PaymentIntent  =  one attempt to charge  (status: requires_payment... -> succeeded/canceled)
Subscription   =  Customer + recurring Price + billing cycle (creates PaymentIntents each period)
```
The shape of your billing maps onto these: you define **Products** and **Prices** for what you offer (a Pro plan with monthly and annual prices), you create a **Customer** for each paying user (linked to your user via metadata), and then either a **PaymentIntent** (for a one-time purchase) or a **Subscription** (for recurring billing, which itself generates PaymentIntents each cycle) collects the money. The **PaymentIntent's status lifecycle** is important to understand, a payment is not instantly "done"; it moves through states (needs a payment method, needs confirmation, processing, then succeeded or canceled), which is *why* you wait for the authoritative `succeeded` (via webhook, D3) rather than assuming success. Modelling your offering with these primitives correctly, the right Products/Prices, Customers linked to your users, the appropriate PaymentIntent or Subscription, is the foundation of a clean Stripe integration.

## Mapping Stripe to your app
The crucial integration detail is the *mapping* between Stripe's objects and your application's data, because your app and Stripe each have their own view of the user and the billing, and they must stay linked. You store the **Stripe customer ID** on your user record (and your **user ID** in the Stripe customer's metadata), so you can go from a Stripe event (this customer's payment succeeded) to *your* user (grant access to user #42) and vice versa, this two-way link is what lets webhooks (which reference Stripe objects) update *your* app's state (which references your users). Similarly, you track subscription status and the relevant Stripe IDs on your side, so your app knows each user's current billing state. Getting this mapping right is essential because it is the bridge between Stripe's billing world and your app's user/access world: when a webhook says "subscription X for customer Y renewed," you use the mapping to find *your* user and update *their* access. A clean integration keeps this mapping accurate and uses Stripe's objects (Customer, Product, Price, PaymentIntent, Subscription) as the model of the billing relationship, with your database holding the links and the resulting access state. Understanding the primitives *and* how they map to your app is what makes the rest of the integration (webhooks, subscriptions, refunds) coherent.

## Where this fits
You understand Stripe's primitives, Customer (linked to your user), Product (what you sell), Price (how, recurring or one-time), PaymentIntent (one payment attempt with a status lifecycle), Subscription (recurring billing), and how they map to your app via stored IDs, the model of your billing. Tomorrow you handle the source of truth: webhooks.

items.title: Webhooks
items.body:
## Webhooks: how Stripe tells your server the truth
Yesterday's principle, webhooks are the source of truth, becomes concrete today. A **webhook** is a server-to-server notification: when an event happens in Stripe (a payment succeeded, a subscription renewed, a refund processed), Stripe sends an HTTP POST to a URL on *your* server (a webhook endpoint), and your server reacts to it. This is how your app learns, authoritatively, what actually happened:
```text
1. Stripe processes an event (e.g. payment_intent.succeeded)
2. Stripe POSTs the event to YOUR webhook endpoint (e.g. POST /api/stripe/webhook)
3. your server VERIFIES the event is really from Stripe (signature check)
4. your server updates its state based on the event (grant access, mark paid, etc.)
```
So you build a webhook endpoint that receives Stripe's events and drives your app's state from them, this endpoint, not your checkout API call, is where you grant access, record the payment, and update the subscription status, because it reflects what *truly* happened.

## Why webhooks, not the API response
Understanding *why* the webhook is authoritative (and the API response is not) is the heart of correct payment handling:
- **Payments are asynchronous and span systems:** a payment involves the customer's bank, possible authentication challenges (3D Secure), and Stripe's processing, much of which happens *after* and *outside* your initial API call, so the response to your call does *not* know the final outcome. The payment might still be processing, or get declined by the bank after your call returned.
- **Some events have no API call of yours at all:** a subscription *renewal* next month, a payment that fails on retry, a dispute, these happen on Stripe's schedule with no request from your app, so the *only* way you learn about them is the webhook. There is no API response to check because you did not make a call.
- **The client cannot be trusted:** anything in the browser can be manipulated, so granting access based on a client-side "payment succeeded" signal is insecure (a user could fake it). The webhook is a *server-to-server*, *signature-verified* message from Stripe, which is trustworthy.
So the webhook is the authoritative, complete, secure source of what happened, and building your payment logic around webhooks (grant access when the `succeeded` webhook arrives) rather than around your own API responses or client signals is what makes the integration correct. This is why the principle is stated so emphatically: the most common payment bugs (granting access for unpaid/failed payments, missing renewals, not handling failures) come from trusting the wrong signal instead of the webhook.

## Building webhooks correctly: verify and be idempotent
Two disciplines make webhook handling correct and secure:
- **Verify the signature:** Stripe signs each webhook, and your endpoint must *verify* that signature (using your webhook secret) before trusting the event, otherwise an attacker could POST fake "payment succeeded" events to your endpoint and get free access. Signature verification ensures the event genuinely came from Stripe. This is non-negotiable security.
- **Be idempotent:** Stripe may send the *same* webhook more than once (retries, network issues), so your handler must be **idempotent**, processing the same event twice must not cause double effects (don't grant access twice, don't double-count). You achieve this by tracking processed event IDs (ignore an event you have already handled) or designing the update to be safe to repeat. Idempotency is essential because webhook delivery is "at least once," not "exactly once."
Also, your endpoint should respond quickly (acknowledge receipt fast, do heavy work async if needed) so Stripe does not consider it failed and retry unnecessarily. Building the webhook endpoint with signature verification (security) and idempotency (correctness under retries), and driving your app's state from the verified events, is the core of a correct Stripe integration. Get this right, and payments are reliable; get it wrong (trust unverified events, or double-process), and you have security holes or billing bugs.

## Where this fits
You understand webhooks as Stripe's authoritative, server-to-server, signature-verified notifications of what actually happened, why they (not API responses or client signals) are the source of truth (payments are async, cross-system, and the client is untrusted), and how to handle them correctly (verify the signature, be idempotent under retries). Tomorrow you handle ongoing billing: the subscription lifecycle.

items.title: Subscription lifecycle
items.body:
## Subscriptions: billing over time
Many apps (including SaaS like FORGE) charge *recurring* subscriptions, and a **Subscription** has a *lifecycle* that unfolds over time, far more than a one-time payment, and handling that lifecycle correctly is what keeps access and billing in sync. A subscription moves through states driven by events (mostly delivered via webhooks):
```text
created -> active -> (renews each period) -> ...
  active                  paying, access granted
  past_due                a renewal payment failed; retrying
  canceled                ended (by user or after failed retries); revoke access
  trialing                in a free trial
  (also: paused, incomplete, etc.)
```
Each state change (a renewal succeeds, a payment fails, the user cancels, a trial ends) arrives as a webhook, and your app must react, grant access on `active`, handle `past_due` (warn the user, maybe restrict), revoke access on `canceled`, so your app's access state always matches the subscription's real billing state.

## Why the lifecycle matters: keeping access in sync with billing
The reason subscription lifecycle handling is its own (substantial) concern is that **a subscription's billing state and your app's access state must stay synchronised over time, through many events you do not directly initiate**, and getting this wrong is a common, costly source of bugs in both directions:
- **Granting access you should not:** if you fail to handle cancellation or a failed renewal, a user keeps paid access *without paying*, you lose revenue and give away your product. (e.g. their card expires, the renewal fails, the subscription goes `past_due` then `canceled`, but if you ignore those webhooks, they keep their Pro features for free.)
- **Revoking access you should not:** if you mishandle the states, you might cut off a *paying* user (e.g. treating a temporary `past_due` as immediate cancellation, or missing a successful renewal), which is a terrible experience for a paying customer.
So you must handle the *full* lifecycle: react to renewals (continue access), to `past_due` (the renewal failed, give a grace period and prompt the user to update payment, Stripe retries), to cancellation (revoke access, at the right time, often at period end), to trials (grant access during the trial, handle its end). This is driven by webhooks (the source of truth, D3) for events like `invoice.payment_succeeded` (renewal worked), `invoice.payment_failed` (renewal failed), and `customer.subscription.deleted` (canceled), each updating your stored subscription status and the user's access. Keeping the two in sync, your app's access exactly reflecting the real billing state at every point in the lifecycle, is the goal, and it requires handling the *ongoing* events, not just the initial purchase.

## Handle the lifecycle thoughtfully, including the human cases
Beyond the mechanics, good subscription handling involves *thoughtful* treatment of the lifecycle states, which is both a correctness and a customer-experience concern. For failed renewals (`past_due`), the kind approach is a *grace period* with clear communication ("your payment failed, please update your card", Stripe's smart retries plus dunning emails help), rather than instant cutoff, because a paying customer's card expiring is common and you want to recover the payment, not lose the customer. For cancellations, you typically keep access until the *end of the paid period* (they paid for it), then revoke. For upgrades/downgrades (changing plans), you handle proration. For trials, you manage the trial-to-paid transition. These reflect that subscriptions are an *ongoing relationship* with billing events that have real customer-experience implications, not just state flags, so handling them well (grace periods, clear communication, fair proration, access until period end) keeps both your billing correct *and* your customers treated fairly. Stripe provides tools for much of this (smart retries, the customer portal for self-service plan changes, dunning), so you lean on those, but *your app* must correctly react to the resulting webhooks to keep access in sync. Mastering the subscription lifecycle, the states, the events that drive them, keeping access synced with billing, and handling the human cases thoughtfully, is essential for any recurring-revenue product, and it is exactly the kind of thing that, done wrong, either bleeds revenue or alienates paying customers.

## Where this fits
You understand the subscription lifecycle: the states (active, past_due, canceled, trialing) driven by webhook events, the imperative to keep your app's access state synced with the real billing state over time (or lose revenue / cut off paying users), and handling the human cases thoughtfully (grace periods, access until period end, clear communication). Tomorrow you handle money going the other way: refunds and disputes.

items.title: Refunds and disputes
items.body:
## Money flowing back: refunds and disputes
Payments are not one-directional, sometimes money goes *back* to the customer, and handling **refunds** and **disputes** correctly is part of a complete, correct payment integration. They are different:
- **Refund:** *you* (the merchant) choose to return a payment to the customer (fully or partially), e.g. for a return, a cancellation, or goodwill. You initiate it (via Stripe's API or dashboard), and you should react to the resulting event (revoke access for the refunded purchase, update your records). Refunds are under your control.
- **Dispute (chargeback):** the *customer* disputes a charge *with their bank* ("I didn't authorise this" / "I didn't get what I paid for"), and the bank pulls the money back, often with a fee, and asks Stripe (and you) for evidence. Disputes are *adversarial* and *costly* (you can lose the money *and* pay a dispute fee), and they arrive as webhook events you must handle (respond with evidence, and update access/records depending on the outcome).

## Why handling these correctly matters
Refunds and disputes matter because they affect *both* your money and your app's state, and mishandling them causes problems in both:
- **Keep access in sync (again):** when a payment is refunded or a dispute is lost, the customer has effectively *un-paid*, so your app should typically *revoke* the access that payment granted (otherwise you have given the product away). These events arrive via webhook (the source of truth), and your app must react, the same access-syncing discipline as subscriptions, now for money flowing back.
- **Disputes are expensive and worth preventing:** a chargeback costs you the payment *and* a fee, and a high dispute rate can get your Stripe account flagged, so disputes are something to *minimise* (through clear billing descriptors, good customer service that handles complaints *before* they become chargebacks, and fraud prevention) and to *respond to* properly (submitting evidence when you have a legitimate charge). Refunds, while a cost, are often *cheaper than a dispute* (a goodwill refund avoids a chargeback fee and an unhappy customer), so handling refund requests promptly and fairly is good business *and* dispute prevention.
- **Records and accounting:** both refunds and disputes affect your revenue records, so tracking them keeps your accounting accurate.
So a complete payment integration handles not just collecting money but *returning* it (refunds) and *defending/recording* contested charges (disputes), keeping access and records correct throughout, driven by the relevant webhooks.

## The discipline: handle the full money lifecycle, prevent problems
The broader lesson is that **a correct payment integration handles the *entire* money lifecycle, including the unhappy and adversarial paths, not just the happy path of collecting payment**, which is the payment-specific version of the "handle the unhappy path" discipline from across the track. The naive integration handles "user pays, grant access" and stops; the complete one handles renewals, failures, cancellations (D4), *and* refunds and disputes (today), keeping access and records correct through *all* of them. Disputes especially teach a real-world, somewhat adversarial concern: customers (and occasionally fraudsters) will dispute charges, and you must be prepared to respond, defend legitimate charges with evidence, and, more importantly, *prevent* disputes by being clear and fair (recognisable billing descriptors so customers don't dispute a charge they don't recognise, responsive support that resolves issues before they escalate to the bank, fraud screening). Refunds, handled promptly and fairly, are part of this, often the right response to a problem, and cheaper than the dispute that an ignored complaint becomes. Treating the full money lifecycle, including refunds and disputes, as part of the integration, with the same webhook-driven, access-syncing correctness, *and* taking a preventive stance toward disputes (clarity, good service, fraud prevention), is what makes a payment system genuinely complete and robust, protecting both your revenue and your customer relationships. Money flowing back is as much a part of payments as money coming in.

## Where this fits
You understand refunds (merchant-initiated returns) and disputes (customer chargebacks via their bank, costly and adversarial), how to handle both correctly (revoke access via webhooks, keep records accurate, respond to disputes with evidence) and *prevent* disputes (clear descriptors, good service, fraud prevention, prompt fair refunds), completing the full money lifecycle. Tomorrow you handle testing all of this safely.

items.title: Testing
items.body:
## Testing payments without spending real money
Payment code is high-stakes and complex (webhooks, subscription states, refunds, failures), so you *must* test it thoroughly, and Stripe provides a complete **test mode** so you can do so without real money. Test mode is a parallel environment with test API keys, test card numbers, and test webhooks, where you exercise the *entire* payment flow using fake cards that simulate every scenario:
```text
test card 4242 4242 4242 4242  -> succeeds
test card 4000 0000 0000 0002  -> declined
test cards for: 3D Secure required, insufficient funds, expired, dispute, etc.
Stripe CLI: forward/trigger webhooks locally to test your webhook handler
```
You test successful payments, declines, authentication challenges, failed renewals, cancellations, refunds, and disputes, *all* in test mode, confirming your integration handles each correctly before any real customer's money is involved.

## Why testing payments is especially critical
Testing matters everywhere, but for payments it is *especially* critical, and understanding why reinforces the week's high-stakes theme:
- **The cost of bugs is real money:** a payment bug does not just produce a wrong pixel, it charges the wrong amount, grants access for free, double-charges a customer, or fails to collect revenue, all of which have direct financial and trust consequences. So the bar for correctness is high, and testing is how you reach it.
- **The unhappy paths are where bugs hide and matter most:** the happy path (a card that just works) is easy; the *failure* cases (declines, failed renewals, disputes, 3D Secure, webhook retries) are complex, easy to get wrong, and *exactly* where real-world payments spend a lot of time (real cards get declined, real renewals fail). So you must test the failure scenarios deliberately, with the test cards that simulate them, not just the happy path, because that is where correctness is hardest and most consequential.
- **Webhook handling needs testing:** since webhooks are the source of truth, you test that your webhook handler correctly processes each event type (and is idempotent, and verifies signatures), using the Stripe CLI to send/trigger test events to your local endpoint. A bug in webhook handling is a bug in your source of truth.
So payment testing is comprehensive (every scenario, especially the failures) and webhook-inclusive, done entirely in Stripe's test mode so it costs nothing and risks nothing, before going live.

## The discipline: thorough testing before real money
The deeper lesson is that **payments demand a higher testing discipline than almost anything else, because the cost of failure is direct and real**, and Stripe's test mode exists precisely to enable that thorough testing safely. The mature approach is to treat going live with payments as something you do only *after* exercising the full flow, including all the failure and edge cases, in test mode and confirming correct behaviour: the happy purchase, the decline, the 3D Secure challenge, the failed renewal and grace period, the cancellation and access revocation, the refund, the dispute, and the webhook handling for all of them. This is the payment-specific application of the verify-the-real-behaviour discipline that has run through the track (test the real thing, especially the failure cases), elevated because money is on the line, a payment integration you have only tested on the happy path is one that *will* mishandle the very common failure cases in production, with financial consequences. So you use test mode to its fullest, simulating every scenario, before a single real charge, and you keep test mode in your toolkit for verifying changes (never test payment changes against real money). Combined with the week's correctness principles (webhooks as truth, idempotency, full lifecycle handling), thorough testing in test mode is what gives you confidence that your payment integration will behave correctly when real customers' money flows through it, which is exactly the confidence that "the easy way to lose all your money" demands you earn. Test exhaustively, then go live.

## Where this fits
You understand testing payments in Stripe's test mode: exercising the *entire* flow, especially the failure and edge cases (declines, 3D Secure, failed renewals, disputes) and the webhook handling, with test cards and the Stripe CLI, costing and risking nothing, with the discipline that payments demand thorough testing before real money because failures cost real money. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship a correct payment integration.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a correct payment integration
You assemble the week into a working, correct Stripe integration (for Bean Forge, a SaaS, or any app that charges), demonstrating payments done right:
- the right **primitives** modelling your billing (Customers linked to your users, Products/Prices, PaymentIntents or Subscriptions).
- **webhooks as the source of truth** (a signature-verified, idempotent webhook endpoint driving your app's state), never trusting client/API-response signals.
- correct **subscription lifecycle** handling (access synced with billing through renewals, failures, cancellations) and **refund/dispute** handling.
- thoroughly **tested in test mode** across the failure cases before going live.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Stripe integration: webhook-driven, lifecycle-correct, tested in test mode"
git push   # (with Stripe keys as env secrets, never committed)
```

## The deliverable is correctness you can trust with money
What makes this project demonstrate real competence is that the payment integration is *correct and trustworthy enough to handle real money*, which rests on the principles, not just on a checkout that works once. The strongest version is webhook-driven (access and billing state come from Stripe's verified webhooks, the source of truth, not from client signals or API responses), handles the *full* lifecycle (renewals, failures with grace periods, cancellations, refunds, disputes, keeping access correctly synced throughout), is *secure* (signature-verified webhooks, keys as env secrets, no card data touching your server), and is *thoroughly tested* (every scenario exercised in test mode, especially failures). The proof is that it does the *right* thing in the cases that matter and are easy to get wrong: a failed renewal does not silently keep granting free access, a faked client signal does not unlock paid features, a duplicate webhook does not double-charge or double-grant, a refund revokes access. Demonstrating that you understand *why* webhooks are the source of truth and have built a correct, secure, lifecycle-complete, well-tested integration, rather than a naive happy-path checkout, is the deliverable, and it is exactly the competence that lets a business trust you with its revenue.

## What payments established
Step back: you have learned to handle money correctly, one of the highest-stakes and most valuable backend skills. You understand why you use Stripe rather than build payments (PCI, fraud, the regulated machinery, the strongest build-vs-buy case), Stripe's primitives and how they map to your app, and, above all, the central correctness principle that *webhooks, not API responses, are the source of truth*, which drives correct handling of payments, the full subscription lifecycle (keeping access synced with billing), refunds, and disputes, all verified by thorough testing in test mode. The throughline is *correctness under high stakes*: payments are where bugs cost real money and trust, so the discipline, webhook-driven truth, idempotency, full-lifecycle handling, security, exhaustive testing, is elevated, and mastering it is what makes you able to build the revenue systems real businesses depend on. This is FORGE's concern too (it has Stripe in its plan), so it is directly real-world relevant.

## Where this fits
You shipped a correct, secure, well-tested Stripe payment integration built on the source-of-truth principle, the high-stakes skill of handling money. Next week you handle another piece of real-product infrastructure: **email**, transactional (password resets, receipts, the email a user *expects*) and marketing, plus the deliverability, templates, unsubscribe handling, and regulations that determine whether your email reaches the inbox at all, because, as the title warns, getting email right is harder than it looks.

items.body: A user pays successfully, the Stripe Checkout redirect sends them to your /success page, and your success page marks them as Pro. What is the failure mode here? If the user closes the browser immediately after payment but before the redirect fires, your success page never loads, and the user is never marked as Pro. weeks.title: Email, Transactional, Marketing, and Why Your Inbox Hates You
weeks.context:
Email is infrastructure. When a user signs up, forgets their password, makes a purchase, or triggers any significant event, your application sends email. Getting email right means understanding the difference between transactional email and marketing email, the infrastructure that determines whether your message reaches the inbox, and the regulations that govern what you can send.

Transactional email is triggered by user action: welcome email, password reset, order confirmation, invoice. The user expects it. Send it from a transactional email provider: Resend, Postmark, or AWS SES. These providers optimise for deliverability on triggered, one-to-one messages.

Marketing email is bulk: newsletters, product announcements, promotional campaigns. Use a marketing email provider: Loops (good for SaaS), Mailchimp, or ConvertKit. The distinction matters because bulk email and transactional email have different sending patterns, ISPs treat them differently. Mixing them harms your transactional deliverability.

Deliverability: the science of getting email into the inbox. The three DNS records you must configure. SPF (Sender Policy Framework): a TXT record that lists the mail servers authorised to send email from your domain. Prevents strangers from sending email that appears to come from you. DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): your email provider generates a key pair. You publish the public key as a DNS TXT record. The provider signs outgoing emails with the private key. Recipients verify the signature. Proves the email was not altered in transit. DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance): a policy that tells receiving servers what to do with email that fails SPF and DKIM checks, reject it, quarantine it, or report it. Start with p=none (report only), move to p=quarantine, then p=reject.

Regulations. CAN-SPAM (US): all commercial email must include a physical mailing address and an unsubscribe link. The unsubscribe must work within 10 business days. GDPR (EU): you need consent to send marketing email to EU residents. Pre-ticked checkboxes do not count. Keep a record of when and how consent was given.

This week you add transactional email to Bean Forge: welcome email on signup, password reset flow (token generation, email dispatch, token verification), and order confirmation.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Email is infrastructure
Email is not a nice-to-have, it is *infrastructure* that real applications depend on: when a user signs up, forgets their password, makes a purchase, or triggers any significant event, your application sends email. Getting email right, the title hints it is harder than it looks ("why your inbox hates you"), means understanding three things: the difference between **transactional** and **marketing** email (two different systems), the **infrastructure** that determines whether your message actually reaches the inbox (deliverability), and the **regulations** that govern what you may send. This week you build email correctly, learning that "send an email" is deceptively simple-sounding but involves real subtlety to do well.

## The fundamental split: transactional vs marketing
The most important distinction, which shapes everything, is between **transactional** and **marketing** email, they are *different systems* with different purposes, providers, and rules:
- **Transactional email** is *triggered by a user action* and *expected* by the user: a welcome email, a password reset, an order confirmation, an invoice. The user just did something and expects this email as a direct result. It is one-to-one, timely, and the user *wants* it.
- **Marketing email** is *bulk* and *promotional*: newsletters, product announcements, campaigns sent to many users. The user did not trigger each one; you are reaching out to them.
These require *different providers* optimised for their different needs:
- Transactional providers (**Resend**, **Postmark**, **AWS SES**) optimise for *deliverability of triggered, one-to-one messages*, getting the password reset to the inbox *fast and reliably*.
- Marketing providers (**Loops** (good for SaaS), **Mailchimp**, and others) optimise for *bulk sending, campaigns, list management, and unsubscribe handling*.

## Why the distinction matters so much
Understanding *why* transactional and marketing email are separate, and must not be mixed, is the key insight that prevents a cascade of problems:
- **Deliverability depends on reputation, and mixing them hurts it:** email providers (Gmail, etc.) decide whether to deliver your mail to the inbox or spam based partly on your sending *reputation*, and transactional and marketing email have very different sending patterns and engagement. Mixing them (sending marketing blasts from the same domain/setup as your critical password resets) can *damage the reputation* that gets your *transactional* email delivered, so a marketing campaign that gets marked as spam could cause your password-reset emails to land in spam too, a disaster (users locked out because they never get the reset). Keeping them separate (different providers, often different sending domains/subdomains) *protects* the deliverability of your critical transactional mail.
- **Different rules apply:** marketing email is heavily regulated (consent, unsubscribe requirements, D5), while transactional email (expected, triggered) has different obligations, so treating them the same risks compliance problems.
- **Different optimisations:** the providers are *built* for their respective jobs (fast one-to-one delivery vs bulk campaigns with list management), so using the right one for each gets you better results.
So you use a *transactional* provider for the email users *expect* (and must receive, like password resets), and a *marketing* provider for *bulk* outreach, keeping them separate to protect deliverability and meet the right rules. Getting this split right is the foundation of doing email well, and conflating them is a common, damaging mistake.

## Where this fits
This week handles email infrastructure in the Real-World Features phase: transactional vs marketing email (different systems), deliverability (reaching the inbox), templates, unsubscribe, plain-text fallback, the capabilities every real product needs. It builds on your backend (you trigger emails from server events). Today's orientation: email is infrastructure; the fundamental split is transactional (triggered, expected, critical, e.g. password resets) vs marketing (bulk, promotional), which use different providers and must be kept separate to protect the deliverability and compliance of each. Tomorrow you build transactional email.

items.title: Transactional email
items.body:
## Transactional email: the messages users expect
You start with **transactional email**, the most critical kind, because it includes things like password resets that users *must* receive (a failed password-reset email means a locked-out user). You send it through a transactional provider (Resend, Postmark, AWS SES) via their API, triggered by an event in your app:
```js
// triggered by a user action (e.g. password reset requested)
await resend.emails.send({
  from: 'Bean Forge <noreply@beanforge.com>',
  to: user.email,
  subject: 'Reset your password',
  html: renderResetEmail(resetLink),     // the email content
});
```
Your server, on the relevant event (signup, password reset, order placed), calls the provider's API to send the appropriate email to the user, and the provider handles the actual delivery, optimised for getting these one-to-one, triggered messages to the inbox reliably.

## Why use a provider, and treat email sending as reliable infrastructure
You use a transactional email *provider* rather than sending email yourself (e.g. running your own mail server) for the same build-vs-buy reasons that applied to auth and payments, email deliverability is hard, specialised infrastructure:
- **Deliverability expertise:** getting email to the inbox (not spam) requires reputation management, correct authentication (D3), and infrastructure that providers specialise in, running your own mail server and achieving good deliverability is genuinely difficult and a constant battle.
- **Reliability and scale:** providers handle retries, bounces, and high volume reliably.
- **Tooling:** they provide sending APIs, delivery tracking, bounce/complaint handling, and analytics.
So you integrate a provider's API and let them handle the hard delivery infrastructure, focusing on *what* to send and *when*. And you treat transactional email as *reliable infrastructure* your app depends on: because some transactional emails are *critical* (password reset, email verification, payment receipts), you handle their sending robustly, with error handling (what if the send fails?), and you recognise that a user not receiving a critical email is a real failure (a locked-out user, a confused customer). This means triggering emails reliably from your server events, handling send failures, and choosing a dependable provider, treating email sending with the seriousness its criticality warrants.

## Trigger emails from server events, reliably and asynchronously
The architectural pattern for transactional email is to **trigger it from your server in response to events, reliably and usually asynchronously**, which is worth getting right. Emails are triggered by application events (a user signed up -> send welcome; requested a reset -> send reset link; placed an order -> send confirmation), so your server-side event handling calls the email provider at the right moment. Two practical considerations: First, *don't block the user's request on the email send*, sending an email involves a network call to the provider that could be slow or fail, so you typically send it *asynchronously* (after responding to the user, or via a background job/queue) so the user's action (signup, order) completes promptly regardless of email timing, and a slow email does not slow the user. Second, *handle failures*, the send might fail (provider down, invalid address), so for critical emails you handle the error (retry, log, alert) rather than silently losing it, because a lost password-reset email is a real problem. For high-reliability needs, emails are often queued (a background queue with retries) so a transient failure does not lose the email. This connects to the async and process patterns from the backend phase: email sending is I/O that you handle asynchronously and robustly, as part of your server's event handling, because it is infrastructure users depend on. Getting transactional email right, triggered reliably from events, sent asynchronously so it doesn't block, with failure handling for critical messages, through a deliverability-optimised provider, is the foundation, because these are the emails that *matter most* (the ones users need), and they must arrive.

## Where this fits
You can send transactional email, the triggered, expected, often-critical messages (welcome, password reset, receipts), through a deliverability-optimised provider's API, triggered reliably and asynchronously from your server's events with failure handling for the critical ones, treating it as the reliable infrastructure it is. But sending is only half, the email must *reach the inbox*, which is tomorrow's hard problem: deliverability.

items.title: Deliverability
items.body:
## Deliverability: actually reaching the inbox
Sending an email is easy; getting it *delivered to the inbox* (not spam, not blocked) is the hard part, and **deliverability** is the set of factors that determine whether your message arrives. The receiving mail systems (Gmail, Outlook) decide whether to inbox, spam-folder, or reject your email based on signals about your *legitimacy* and *reputation*, and the foundational technical signals are **email authentication** records you set up in your domain's DNS:
```text
SPF   - says which servers are allowed to send email for your domain
DKIM  - cryptographically signs your emails so the recipient can verify they're really from you
DMARC - tells receivers what to do with email that fails SPF/DKIM (and reports on it)
```
These three (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) prove your email genuinely comes from your domain and is not forged, and *without them properly configured, your email is far more likely to be marked as spam or rejected*, because unauthenticated email looks suspicious (spammers forge senders, so authentication is how you prove you are legitimate).

## What drives deliverability beyond authentication
Authentication is necessary but not sufficient, and understanding the *full* picture of deliverability shows why "why your inbox hates you" is a real problem:
- **Sender reputation:** mail providers track your domain's/IP's reputation based on your sending behaviour, do recipients open and engage, or mark you as spam? do you send to invalid addresses (bounces) or spam traps? A good reputation gets you the inbox; a bad one (lots of spam complaints, bounces, low engagement) gets you the spam folder or blocked. Reputation is *earned over time* and *damaged* by bad practices (which is exactly why mixing marketing and transactional, D1, is dangerous, marketing's spam complaints damage the reputation your transactional email needs).
- **Engagement:** recipients opening, reading, and *not* deleting/spam-flagging your email signals to providers that it is wanted, improving deliverability; mail that is ignored or flagged hurts it. So sending email people actually *want* (and not to people who don't) is itself a deliverability factor.
- **Content and list hygiene:** spam-like content (certain words, all-image emails, bad formatting) can trip spam filters, and sending to invalid or unengaged addresses (poor list hygiene) generates bounces and complaints that hurt reputation.
So deliverability is a *combination* of technical authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC proving legitimacy), earned reputation (good sending behaviour over time), engagement (sending wanted email), and hygiene (clean lists, decent content), and *all* of these affect whether your message reaches the inbox.

## Why deliverability is a real, ongoing concern
The deeper lesson is that **deliverability is a genuine, often-underestimated problem, and reaching the inbox is not guaranteed just because you sent the email**, which is the surprising reality behind "your inbox hates you." Many developers assume "I called the send API, so the email arrived", but the email may well be in spam, or blocked, especially if authentication is missing or reputation is poor, and the user simply never sees it (a locked-out user who never got the reset, with no error on your side). So you treat deliverability as something to *actively ensure*: set up SPF/DKIM/DMARC correctly (the technical foundation, often handled with your provider's guidance), use a reputable provider (their infrastructure and shared reputation help), protect your reputation (keep marketing and transactional separate, maintain list hygiene, send wanted email, monitor bounce and complaint rates), and *monitor* deliverability (providers report delivery, bounce, and spam rates so you can see if you have a problem). This is the email-specific version of the recurring "verify the real-world outcome, don't assume" discipline, sending is not delivering, and you must ensure and monitor actual delivery. Good deliverability is what makes email reliable infrastructure (the critical password reset *actually* reaches the user); poor deliverability silently breaks it (emails vanish into spam). Understanding the factors, authentication, reputation, engagement, hygiene, and actively managing them is what separates email that works from email that mysteriously "doesn't arrive," and it is a real, ongoing operational concern, not a one-time setup.

## Where this fits
You understand deliverability: the factors that determine whether email reaches the inbox, technical authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC proving legitimacy), earned sender reputation, engagement, and list hygiene, and that sending is not delivering, so you actively ensure and monitor delivery rather than assuming it. Tomorrow you handle making emails look good and feel personal: templates and personalisation.

items.title: Templates and personalisation
items.body:
## Email templates and personalisation
Emails need to *look good* and feel *relevant*, and that means **templates** (reusable, well-designed email layouts) with **personalisation** (filling in the recipient's specific details). A template defines the email's structure and style once, and you inject the per-recipient data:
```text
template (reusable):   header, body layout, footer, styling
personalisation:       "Hi {{name}}", the specific order details, the reset link, etc.
-> rendered per recipient: "Hi Amina, your order #1234 has shipped..."
```
You build templates for each email type (welcome, reset, receipt) and render them with the recipient's data, so each email is consistent in design but personalised in content. Tools and providers offer template systems (and React-based email frameworks like React Email let you build templates with components, the same component model you know).

## Why email templates are their own (annoying) challenge
A crucial, practical reality: **email HTML is *not* like web HTML, it is far more constrained and inconsistent**, which is why email templating is its own skill and a known pain point. Email clients (Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail, and dozens more) render HTML *very* inconsistently and support only a *limited, old* subset of HTML/CSS, Outlook especially is notorious for poor, quirky rendering. This means the modern CSS and layout techniques you use on the web (flexbox, grid, modern selectors) often *do not work* in email, and you are forced back to older, more robust techniques (table-based layouts, inline styles) to get consistent rendering across clients. So building an email that looks good *everywhere* is genuinely harder than building a web page, you must use the constrained, compatible subset and test across many clients. This is why you lean on *email-specific* tools and frameworks (React Email, MJML, or your provider's templates) that handle the cross-client compatibility for you (generating the table-based, inline-styled, broadly-compatible HTML), rather than hand-writing email HTML with modern web techniques that will break in Outlook. Understanding that email rendering is a constrained, inconsistent environment, requiring compatible techniques and cross-client testing, is what saves you from the frustration of an email that looks perfect in Gmail and broken in Outlook.

## Personalisation, relevance, and not overdoing it
Personalisation, filling in the recipient's details, matters because *relevant* email is more useful, more engaging, and (back to D3) better for deliverability (engagement helps reputation), but the lesson is to personalise *meaningfully* and respect the user, not creepily or excessively. Good personalisation makes the email genuinely relevant and useful: the recipient's name, their specific order, their actual reset link, the details *they* need, which makes the email clearly *for them* and actionable. This is valuable and expected (an order confirmation *should* have your order details). The discipline is to keep personalisation *purposeful and respectful*: use the data to make the email *useful to the recipient* (relevant content, the right details), not to be invasive ("we noticed you were looking at X at 2am") or manipulative, and be mindful that using personal data carries responsibility (privacy, which connects to the broader data-responsibility themes). Combined with good templates (consistent, well-designed, cross-client-compatible), thoughtful personalisation produces email that is professional, relevant, and effective, the recipient gets a well-designed message with exactly the information they need. The combination, robust cross-client templates plus meaningful personalisation, is what makes transactional (and marketing) email both look good and feel relevant, which improves both the user experience and deliverability. Getting templates right (compatible, tested) and personalisation right (relevant, respectful) is the craft of email content.

## Where this fits
You can build email templates (reusable, well-designed) and personalise them, using email-specific tools because email HTML is a constrained, inconsistent environment requiring compatible techniques (tables, inline styles) and cross-client testing, with personalisation that is meaningful and respectful. Tomorrow you handle a legal and ethical requirement, especially for marketing email: unsubscribe.

items.title: Unsubscribe
items.body:
## Unsubscribe: a legal and ethical requirement
For marketing email (and bulk email generally), letting recipients **unsubscribe** is not optional, it is a *legal requirement* and an ethical baseline. Laws governing commercial email (CAN-SPAM in the US, GDPR/PECR in Europe, CASL in Canada, and others) require that marketing emails include a clear, working way to opt out, and that you *honour* unsubscribe requests promptly:
```text
every marketing email MUST:
  - include a clear, visible unsubscribe link
  - honour the unsubscribe promptly (stop sending to that person)
  - (often) not require login or hoops to unsubscribe; one click
```
So your marketing email system must include an unsubscribe mechanism, and unsubscribing must *actually work*, the person stops receiving marketing email, reliably and quickly.

## Why unsubscribe matters: law, deliverability, and respect
Unsubscribe handling matters on three levels, and understanding all three shows it is far more than a checkbox:
- **Legal compliance:** the regulations *require* it, and violations carry real penalties (fines can be substantial). A clear unsubscribe link and honouring opt-outs is a legal obligation for marketing email, full stop.
- **Deliverability (back to D3):** if people *cannot* easily unsubscribe, they will instead mark your email as *spam*, which is far worse for you, spam complaints directly damage your sender reputation (D3) and hurt the deliverability of *all* your email (including transactional). So an easy unsubscribe is actually *protective*: a person who unsubscribes quietly is much better for your reputation than one who hits "spam" because they couldn't find the unsubscribe. Making unsubscribe easy *reduces* spam complaints, which *helps* deliverability.
- **Respect and trust:** honouring people's choice to stop hearing from you is basic respect, and respecting it builds trust (while ignoring it, or making it hard, destroys trust and brand reputation). Forcing email on people who don't want it is both wrong and counterproductive.
So unsubscribe is a legal requirement, a deliverability protector, *and* an ethical baseline, the rare case where the legal, technical, and ethical reasons all point the same way: make unsubscribe easy and honour it promptly.

## The broader principle: consent and respecting choice
The deeper lesson unsubscribe teaches is about **consent and respecting the user's choices in communication**, which extends through responsible email (and software) practice generally. The foundation is that marketing email should go to people who have *consented* to receive it (opted in), not purchased lists or non-consenting recipients, sending wanted email to people who agreed to it is both the legal/ethical standard (especially under consent-based regimes like GDPR) *and* the deliverability-smart approach (engaged, consenting recipients improve reputation; unwanted email to non-consenting people generates complaints and ruins it). And once someone is on your list, respecting their choice to *leave* (easy unsubscribe, promptly honoured) is the other half of consent. This reflects a respectful posture toward users that runs through the responsible-engineering themes of the whole track: you communicate *with consent*, you make opting out *easy*, and you *honour* people's choices, treating recipients as people whose preferences matter, not targets to be blasted. It also aligns incentives nicely, the respectful approach (consent-based sending, easy unsubscribe) is *also* the one that protects your deliverability and keeps you legal, so there is no tension between doing right by users and doing well operationally. Understanding unsubscribe (and consent) as a legal requirement, a deliverability protector, and an ethical practice, all reinforcing each other, is what makes your email program both compliant and effective, and it embodies the broader principle of respecting users' communication choices. Make unsubscribe trivial, honour it immediately, and only send wanted email in the first place.

## Where this fits
You understand unsubscribe as a legal requirement (CAN-SPAM, GDPR, etc.), a deliverability protector (easy unsubscribe reduces reputation-damaging spam complaints), and an ethical baseline (respecting people's choice), reflecting the broader principle of consent-based, choice-respecting communication. Tomorrow you handle a robustness detail that aids both deliverability and accessibility: plain-text fallback.

items.title: Plain-text fallback
items.body:
## Plain-text fallback: robustness and reach
A well-built email is sent as *both* an HTML version *and* a **plain-text** version (a "multipart" email), with the recipient's client showing whichever it can. The **plain-text fallback** is the plain version of your email's content, no HTML, no styling, just the text, included alongside the HTML:
```text
multipart email:
  - HTML part:        the nicely-designed, styled version (most clients show this)
  - plain-text part:  the same content as plain text (fallback)
recipient's client picks the version it can display / prefers
```
So every email carries both, and you ensure the plain-text part is a *good*, complete representation of the email's content and purpose (with links as visible URLs, the key information present), not an empty or broken afterthought.

## Why plain-text fallback matters
Including a proper plain-text version matters for several concrete reasons that connect to the week's themes:
- **Deliverability (back to D3):** spam filters are *suspicious of HTML-only emails* (a common spammer pattern is HTML-only, often image-heavy, mail), and including a proper plain-text alternative is a *positive* signal that helps deliverability. An email with no plain-text part is more likely to be flagged; one with a good plain-text version looks more legitimate. So plain-text fallback is partly a deliverability practice.
- **Reach and robustness:** some recipients/clients prefer or only show plain text (certain email clients, accessibility tools, smartwatches, text-only contexts, users who disable HTML), and if your email has *no* plain-text version, those recipients see nothing useful (a blank or garbled message). The plain-text fallback ensures your message is readable *everywhere*, regardless of the client's HTML support, which is exactly the robustness that critical transactional email (a password reset must be readable!) requires.
- **Accessibility:** plain text is inherently accessible (screen readers, etc.), so a good plain-text version serves users with assistive technology and varied setups.
So plain-text fallback is a robustness-and-reach practice: it improves deliverability (a positive signal vs suspicious HTML-only), ensures your message is readable in *any* client or context (critical for important emails), and aids accessibility, for the small cost of also writing the content as plain text.

## The principle: robustness through graceful degradation
The broader lesson plain-text fallback teaches is **robustness through graceful degradation**, building your communication to *still work* when the rich version cannot be used, which is a recurring engineering principle. Just as a well-built website degrades gracefully (semantic HTML readable even if CSS fails, W1; a form that works even without JavaScript, W3), a well-built email degrades gracefully to plain text when HTML cannot be shown, so the *message gets through regardless of the recipient's environment*. This matters most for the *critical* emails (a password reset, an important notification) that *must* be readable, you cannot have a locked-out user fail to read their reset email because their client showed only the broken HTML, so the plain-text fallback guarantees the essential message and links are available no matter what. It is the email-specific application of the "make it work even when the ideal conditions aren't met" robustness that distinguishes professional, resilient systems from fragile ones that only work in the happy case. Including a thoughtful plain-text version (not a throwaway) embodies this: you ensure your communication reaches and serves *every* recipient, in *any* client, which is both robust and respectful (and, conveniently, also helps deliverability). Combined with the week's other practices, transactional/marketing separation, deliverability setup, good templates, consent and unsubscribe, plain-text fallback rounds out an email program that is reliable, compliant, well-designed, and robust, reaching the inbox and being readable for everyone. Graceful degradation to plain text is a small detail that reflects the larger discipline of building robust, inclusive systems.

## Where this fits
You understand plain-text fallback: sending email as both HTML and a proper plain-text version, which helps deliverability (vs suspicious HTML-only), ensures readability in any client or context (crucial for important emails), and aids accessibility, embodying robustness through graceful degradation. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship a complete email system.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a reliable email system
You assemble the week into a working email system for a real app, demonstrating email done right:
- **transactional email** for the messages users expect/need (welcome, password reset, receipts), through a deliverability-optimised provider, triggered reliably and asynchronously from server events.
- **deliverability** set up (SPF/DKIM/DMARC, reputable provider) and the transactional/marketing **separation** to protect it.
- good **templates** (cross-client-compatible) with meaningful **personalisation**, a working **unsubscribe** for any marketing email, and **plain-text fallbacks**.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Email system: transactional via provider, deliverability, templates, unsubscribe, plain-text"
git push
```

## The deliverable is email that actually arrives and works
What makes this project demonstrate real competence is that the email *actually reaches the inbox and serves the user*, which, as the week showed, is harder than just calling a send API. The strongest version is *deliverable* (authentication set up, transactional separated from marketing to protect reputation, so the critical emails actually arrive), *reliable* (triggered robustly from events, failures handled, so a password reset is not silently lost), *well-built* (cross-client-compatible templates that look right everywhere, personalised relevantly, with plain-text fallbacks for robustness), and *compliant/respectful* (consent-based, easy unsubscribe honoured). The proof is that the email *works end-to-end in reality*: a user requests a password reset and *actually receives a readable email with a working link in their inbox* (not spam, not broken in their client), which is the whole point and exactly what naive implementations get wrong (the email vanishes into spam, or renders broken, or is silently lost). Demonstrating that you understand email as *infrastructure that must reliably reach and serve users*, with the deliverability, reliability, compatibility, and compliance that requires, rather than just "I called sendEmail()", is the deliverable, and it is the competence that makes email a dependable part of a real product.

## What email established
Step back: you have learned email as the *infrastructure* it is, with the real subtlety that "why your inbox hates you" implies. You understand the fundamental transactional/marketing split (different systems, kept separate to protect deliverability and compliance), how to send transactional email reliably (provider-based, event-triggered, async, failure-handled), the hard problem of deliverability (authentication, reputation, engagement, hygiene, and that *sending is not delivering*), cross-client-compatible templates with respectful personalisation, the legal-ethical-deliverability necessity of consent and unsubscribe, and robustness via plain-text fallback. The throughline is that email *only works if it reliably reaches and serves the recipient*, which requires deliberate attention to deliverability, reliability, compatibility, and compliance, far more than the simple-sounding "send an email." This is real-product infrastructure (FORGE needs password resets, notifications, etc.), and getting it right is what makes the difference between email that works and email that mysteriously fails.

## Where this fits
You shipped a reliable email system that actually reaches the inbox and serves users, the real-product infrastructure of transactional and marketing email done right. Next week you handle another product capability: **file uploads, object storage, and CDNs**, how to store and serve files (images, documents, uploads) properly, because storing files is *not* the same as storing data, and doing it right (object storage, presigned uploads, CDNs, validation) is essential for any app that handles user files.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You send a password reset email with a token. The email contains a link to /reset-password?token=abc123. How do you implement this securely? Generate the token with crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex'). Hash it before storing in the database (use SHA-256, it does not need to be bcrypt because password reset tokens are long-lived and random, not user-chosen). Store the hash, the userId it belongs to, and an expiry (15 minutes from now). Send the raw token in the email link. When the user clicks the link, hash the token from the URL, look up the hash in the database, verify it has not expired, then allow the password reset and delete the token. The reason you store the hash: if your database is breached, the attacker cannot use the stored tokens to reset passwords.
