items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Testing is how you change code without fear
Here is the core idea, and the reason testing matters: **testing is how you change code without being afraid.** An untested codebase is one where *every* change might break something that worked before, and the only way to know is to manually click through every feature after every change, slow, unreliable, and increasingly impossible as the app grows. Tests make refactoring *possible* (change the code, run the tests, know instantly if you broke anything), make onboarding new developers faster (they can change code confidently, the tests catch mistakes), and, only half-jokingly, make you sleep better (you ship knowing the tests passed). This week you learn the types of tests, when to use each, and how to test the different layers of a web app, building the safety net that lets you move fast *and* not break things.

## Three types of tests: the testing pyramid
There are three main types of tests, differing in *scope*, *speed*, and *cost*, and understanding them is the foundation:
- **Unit tests:** verify a *single function in isolation*, mocking its dependencies. They run in *milliseconds* and are cheap to write. Use them for *pure business logic*: price calculations, data transformations, validation functions, the focused logic where you want to verify many cases fast. Their limit: a unit test *cannot* tell you the system works *end-to-end* (it tests one piece in isolation).
- **Integration tests:** verify that *multiple units work together*, your API route actually calling the database, your auth middleware protecting a route. They are slower (they exercise real interactions) but verify the *connections* between parts, which is where many real bugs live (the pieces work alone but not together).
- **End-to-end (E2E) tests:** verify the *whole system* from the user's perspective, driving a real browser through a real flow (sign up, add to cart, checkout). They are the slowest and most expensive, but they verify the app *actually works* as a user experiences it.
```text
        /\        E2E (few): whole-system, user flows, slow, expensive
       /  \       Integration (some): units working together (API+DB), medium
      /____\      Unit (many): single functions, fast, cheap
   the TESTING PYRAMID: many fast cheap unit tests, fewer slow expensive E2E
```

## Why the pyramid shape, and what testing buys you
The pyramid shape, *many* unit tests, *fewer* integration tests, *few* E2E tests, is the recommended balance, and understanding why frames the week. You want *many* unit tests because they are fast and cheap (run in milliseconds, so you run them constantly) and pinpoint failures precisely (a failing unit test points at the exact broken function), so they catch most logic bugs cheaply. You want *some* integration tests for the critical connections (does the API actually save to the database? does auth actually protect this route?), because unit tests miss integration bugs. You want *few* E2E tests, only for the *most critical* user flows (signup, checkout), because they are slow and expensive to write and run, and brittle, but they give the ultimate confidence that the whole thing works. Inverting the pyramid (lots of slow E2E tests, few unit tests) gives slow, brittle, expensive test suites that people stop running, exactly what you don't want. The payoff of getting this right is the fearless-change capability: a good test suite (well-balanced per the pyramid) runs fast enough to use constantly, catches regressions before they reach users, and gives you the confidence to refactor, add features, and ship quickly without manually re-verifying everything. Tests are not bureaucracy; they are the safety net that makes sustainable, fast development possible, the difference between a codebase you can confidently evolve and one you are afraid to touch.

## Where this fits
This opens the **Performance & DX phase** (W17-20): testing (this week), performance, CI/CD, and observability, the engineering practices that make an app reliable, fast, and maintainable. Testing comes first because it is the foundation of confident change, and CI (W19) runs these tests automatically. Today's orientation: testing lets you change code without fear; the three types (unit, integration, E2E) trade scope for speed/cost, balanced as a *pyramid* (many fast unit tests, few slow E2E), giving the safety net for fast, sustainable development. Tomorrow you go deeper on the testing pyramid and what to test at each level.

items.title: Testing pyramid
items.body:
## The testing pyramid: what to test at each level
Yesterday introduced the three test types; today you learn *what* to test at each level, which is the real skill, because testing the *right* things at the *right* level is what makes a test suite valuable rather than a burden. The guidance per level:
- **Unit tests, for pure logic:** test the *self-contained logic* that has clear inputs and outputs, price/total calculations, data transformations, formatting, validation rules, business rules. These are perfect for unit tests: fast, easy to test many cases (including edge cases), and they isolate the logic. *Don't* unit-test trivial code (a getter) or things that are really about integration.
- **Integration tests, for the connections:** test that *units work together correctly* across a boundary, your API endpoint actually reads/writes the database correctly, your auth middleware actually blocks unauthorised requests, a service correctly calls another. Focus on the *critical interactions* where real bugs hide (the API-to-database path, the auth checks).
- **E2E tests, for critical user journeys:** test the *handful of most important end-to-end flows* that *must* work, sign up and log in, the core feature, checkout/payment. These are the flows where a break is catastrophic, so they earn the expensive E2E coverage; don't E2E-test every minor path.

## Testing behaviour, not implementation
The single most important principle for *good* tests, which separates tests that help from tests that hinder, is **test behaviour, not implementation.** A good test verifies *what the code does* (its observable behaviour, its inputs and outputs, what the user sees) rather than *how* it does it internally (the specific functions it calls, its internal structure). Why this matters enormously:
- **Implementation-coupled tests break on refactoring:** if a test checks internal details (this function called that one), then *refactoring* the code (changing the internals while keeping the behaviour) breaks the test even though nothing actually broke, which defeats the whole purpose (tests should let you refactor freely, not punish it). Tests coupled to implementation are *brittle* and make refactoring painful, the opposite of what tests are for.
- **Behaviour-focused tests are robust and meaningful:** a test that checks *behaviour* (given this input, the function returns this output; when the user does this, they see that) keeps passing through any internal refactor that preserves behaviour, and *fails* only when behaviour actually changes, which is exactly when you want to know. Such tests are robust, meaningful (they test what actually matters, the behaviour), and they enable fearless refactoring.
So you write tests that assert *behaviour and outcomes*, not internal mechanics, at every level (a unit test checks a function's output for given inputs, not which helpers it called; an E2E test checks the user can complete the flow, not the internal steps). This principle, test what the code *does*, not *how*, is what makes a test suite a help (catching real behaviour regressions while permitting refactoring) rather than a hindrance (breaking on every internal change). It is the most important habit for writing tests that you'll actually keep and value.

## Test the right things: coverage that matters
The other key judgement is *what's worth testing*, because the goal is *valuable* coverage, not maximal coverage. You prioritise testing:
- **Critical paths and core logic:** the things that *must* work (the payment flow, the core feature, the security checks) and the *complex logic* most likely to have bugs (intricate calculations, edge-case-heavy validation). High-value, bug-prone, critical code earns thorough testing.
- **Things that have broken or are easy to break:** bug-prone areas, past bugs (a regression test so it doesn't recur), and tricky edge cases.
And you *don't* obsess over testing trivial code (simple getters, framework glue) or chase 100% coverage for its own sake, coverage *percentage* is a weak goal (you can have 100% coverage of meaningless tests, or 70% coverage of exactly the critical paths, the latter is far better). The mature view is that test *value* matters more than test *count* or *coverage percentage*: a focused suite that thoroughly tests the critical, complex, bug-prone parts (at the right pyramid level, testing behaviour) provides far more confidence per unit of effort than a sprawling suite of trivial or brittle tests. So you invest testing effort where it pays, the critical paths, the complex logic, the things that break, with behaviour-focused tests at the appropriate level, which gives you a *valuable, maintainable* safety net rather than a large, brittle, low-value one. Testing the right things, the right way, at the right level, is the skill that makes testing worthwhile.

## Where this fits
You understand what to test at each pyramid level (unit for pure logic, integration for critical connections, E2E for key user journeys), the crucial principle of *testing behaviour not implementation* (so tests are robust and enable refactoring), and prioritising *valuable* coverage (critical paths, complex/bug-prone logic) over coverage percentage. Tomorrow you learn to test UI components with Testing Library.

items.title: Test databases
items.body:
## Testing with a database: test databases
Integration tests (and some others) need to test code that *uses the database*, your API route that saves an order, your query logic, and you can't test these against your *real* (production or development) database without making a mess. The solution is a **test database**: a separate, disposable database used only for tests, where each test (or test run) starts from a known clean state, does its thing, and is cleaned up, so tests are *isolated* and *repeatable*:
```text
test setup:    spin up / connect to a TEST database (separate from dev/prod)
each test:     start from a known state -> run the code under test (real DB operations)
               -> assert -> clean up (reset) so the next test starts clean
```
This lets integration tests exercise *real* database operations (so they actually verify the database interaction works) while staying isolated (one test's data doesn't pollute another's) and repeatable (every run starts clean, same result).

## Why test databases, and the isolation challenge
Understanding *why* a dedicated, isolated test database is needed shows the core challenge of testing stateful code:
- **You must test real database behaviour:** for an integration test to be meaningful (does my API actually save correctly? does my query return the right rows?), it should run against a *real* database (or a close equivalent), not a fake, because the bugs you're catching are in the *actual* database interaction (a wrong query, a constraint violation, a transaction issue), which a mock wouldn't exercise. So you test against a real (test) database.
- **But tests must be isolated and repeatable:** the *challenge* with database tests is *state*, the database holds state that persists between tests, so without care, one test's data affects another (test order matters, tests interfere), and tests aren't repeatable (running twice gives different results because data accumulated). This *shared mutable state* is what makes testing stateful code hard, and it's why you need *isolation*: each test must start from a *known* state and not be affected by others. Techniques: reset the database (or use transactions that roll back) between tests, so each starts clean; use a separate test database so tests never touch dev/prod data; and ensure tests don't depend on each other's data.
- **Never test against production data:** obviously, you use a *separate* test database, never the real one, both to avoid corrupting real data and so tests can freely create/destroy data.
So a test database gives you *real* database testing (meaningful integration tests) with *isolation and repeatability* (each test independent and deterministic), by being separate, reset between tests, and disposable. Managing test state, ensuring each test starts clean and stays isolated, is the key skill for testing database-backed code, and it's a specific instance of the broader challenge of testing stateful systems.

## Approaches and the practical setup
Practically, there are a few approaches to test databases, and the judgement is to choose what gives real-enough testing with good isolation conveniently:
- **A real database instance for tests** (e.g. a Postgres in a Docker container spun up for the test run, often via tools like Testcontainers): tests run against actual Postgres, maximally realistic, with the test database reset between tests (truncate tables, or wrap each test in a transaction that rolls back, a clean way to isolate). This is the gold standard for integration tests, real database, well isolated.
- **An in-memory or lightweight database** (e.g. SQLite for tests): faster and simpler, but *less* realistic (different database than production, so some behaviours/bugs differ), so it trades fidelity for speed, acceptable for some logic but risky where production-Postgres-specific behaviour matters.
The recommended approach for meaningful integration tests is to test against a *real* database matching production (Postgres in a container), reset between tests for isolation, because it catches the *actual* database-interaction bugs while staying isolated and repeatable. You also keep these (slower) integration tests fewer than your (fast) unit tests, per the pyramid, the unit tests cover pure logic fast, the integration tests cover the critical database interactions thoroughly but in smaller number. Setting up a proper test database (separate, real-ish, isolated, reset between tests) is what makes your integration tests trustworthy and repeatable, so you can confidently verify that your database-backed code actually works, which is exactly the kind of integration bug (the API doesn't save correctly, the query is wrong) that unit tests miss and users would otherwise hit.

## Where this fits
You can test database-backed code with a test database: a separate, real-ish (e.g. Postgres in a container), isolated database that's reset between tests so integration tests exercise *real* database operations while staying isolated and repeatable, the key being managing test state for isolation. Tomorrow you handle full end-to-end testing with Playwright.

items.title: Mocks vs the real thing
items.body:
## Mocks vs the real thing: a key testing decision
A recurring decision in testing is whether to use a **mock** (a fake stand-in for a dependency) or the **real thing**, and getting this judgement right is central to writing good, trustworthy tests. A *mock* replaces a real dependency (a database, an external API, a service) with a controlled fake that returns predetermined responses:
```text
real:  test calls the actual dependency (real database, real Stripe API, real email service)
mock:  test uses a FAKE that you control (returns canned data, records calls)
```
The trade-off is fundamental: mocks make tests *faster, more isolated, and deterministic* (no real database/network, controlled responses, fast), but *less realistic* (you're testing against a fake, which might behave differently from the real thing); using the real dependency is *more realistic* (you test actual behaviour) but *slower, harder to set up, and less deterministic* (real systems are slow, have state, can fail). Choosing well, when to mock and when to use the real thing, is a key skill.

## When to mock, and when to use the real thing
The judgement follows from what each test *level* is trying to verify, which ties back to the pyramid:
- **Mock for unit tests (isolation):** unit tests verify *one function in isolation*, so you *mock its dependencies* (the database, external services) to isolate the logic under test, this is the *point* of a unit test (test this function's logic, not its dependencies), and mocking keeps it fast and focused. So unit tests mock freely.
- **Use the real thing for integration tests (that's the point):** integration tests verify that units *work together with real dependencies* (your API actually using the real database), so here you *want* the real (test) database, mocking it would defeat the purpose (you'd be testing against a fake, not verifying the real integration works). So integration tests use real dependencies (a test database, D4) for the things being integrated.
- **Mock *external, third-party* services even in integration/E2E (usually):** for dependencies *outside your control* (Stripe, an email provider, a third-party API), you usually *mock* them even in higher tests, because you can't (and shouldn't) hit the real Stripe/email service in every test run (slow, costs money, has side effects, unreliable), and Stripe's *test mode* (W13) or a mock provides controlled responses. So external services are typically mocked/stubbed (or use their sandbox), while *your own* dependencies (your database) are real in integration tests.
The principle: **mock what you're *not* testing and what's external/expensive/uncontrollable; use the real thing for what you *are* testing and what you control.** Unit tests mock dependencies (isolating the logic); integration tests use your real components (your database) to verify they work together but mock external third parties; E2E tests use the real app but may mock external services. This gives you the right *fidelity* at each level, fast isolated unit tests (mocked), realistic integration tests (real internals), and full E2E (real app), with external services controlled (mocked/sandboxed) throughout.

## Why over-mocking is a trap
The deeper lesson, and a common pitfall, is that **over-mocking makes tests pass while the real system fails**, which is the danger to avoid. If you mock *too much*, especially mocking the very things you should be testing, your tests verify that your code works *against your fakes*, not against reality, so they can all pass while the actual integration is broken (your mock of the database returns what you expect, but the real database query is wrong, and your test never catches it because it used the mock). This is a real and insidious problem: a test suite that's all green but doesn't actually verify the system works, because it mocked away the real behaviour. Over-mocking gives *false confidence*, the worst kind, because you *trust* the tests but they aren't testing reality. So the discipline is to mock *judiciously*: mock what genuinely should be mocked (external services, the dependencies of a unit under test) but use the *real thing* for what you're actually verifying (your database in integration tests, the full app in E2E), so that your tests verify *real* behaviour where it matters. The balance is the point: enough mocking for fast, isolated, deterministic tests where appropriate (units, external services), but real dependencies where realism matters (integration with your own database, E2E), so the suite is both *efficient* and *trustworthy* (it actually catches real failures). Getting the mocks-vs-real balance right per test level is what makes a test suite genuinely protective rather than falsely reassuring, and it's the judgement that distinguishes effective testing from green-but-meaningless test suites.

## Where this fits
You understand the mocks-vs-real decision: mock what you're not testing and what's external/expensive (dependencies of a unit, third-party services), use the real thing for what you *are* testing and control (your database in integration tests, the app in E2E), avoiding over-mocking that makes tests pass while reality fails. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship a tested codebase.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a tested codebase
You assemble the week into a real codebase with a well-balanced test suite, demonstrating testing done right:
- **unit tests** for the pure business logic (calculations, validation, transformations), fast and focused.
- **integration tests** for critical connections (API + real test database, auth protection), using real internal dependencies.
- a few **E2E tests** (Playwright) for the critical user journeys (auth, core flow, payment), robust and focused.
- all written to *test behaviour, not implementation*, with judicious mocking (external services mocked, your own components real where it matters).
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Test suite: balanced pyramid (unit/integration/E2E), behaviour-focused, judicious mocks"
git push
```

## The deliverable is confidence to change code
What makes this project demonstrate real competence is that the test suite delivers the thing testing is *for*: the *confidence to change code without fear*. The strongest version is a *well-balanced* suite (the pyramid: many fast unit tests, some integration tests, a few E2E tests) that tests the *right things* (critical paths, complex logic, the things that break) the *right way* (behaviour not implementation, judicious mocking), so it's *fast* (runs quickly enough to use constantly), *trustworthy* (it actually catches real regressions, not falsely green from over-mocking), and *maintainable* (behaviour-focused tests survive refactoring). The proof is the capability it provides: you can make a change, run the tests, and *know in seconds* whether you broke anything, which means you can refactor freely, add features confidently, and ship without manually re-verifying everything, exactly the fearless-change ability that the week opened with. Demonstrating that you can build a test suite that genuinely provides this confidence (balanced, valuable, robust, trustworthy), rather than a brittle or meaningless one, is the deliverable, and it's the foundation of sustainable development, which CI (W19) will run automatically on every change.

## What testing established
Step back: you have learned testing as the foundation of *confident, sustainable change*, not as a chore. You understand the three test types and the pyramid (many fast unit tests, some integration, few E2E) that balances confidence against cost, *what* to test at each level (pure logic, critical connections, key user journeys) and *what's worth testing* (critical/complex/bug-prone code, not coverage for its own sake), the crucial principle of *testing behaviour not implementation* (robust, refactor-enabling tests), how to test each layer (Testing Library for components the user's way, test databases for isolated integration tests, Playwright for E2E), and the mocks-vs-real judgement (mock the external and the not-under-test, use real for what you verify, avoid false-confidence over-mocking). The throughline is that *good tests let you change code without fear*, and achieving that requires testing the right things, the right way, at the right level, a real skill that makes the difference between a safety net and a burden. This is the foundation the rest of the Performance & DX phase builds on (CI runs these tests; confident change underlies everything).

## Where this fits
You shipped a balanced, behaviour-focused, trustworthy test suite that provides the confidence to change code without fear, the foundation of sustainable development. Next week you make the app *fast*: **performance, Web Vitals and bundle size**, measuring and optimising the load speed and responsiveness (Core Web Vitals: LCP, CLS, INP) that determine user experience and even search ranking, because performance *is* user experience, and a slow app loses users before they see the product.

weeks.title: Performance, Web Vitals and Bundle Size
weeks.context:
Performance is user experience. A page that takes 5 seconds to load loses users before they see the product. Core Web Vitals are Google's performance metrics and a ranking signal for search. The three that matter: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), how fast the main content appears; Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), how much the page jumps around while loading; Interaction to Next Paint (INP), how fast the page responds to user interactions.

LCP targets: under 2.5 seconds is good, 2.5-4.0 seconds needs improvement, over 4.0 seconds is poor. The LCP element is usually the hero image or the main heading. Optimise it by: preloading the LCP image (link rel="preload"), serving images in WebP or AVIF format, using a CDN so the image is served from an edge location close to the user, and using the Next.js Image component which does all of this.

Bundle size is the other major performance lever. Every kilobyte of JavaScript downloaded, parsed, and executed delays interactivity. Your users on slow connections pay for every unused import. Measure bundle size with next build (it shows route bundle sizes) and the next-bundle-analyzer package. Common problems: importing an entire utility library when you only need one function (import { format } from 'date-fns' is fine; import _ from 'lodash' pulls in 70KB), not code-splitting large components (dynamic imports load them lazily), shipping polyfills for browsers you do not support.

Server components in Next.js App Router are a performance win: they render on the server and ship zero JavaScript to the browser. Use server components for anything that does not require interactivity (fetching data, static content). Move interactivity down to leaf components that can be marked 'use client'. This "islands architecture" minimises client-side JavaScript.

Caching is the most impactful optimisation. Next.js caches at multiple levels: build-time static generation (fastest), route-level caching with revalidate, and request memoization. Understand which cache is active for each page and when it is invalidated. Database query caching: use Redis or a query-level cache for expensive queries that do not need to be real-time. HTTP caching: set Cache-Control headers correctly so browsers and CDNs cache static assets.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Performance is user experience
This week's premise is direct: **performance *is* user experience.** A page that takes 5 seconds to load *loses users before they even see the product*, people abandon slow pages, and a slow app feels broken no matter how good its features are. Beyond UX, performance is a *business* concern: it affects conversion, retention, and even *search ranking* (Google uses performance as a ranking signal). This week you learn to *measure* and *optimise* web performance, the **Core Web Vitals** (Google's standardised performance metrics), image and database and caching optimisations, and real-user monitoring, so your app is genuinely *fast* for real users, which is one of the most impactful things you can do for its success.

## Core Web Vitals: the metrics that matter
You optimise what you measure, and the standard, meaningful performance metrics are Google's **Core Web Vitals**, three metrics capturing the key aspects of perceived performance:
- **Largest Contentful Paint (LCP):** how fast the *main content* appears, the time until the largest element (usually the hero image or main heading) is rendered. It measures *loading speed*, how quickly the user sees the meaningful content. Target: *under 2.5s is good*, 2.5-4s needs work, over 4s is poor.
- **Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS):** how much the page *jumps around* while loading, the visual stability. A page where content shifts as things load (an image loads and pushes text down, you go to click and the button moves) is jarring and frustrating. It measures *visual stability*; you want minimal shifting.
- **Interaction to Next Paint (INP):** how fast the page *responds to user interactions*, the responsiveness, when the user clicks or types, how quickly does the page react. It measures *interactivity*; a sluggish page (clicks that lag) feels broken.
Together, LCP (does content appear fast?), CLS (is it visually stable?), and INP (does it respond fast?) capture the dimensions of performance users actually feel.

## Why measure with these specific metrics
Understanding *why* Core Web Vitals are the right metrics frames the whole week:
- **They measure *perceived*, user-centric performance:** rather than abstract numbers, these capture what users actually *experience*, how fast they see content (LCP), whether the page is annoyingly jumpy (CLS), and whether it responds to them (INP). They're designed around the *user's* perception of speed and smoothness, which is what matters (the perceived-performance theme from across the tracks).
- **They're standardised and actionable:** being a defined standard (with clear "good/needs-improvement/poor" thresholds), they give you concrete targets to hit and a common language, and each maps to *specific* optimisations (LCP -> optimise the main content's loading; CLS -> reserve space for elements; INP -> reduce blocking work), so measuring them tells you *what to fix*.
- **They have real consequences:** Google uses them as a *search ranking signal*, so poor Core Web Vitals can hurt your search visibility (a direct business impact), and they correlate with user behaviour (bounce, conversion), so improving them improves real outcomes.
So you measure performance with Core Web Vitals because they capture *user-perceived* performance in a *standardised, actionable* way with *real consequences*, making them the right target for optimisation. The discipline, as with all the track's performance and quality work, is *measure first* (know your Core Web Vitals) then *optimise* the specific problems they reveal, rather than guessing. This week is that loop: measure the Vitals, identify what's hurting them, apply the targeted optimisations, re-measure.

## Where this fits
This week is performance in the Performance & DX phase: measuring (Core Web Vitals) and optimising (images, database queries, caching) the speed that *is* user experience and affects ranking, with real-user monitoring to track it. It builds on image optimisation (W15) and connects to the perceived-performance themes throughout. Today's orientation: performance is UX (and business and ranking); you measure it with Core Web Vitals, LCP (loading), CLS (stability), INP (responsiveness), which capture user-perceived performance in a standardised, actionable way, then optimise what they reveal. Tomorrow you go deeper on the Vitals and how to improve each.

items.title: Core Web Vitals
items.body:
## Improving each Core Web Vital
Today you learn the *specific* optimisations for each Core Web Vital, because each maps to concrete fixes, which is what makes them actionable:
- **LCP (loading speed)** is dominated by how fast the *main content* (usually the hero image or heading) loads, so you improve it by speeding up that critical content: *preload* the LCP image (`<link rel="preload">` so it starts loading immediately), serve images in *modern formats* (WebP/AVIF, smaller, W15) and *optimised sizes*, serve from a *CDN* (close to the user, W15), use the framework's image handling (Next.js `<Image>`, FORGE's stack), and reduce anything blocking the content's render (render-blocking resources, slow server response). Get the main content to appear fast.
- **CLS (visual stability)** is caused by elements *shifting* as the page loads, so you fix it by *reserving space* for things before they load: set explicit *dimensions* on images and embeds (so their space is held and text doesn't jump when they load), reserve space for ads/dynamic content, avoid inserting content above existing content, and ensure fonts don't cause big shifts. Hold the layout stable so nothing jumps.
- **INP (responsiveness)** is hurt by the *main thread being blocked* (busy JavaScript) when the user interacts, so you improve it by reducing and breaking up heavy JavaScript work: minimise and split large JS bundles (less to parse/execute), avoid long-running tasks that block interaction (break them up, defer non-critical work), and keep the main thread free to respond to clicks/input quickly. Keep the page responsive to the user.

## The big lever: JavaScript and bundle size
A theme connecting INP (and load performance generally) is **bundle size**, the amount of JavaScript you ship, which is one of the biggest performance levers, and the week's title pairs it with Web Vitals for good reason. Every kilobyte of JavaScript must be *downloaded, parsed, and executed* by the user's device, and excessive JS hurts performance multiple ways: slower download (especially on mobile/slow networks), slower parse/execute (especially on low-end devices), and a blocked main thread (hurting INP and interactivity). So *reducing bundle size* is a high-impact optimisation:
- **Code splitting:** don't ship *all* your JavaScript up front, *split* it so each page/route loads only the JS it needs (and load the rest on demand). Frameworks (Next.js) do this automatically by route, and you can lazy-load heavy components. This means the initial load downloads/executes far less JS.
- **Avoid bloat:** be mindful of *dependencies* (a heavy library for a small task adds to every user's bundle, so choose lean libraries, or avoid the dependency), remove unused code, and analyse your bundle (tools show what's *in* it, often revealing a surprisingly large dependency you can trim or replace).
- **Ship less to the client:** the server-component model (Next.js, W6) helps here, components that render on the server ship *no* JS to the browser, so keeping interactivity to small client islands minimises the bundle. This is a concrete payoff of the server/client architecture.
So managing bundle size, code splitting, avoiding heavy dependencies, shipping less JS to the client (server components), is a central performance discipline, because JavaScript is expensive (download + parse + execute + main-thread blocking) and shipping less of it improves load speed *and* interactivity (INP). Watching and reducing your bundle is one of the most effective performance habits.

## Optimise from measurement, targeting the real problem
The overarching discipline, the same *measure-then-optimise* rigor from every performance lesson in the track, is to optimise *based on what you measure*, targeting the *actual* problem rather than guessing. You measure your Core Web Vitals (tools like Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights, and the browser devtools give you LCP, CLS, INP and *what's causing* them), *identify* which Vital is poor and *why* (Lighthouse will tell you: "your LCP is slow because of this large unoptimised image"; "CLS is high because this image has no dimensions"; "reduce JavaScript to improve INP"), and apply the *targeted* fix for *that* specific problem, then re-measure to confirm. This avoids the trap of random, untargeted optimisation (tweaking things that weren't the bottleneck) and focuses effort where it actually helps, exactly the disciplined approach (find the real bottleneck via measurement, fix that) that recurs in React performance, ML performance, and database indexing. Because the tools tell you *which* Vital is bad and *what's* causing it, performance optimisation becomes a clear loop: measure the Vitals, read what's hurting them, fix the specific causes (optimise the LCP image, set dimensions to fix CLS, cut JS to fix INP), re-measure. Following the metrics to the real problems, rather than guessing, is what makes performance work effective and efficient.

## Where this fits
You know how to improve each Core Web Vital, LCP (speed up the main content: preload, optimise images, CDN), CLS (reserve space, set dimensions), INP (reduce/split JavaScript, free the main thread), with bundle size (code splitting, lean dependencies, server components) as a major lever, all driven by *measuring* the Vitals and targeting the actual cause. Tomorrow you go deeper on images, often the biggest performance factor.

items.title: Image optimisation
items.body:
## Images: usually the biggest performance factor
Images deserve their own focus because they are typically the *largest* assets on a page and thus the biggest factor in load performance (and LCP especially), you covered the *how* in W15 (object storage, optimisation, CDN); here you focus on images *as a performance optimisation*. The core techniques, now framed around performance:
- **Serve the right size:** never serve an image larger than it's displayed (a 4000px image into a 400px slot wastes enormous bandwidth), use *responsive images* so each device gets an appropriately-sized version.
- **Modern formats:** WebP/AVIF are far smaller than JPEG/PNG at the same quality, so serving modern formats is a large, free saving.
- **Compress appropriately:** balance quality against size (often you can compress significantly with no visible difference).
- **Lazy-load below-the-fold images:** images *not* initially visible (further down the page) should load *only when needed* (as the user scrolls near them), so they don't slow the *initial* load, `loading="lazy"` (or the framework's handling) does this. Only the above-the-fold images load up front.
- **Prioritise the LCP image:** conversely, the *main* (LCP) image should load *fast* (preload, high priority), since it determines LCP.

## Why images dominate, and the lazy-loading insight
Understanding *why* images are so impactful, and the lazy-loading idea, deepens the performance picture:
- **Images are usually the bulk of page weight:** on most pages, images vastly outweigh the HTML, CSS, and even JavaScript in bytes, so unoptimised images are usually the *single biggest* cause of slow loads, which is why optimising them often improves performance more than anything else, and why LCP (often an image) is so image-dependent. A page heavy with large images will be slow no matter what else you do, so images are the first place to look for load-performance wins.
- **Lazy loading: only load what's needed now:** a key insight is that you don't need to load images the user *can't see yet*, the ones below the fold, far down the page, are not needing to load during the *initial* render, so *lazy loading* (deferring them until the user scrolls near) makes the initial load much lighter and faster (only the visible images load up front), while the rest load just-in-time as the user scrolls. This dramatically reduces initial load weight for image-heavy pages, since you're not downloading dozens of images the user may never scroll to. It's a "load only what's needed now" optimisation (the same principle as code splitting for JS), applied to images.
- **The LCP image is the exception, prioritise it:** while you lazy-load below-the-fold images, you do the *opposite* for the LCP image (the main, above-the-fold content image), you *prioritise* it (preload, high priority) so it appears *fast*, because it determines LCP. So the strategy is split: prioritise the critical (LCP) image, lazy-load the non-critical ones.
This combination, optimise all images (size, format, compression), prioritise the LCP image, lazy-load the rest, is what makes image-heavy pages fast: the initial view loads quickly (light, with the main image prioritised) and the rest streams in as needed.

## Automate it, and the framework helps
The practical guidance, consistent with W15, is to *automate* image performance rather than hand-optimising, and modern frameworks make this largely automatic. Tools and services (image CDNs, Next.js `<Image>` which FORGE uses) handle the optimisation (right size per device, modern format, compression), lazy loading (below-the-fold images deferred automatically), and even prioritisation (marking the LCP image) for you, so you get the performance wins without manually optimising every image. For example, Next.js's `<Image>` component automatically serves optimised, responsive, modern-format images, lazy-loads them by default, and lets you mark the priority (LCP) image, encoding the best practices. So the recommendation is to use the framework's/service's image handling, which automates the size/format/compression/lazy-load/priority optimisations, giving you fast images by default rather than requiring per-image manual work. This is the highest-leverage performance practice for most apps (since images dominate), and it's largely a matter of *using the right tools correctly* (the framework's image component, an image CDN) rather than heroic manual effort. Combined with the W15 storage/serving architecture and the framework's automation, you get images that are optimised, responsive, lazy-loaded, prioritised correctly, and CDN-served, which is most of what makes a page load fast. Getting images right is often the single biggest performance win available, and the tools make it achievable.

## Where this fits
You understand images as the biggest performance factor: optimise all (size, format, compression), prioritise the LCP image (preload), lazy-load the rest (load only what's visible now), largely automated by frameworks/image services (Next.js `<Image>`, image CDNs), which is the highest-leverage load-performance practice since images dominate page weight. Tomorrow you optimise the backend side: database query performance.

items.title: Database query optimisation
items.body:
## Backend performance: database query optimisation
Performance isn't only frontend, a slow *server* response (often a slow *database query*) delays everything (it directly hurts LCP, since the content can't render until the server responds), so **database query optimisation** is a key backend performance concern. The most common backend performance problems are slow or excessive database queries:
- **Missing indexes (W10):** a query filtering/sorting on an unindexed column does a *full table scan*, slow on large tables, and adding the right *index* makes it fast. The single most common database performance fix is adding a missing index on a frequently-queried column (revisit W10's indexing, now as performance work).
- **The N+1 query problem:** the classic ORM performance trap, fetching a list and then making a *separate* query for each item's related data (1 query for the list + N queries for the items = N+1 queries), turning one logical operation into hundreds of database round-trips. The fix is to fetch the related data *together* (a join, or Prisma's `include`), turning N+1 queries into 1 or 2. This is a *very* common, often-invisible cause of slow pages.
- **Fetching too much:** selecting all columns/rows when you need few, transfer and process only what you need (select specific fields, paginate, W11).

## Why database queries are a common, hidden bottleneck
Understanding *why* database performance is so often the culprit, and so easy to get wrong, shows its importance:
- **It directly gates the whole response:** the page (or API response) often can't be produced until the database returns the data, so a slow query directly slows the user's whole experience (a 2-second query means at least a 2-second wait), making database performance a frequent root cause of slow apps. Frontend optimisations can't help if the server is waiting on a slow query.
- **The problems are often invisible until scale:** the N+1 problem and missing indexes frequently *don't show* in development (with little data, even a full scan or N+1 queries are fast), then become severe in *production* with real data volume, exactly the "works locally, slow at scale" trap (the same as W11's pagination, W10's indexes). So these issues lurk until real data exposes them, which is why understanding them *in advance* (and measuring) matters.
- **ORMs make N+1 easy to cause accidentally:** the convenience of an ORM (Prisma) can *hide* that accessing related data in a loop triggers a query each time, so the N+1 problem is *easy to write without realising*, which is why you must be deliberate about fetching related data together (`include`). The abstraction's convenience can mask the performance cost, the "understand the layer beneath the ORM" lesson from W10.
So database query optimisation, adding indexes, eliminating N+1 queries (fetch related data together), fetching only what's needed, is a high-impact, often-overlooked performance area, because slow queries directly gate the user's experience and the problems often hide until production scale. Backend performance is as important as frontend; a beautifully-optimised frontend still feels slow if the server takes 2 seconds to respond because of a missing index or an N+1 query.

## Find and fix queries by measuring
The discipline, again, is *measure to find the slow queries, then fix the specific ones*, not guess, the same measure-then-optimise loop. You find slow queries by measuring: the database's *query analysis* (`EXPLAIN` shows whether a query uses an index or does a full scan, W10), *slow-query logs* (the database logs queries taking too long), and *APM/observability* tools (W20) that show which queries/endpoints are slow in production. These tell you *which* queries are the bottleneck and *why* (full scan -> add an index; many similar queries -> N+1, fetch together; large result -> select less), so you apply the *targeted* fix to the *actual* slow query rather than optimising blindly. This is the backend version of following the metrics to the real problem: measure to identify the specific slow query, diagnose its cause (missing index, N+1, over-fetching), apply the matching fix, and re-measure. Often a single fix (one index, one `include` to kill an N+1) dramatically speeds up a page, which is why database optimisation is so high-leverage, the bottleneck is frequently one slow query, and fixing it transforms the response time. Combined with the frontend optimisations, eliminating backend (database) bottlenecks ensures the *whole* path, from request through the server and database to the rendered page, is fast, which is what real performance requires. A fast frontend on a slow backend is still a slow app, so optimising the database queries (found by measurement, fixed specifically) is an essential half of the performance picture.

## Where this fits
You understand database query optimisation: adding indexes (avoid full scans), eliminating the N+1 problem (fetch related data together), and not over-fetching, found by measuring (EXPLAIN, slow-query logs, APM) and fixed specifically, because slow queries directly gate the response and the problems hide until production scale. Tomorrow you handle caching API responses to avoid repeated work.

items.title: API response caching
items.body:
## API response caching: don't recompute what hasn't changed
A powerful performance technique is **caching**: storing the result of expensive work (a database query, an API response, a computation) so that *repeated* requests for the *same* thing return the cached result instantly instead of recomputing it. If many users request the same data (the menu, a popular product, a dashboard), computing it fresh every time is wasteful, caching computes it *once* and serves the stored result to subsequent requests:
```text
without caching:  every request -> run the (expensive) query/computation -> respond (slow, repeated work)
with caching:     first request -> compute -> STORE result
                  subsequent requests -> return STORED result instantly (no recompute)
```
Caching can happen at many layers: in-memory or Redis caching of query/computation results on the server, HTTP caching (cache headers, CDN caching of responses), and framework-level caching (Next.js caches, FORGE's stack). The idea is the same, avoid redoing work whose result you already have.

## Why caching is powerful, and the layers
Understanding caching's power and where it applies shows why it's a key performance tool:
- **It eliminates repeated expensive work:** for data that's *requested repeatedly* and *doesn't change every request* (the menu, popular content, reference data), caching turns N expensive computations into *one* (compute once, serve from cache N-1 times), a massive saving in both *response time* (cache hits are instant) and *server/database load* (far fewer expensive operations). For read-heavy data, caching is one of the highest-impact optimisations.
- **Multiple layers, each valuable:** caching applies at several levels, each helping: *server-side* (cache query results in memory/Redis so the database isn't hit repeatedly for the same data), *HTTP/CDN* (cache responses at the CDN edge so requests don't even reach your server, the same edge-caching idea as files in W15, applied to API/page responses), and *framework* (Next.js's data/route caching). Combining them, fast responses served from cache, often from the edge, near the user, gives excellent performance for cacheable content.
- **It reduces load and cost:** beyond speed, caching reduces work on your server and database (fewer queries) and can reduce cost (less compute, and with CDN caching, less origin traffic), so it helps performance *and* scalability *and* cost together.
So caching is a high-leverage technique for *read-heavy, repeatable* requests: compute once, serve many times from the cache, dramatically improving response time and reducing load, applied at the server, HTTP/CDN, and framework layers.

## The hard part: cache invalidation and what to cache
The famous catch, "there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things", is real: the difficulty of caching is **invalidation**, knowing *when* the cached data is *stale* and must be refreshed, because serving *outdated* data is the risk caching introduces. If you cache the menu and then the menu changes, the cache must be *invalidated* (cleared/refreshed) or users see the old menu, so the challenge is keeping the cache *fresh enough* while still getting the caching benefit. This is the same *freshness-vs-staleness* trade-off from TanStack Query's stale time (W8), now on the server: you balance *how long* to cache (longer = more cache hits, better performance, but more staleness risk) against *how fresh* the data needs to be, and you *invalidate* the cache when the underlying data changes (e.g. clear the menu cache when the menu is updated). The judgement is *what* to cache and *for how long*, based on the data: cache data that's *read often* and *changes rarely* (reference data, popular content) for longer (big win, low staleness risk), cache rapidly-changing or critical-freshness data briefly or not at all (the staleness risk outweighs the benefit), and *invalidate* on change where you can. So caching is powerful but requires care: you cache the *right* things (read-heavy, change-tolerant) for the *right* duration, and *invalidate* appropriately, to get the performance benefit *without* serving unacceptably stale data. Getting invalidation right (or choosing appropriate cache durations) is what makes caching safe and effective rather than a source of stale-data bugs. Used judiciously, with attention to freshness, caching is one of the most effective ways to make read-heavy apps fast and scalable.

## Where this fits
You understand API response caching: storing expensive results to serve repeated requests instantly (at server, HTTP/CDN, and framework layers), a high-leverage win for read-heavy data, with the key challenge of *invalidation* (the freshness-vs-staleness trade-off, the same as W8's stale time), cache read-often/change-rarely data for appropriate durations and invalidate on change. Tomorrow you handle measuring performance for *real* users: real-user monitoring.

items.title: Real-user monitoring
items.body:
## Real-user monitoring: performance for actual users
You can measure performance in a *lab* (Lighthouse on your machine), but that doesn't capture how the app performs for *real users* on *their* devices and networks, which vary enormously (a fast laptop on fibre vs an old phone on slow mobile data). **Real-user monitoring (RUM)** measures performance *as real users experience it*, collecting actual Core Web Vitals (and other metrics) from real visitors' browsers in production:
```text
lab testing (Lighthouse):   YOUR device/network -> one synthetic measurement
real-user monitoring (RUM): MANY real users' actual devices/networks -> real-world distribution
                            of LCP, CLS, INP as users actually experience them
```
RUM tools (Vercel Analytics, Google's CrUX, and others) gather Web Vitals from your real users, so you see the *actual* performance distribution across your real audience, not just a synthetic lab number.

## Why real-user data matters beyond lab testing
Understanding *why* you need RUM in addition to lab testing shows the gap it fills:
- **Real conditions vary hugely, and lab testing misses that:** your lab test (on a good device and network) might show great performance, while a chunk of your real users (on older phones, slower networks, different geographies) experience it as *slow*, a reality the lab test entirely misses. RUM reveals the *real distribution* (some users fast, some slow), so you see how performance actually is for your *whole* audience, including the slower-experiencing portion that lab testing hides. The lab gives one optimistic data point; RUM gives the real picture.
- **It catches real-world problems:** performance issues that only appear under real conditions (a slow third-party script in production, a regional CDN problem, poor performance on the devices your users actually have) show up in RUM but not in your lab test. RUM is the "verify the real-world outcome, don't assume" discipline (recurring across the tracks) applied to performance, measure how it *actually* performs for real users, not how it performs for you.
- **It tracks performance over time and catches regressions:** RUM continuously monitors production performance, so you see *trends* (is it getting slower?) and catch *regressions* (a deploy made LCP worse for real users), turning performance into something you *monitor and maintain*, not just optimise once. A change that degrades real-user performance shows up in RUM, so you can catch and fix it.
So RUM complements lab testing: lab testing (Lighthouse) is for *developing and debugging* performance (controlled, repeatable, before deploy), while RUM is for knowing the *actual* performance for *real* users in production (the real distribution, real-world issues, regressions over time). You need both, lab to optimise and verify before shipping, RUM to confirm and monitor the real-world result, because *real users on real devices* are the ground truth that a lab test only approximates.

## Performance as an ongoing, monitored discipline
The deeper lesson RUM teaches is that **performance is not a one-time optimisation but an ongoing, monitored discipline**, the same "it's not done at launch, you monitor and maintain it" theme from the ML/AI observability and drift lessons, now for web performance. Performance can *regress* over time (a new feature adds a heavy dependency, an unoptimised image slips in, a query gets slower as data grows), and without monitoring, this degradation is *invisible* until users complain, exactly the silent-degradation pattern. So you treat performance like any production property you care about: *monitor* it continuously (RUM tracking real-user Web Vitals), set *targets* (the Core Web Vitals thresholds), *alert* or watch for *regressions* (a deploy that worsens real-user LCP), and *maintain* it (keep it within targets as the app evolves). This makes performance a *sustained* quality, not a one-off effort that erodes, you optimise it, then *keep it optimised* by monitoring real users and catching regressions. It also connects to the next week's observability theme (production monitoring generally): real-user performance monitoring is part of *seeing how your app actually behaves in production*, and acting on it. The mature stance is that performance, like reliability and correctness, is something you *measure in production and maintain over time*, because it degrades if unwatched, and RUM is the tool that makes real-user performance visible so you can keep your app fast for the people who actually use it, continuously, not just at launch. Combining lab optimisation (before deploy) with real-user monitoring (in production, ongoing) is what keeps an app genuinely fast for real users over its life.

## Where this fits
You understand real-user monitoring: measuring Core Web Vitals from *real users'* actual devices and networks in production (the real distribution, not a lab approximation), which catches real-world performance problems and regressions that lab testing misses, making performance an *ongoing, monitored discipline* you maintain over time rather than a one-time fix. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship a fast app.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a fast app
You assemble the week into a genuinely fast app, measured and optimised across the stack, demonstrating performance done right:
- good **Core Web Vitals** (LCP, CLS, INP within targets), measured (Lighthouse) and optimised with targeted fixes.
- **optimised images** (right size, modern format, LCP prioritised, rest lazy-loaded) and a managed **bundle size** (code splitting, lean dependencies, server components).
- **fast backend** (indexed queries, no N+1) and **caching** for read-heavy data (with sensible invalidation).
- **real-user monitoring** tracking actual performance in production.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Performance: Core Web Vitals optimised across the stack, RUM in production"
git push
```

## The deliverable is measured, real-world speed
What makes this project demonstrate real competence is *measured, real-world* performance, not just "it feels fast on my machine." The strongest version shows the *measure-optimise-verify* loop applied: you measured the Core Web Vitals, identified the specific problems (a slow LCP image, a layout shift, an N+1 query, a heavy bundle), applied the *targeted* fixes (optimise that image, reserve that space, fix that query, split that bundle), and *verified* the improvement, with *real-user monitoring* confirming it's fast for actual users (not just in your lab). The proof is the *numbers*: good Core Web Vitals (LCP under 2.5s, low CLS, responsive INP) confirmed by both lab tools and real-user data, achieved through targeted optimisations across the whole stack (frontend rendering, images, bundle, backend queries, caching). Demonstrating that you can *measure* performance properly (Core Web Vitals, lab and real-user), *diagnose* the real bottlenecks, *fix* them with targeted optimisations across frontend and backend, and *maintain* it with monitoring, rather than guessing or only checking on your own fast machine, is the deliverable, and it's the competence that makes an app genuinely fast for real users, which directly affects whether they stay, convert, and find it (ranking).

## What performance established
Step back: you have learned to make apps *genuinely fast for real users*, which is core UX and a business/ranking factor. You understand performance *is* user experience (slow loses users), how to *measure* it with Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP, user-perceived, standardised, actionable), the targeted optimisations for each (LCP via image/content speed, CLS via reserved space, INP via reduced JavaScript), the big levers (images, the usual biggest factor, and bundle size), backend performance (indexes, N+1, the often-hidden bottleneck), caching (compute once, serve many, with invalidation), and real-user monitoring (the real-world ground truth, performance as an ongoing monitored discipline). The throughline is the *measure-then-optimise* rigor (follow the metrics to the real bottlenecks, fix specifically, verify) and the recognition that performance is a *maintained* property monitored in production, not a one-time effort. This is one of the highest-impact areas for an app's success, and it spans the whole stack (frontend, images, bundle, backend, caching), making it a comprehensive engineering skill.

## Where this fits
You shipped a measurably fast app, optimised across the stack with good Core Web Vitals confirmed by real-user monitoring, the performance that is user experience. Next week you automate getting changes safely to production: **CI/CD and deploy, shipping on every merge**, the pipeline that runs your tests and deploys your code automatically on every change, so changes go from your editor to users in minutes, with confidence, no manual steps, the practice that makes fast, safe, frequent shipping possible.

weeks.title: CI/CD and Deploy, Shipping on Every Merge
weeks.context:
Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) is the practice of automatically running tests and deploying code on every change. The goal: changes go from your editor to users in production with confidence, in minutes, without manual steps. This week you set up the pipeline that will govern every future change to Bean Forge.

CI (Continuous Integration): every push to the repository triggers an automated pipeline that installs dependencies, runs linting, runs the type checker, runs the test suite, and builds the application. If any of these fail, the pipeline fails and the change is blocked from merging. The point is that you find out within 5 minutes of pushing whether your change is broken, not 2 days later when someone complains.

CD (Continuous Deployment): after CI passes on the main branch, the pipeline automatically deploys to production. For staging environments, deploy on every merge to main. For production, some teams add a manual approval step. With Vercel or Railway, deployment is a single command or a git push, these platforms handle building and serving.

GitHub Actions is the standard CI system for GitHub repositories. A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/ that defines jobs (groups of steps) triggered by events (push, pull_request, schedule). Each job runs on a fresh virtual machine (runner). Steps are shell commands or pre-built actions from the Actions Marketplace.

Environments and secrets: production credentials (DATABASE_URL, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, etc.) must not be in your code. GitHub Actions provides encrypted secrets that you set in the repository settings and reference in workflows as ${{ secrets.SECRET_NAME }}. Set up separate secrets for staging and production environments.

Preview deployments: Vercel and Railway can deploy every pull request to a unique preview URL. This means stakeholders can review changes on a live URL before they merge to main. Each preview has its own environment variables (connected to the staging database, not production).

## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **Hosting**, **Vercel Hobby** is free with no card; Netlify's free tier and GitHub Pages also work.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Shipping on every merge, automatically
This week you build the **CI/CD pipeline**, the automation that runs your tests and deploys your code *automatically on every change*. **Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment** is the practice that makes shipping fast and safe: the goal is that changes go *from your editor to users in production with confidence, in minutes, without manual steps*. You set up the pipeline that will govern every future change to Bean Forge (and any real app), so that committing and pushing a change automatically triggers tests, checks, and deployment, no manual test-running, no manual deploy steps, no "did I remember to run the tests?" The result is the ability to ship changes frequently and confidently, which is how modern software actually ships.

## CI: catch problems automatically, within minutes
**Continuous Integration (CI)** is the first half: *every push triggers an automated pipeline* that validates the change. The pipeline installs dependencies, runs linting (code-style checks), runs the type checker, runs the *test suite* (your W17 tests), and builds the application, and *if any of these fail, the pipeline fails and the change is blocked from merging*:
```text
push to repo  ->  CI pipeline runs automatically:
   install deps -> lint -> type-check -> run tests -> build
   ALL pass  -> the change is OK to merge
   ANY fail  -> pipeline FAILS -> change BLOCKED from merging
```
The crucial value: you find out **within ~5 minutes of pushing** whether your change is broken, *not* two days later when a user complains. CI automatically runs all your checks on every change, so a broken change (failing test, type error, build failure) is caught *immediately*, before it merges, before it reaches anyone, which is exactly what makes the W17 test suite *protective* (the tests run automatically on every change, not just when you remember).

## Why automation here is transformative
Understanding *why* CI/CD matters so much frames the week, it's about *velocity with confidence*:
- **Fast feedback catches problems early:** CI tells you in minutes if you broke something, when it's cheap and easy to fix (you just made the change, it's fresh in mind), rather than days later in production (expensive, hard to trace). Catching problems at push time, automatically, is far better than catching them in production from user reports.
- **Automation removes manual error and toil:** without CI/CD, shipping involves manual steps (remember to run tests, manually deploy) that are slow, tedious, and *error-prone* (you forget to run the tests, you deploy the wrong thing, you skip a step). Automating these means they happen *reliably and consistently* every time, with no human forgetting or mistake. The pipeline does it the same way, every time.
- **It enables frequent, confident shipping:** because every change is automatically tested and (if it passes) deployed, you can ship *frequently* (many small changes) *confidently* (the pipeline caught any breakage), which is far better than infrequent, risky, manual "big bang" deploys. Small, frequent, automated, tested deploys are safer and faster than large, rare, manual ones.
So CI/CD transforms shipping from a slow, manual, risky event into a fast, automated, confident routine, you push, the pipeline tests and deploys, and your change reaches users in minutes if it's good (or is blocked if it's broken). This *velocity with safety* (the same theme as MLOps CI/CD, W21 of ML-eng) is what lets a team (or you) ship continuously and reliably, which is the modern standard and a huge productivity and quality win.

## Where this fits
This week is CI/CD in the Performance & DX phase: automating tests and deployment on every change so shipping is fast, safe, and frequent. It builds directly on testing (W17, the tests CI runs) and is the pipeline every future change flows through. Today's orientation: CI/CD automates testing and deployment on every push, giving fast feedback (find breakage in minutes, not days), removing manual toil and error, and enabling frequent confident shipping, velocity with safety. Tomorrow you clarify the terms: CI vs CD vs CD.

## CI vs CD vs CD: clarifying the pipeline
The terms are confusingly overloaded (CD means two different things), so today you clarify the stages of the pipeline, which helps you understand and design it:
- **CI (Continuous Integration):** *automatically test and validate every change.* Every push runs the checks (lint, type-check, tests, build), and breakage is caught and blocks merging. CI is about *integrating* changes safely, keeping the main branch always in a working, tested state.
- **CD (Continuous *Delivery*):** *automatically prepare every passing change for release.* After CI passes, the change is automatically built and made *ready to deploy* (deployable artifact prepared, perhaps deployed to staging), but the final deploy to *production* may require a *manual approval* (a human clicks "deploy"). So delivery automates *up to* production, with a human gate for the production release.
- **CD (Continuous *Deployment*):** *automatically deploy every passing change to production*, no manual gate. After CI passes, the change is deployed to production *automatically*. This is the fullest automation: push -> test -> deploy to users, all automatic.
```text
CI:                    push -> lint/type/test/build (catch breakage, block bad merges)
CD (Delivery):         CI passes -> auto-prepare for release -> MANUAL approval -> production
CD (Deployment):       CI passes -> AUTO deploy to production (no manual gate)
```

## Understanding the distinction, and choosing
The distinction between Continuous *Delivery* and *Deployment* (the two CDs) is the one worth understanding, because it's a real choice about *how much* to automate:
- **Continuous Delivery (manual production gate):** every change is *always ready* to deploy (automatically built, tested, prepared), but a *human* decides *when* to actually release to production. This gives automation's benefits (always-deployable, tested changes) while keeping a *human checkpoint* before production, useful when you want a person to approve production releases (e.g. timing, a final review, regulatory needs). The change is one click from production, but a human makes that click.
- **Continuous Deployment (fully automatic to production):** every passing change goes to production *automatically*, no human gate, maximum velocity (changes reach users the moment they pass CI). This requires *high confidence* in your automated checks (since nothing human stops a bad change except the tests), so it demands a strong test suite and safety practices (feature flags, easy rollback, monitoring), but it gives the fastest, most automated shipping.
The choice between them is about *confidence and control*: full Continuous Deployment (auto to production) maximises velocity but requires strong automated safety (good tests, rollback, monitoring) since there's no human gate; Continuous Delivery (manual production approval) keeps a human checkpoint, trading a little velocity for control. Many teams start with Delivery (auto everything, manual production click) and move to full Deployment as their confidence (test coverage, monitoring, rollback) grows. You choose based on how much you trust your automated checks and how much control you want over production releases.

## CI is non-negotiable; the CD level is a choice
The key practical takeaways: **CI is essential and non-negotiable** for any real project (automatically testing every change to catch breakage and keep the main branch working is foundational, the safety the tests provide only works if they run automatically on every change), while the *level of CD* (Delivery with a manual gate, or full Deployment) is a *deliberate choice* based on your confidence and needs. Always have CI (automated checks on every push, blocking broken changes). Then decide your deployment automation: at minimum, automate the *delivery* (every passing change is built and ready, deployed to staging, one approval from production), and adopt full *Continuous Deployment* (auto to production) when you have the confidence (strong tests, monitoring, easy rollback) to ship without a human gate. The progression, CI always, then automated delivery, then full automated deployment as confidence grows, is a sensible path, and understanding the distinct stages (integrate/test, deliver/prepare, deploy) lets you build the pipeline deliberately at the automation level that fits your project's maturity and risk tolerance. The deeper point is that these are *stages of increasing automation* toward the goal of "change to production fast and safely," and you adopt as much automation as your confidence supports, with CI as the always-present foundation. Clarifying these terms and stages is what lets you design and discuss your pipeline precisely.

## Where this fits
You can distinguish CI (auto-test every change, non-negotiable), Continuous *Delivery* (auto-prepare, manual production gate), and Continuous *Deployment* (auto to production, needs strong safety), understanding the choice between the two CDs is about confidence and control, with CI always present and the CD level chosen deliberately. Tomorrow you handle a powerful CI/CD feature: preview deploys.

items.title: Preview deploys
items.body:
## Preview deploys: see every change live before merging
A powerful CI/CD feature, especially valuable for confidence, is the **preview deploy**: for *every* pull request (proposed change), the pipeline automatically deploys a *live, isolated version* of the app *with that change*, at a unique URL, so you can *see and test the change running* before merging it:
```text
open a pull request  ->  CI/CD automatically deploys a PREVIEW of the app WITH that change
                         at a unique URL (e.g. pr-123.preview.beanforge.com)
                         -> review/test the change LIVE before merging
```
So before a change is merged (let alone reaches production), there's a *real, running* version of the app *with that change* that you (or reviewers, or stakeholders) can actually *use* and verify, not just read the code diff, but interact with the actual running result. Platforms like Vercel (FORGE's, and Next.js's, home), Netlify, and others provide preview deploys automatically per pull request.

## Why preview deploys are so valuable
Understanding *why* preview deploys matter shows their unique value for confident shipping:
- **See the real result, not just the code:** reading a code diff tells you what *changed* in the code, but a preview deploy lets you *see and test the actual running result* of the change, the real UI, the real behaviour, which catches things the diff doesn't reveal (it looks wrong, it breaks an interaction, it doesn't work as intended). Reviewing the *running* change is far more revealing than reviewing the code alone, exactly the "verify the real behaviour, don't just read the code" discipline, now built into the workflow per change.
- **Isolated and safe:** each preview is a *separate, isolated* deployment (its own URL, not affecting production or other changes), so you can freely test the change without any risk to production or interference from other in-progress changes. You test *this* change in isolation, as it would actually run.
- **Enables real review and collaboration:** because there's a live URL, *anyone* (reviewers, designers, product people, stakeholders) can *try* the change before it ships, providing feedback on the actual experience, not the code. This makes review richer (catch UX/behaviour issues), enables non-technical stakeholders to weigh in (they can *use* it), and builds confidence (everyone's seen it work) before merging. It turns review from "read the diff" into "try the actual change."
So preview deploys give you a *live, isolated, per-change* version of the app to *verify the real result before merging*, which dramatically improves confidence (you've *seen* the change work, not just read it), enables better review (test the running change, involve stakeholders), and catches real-world issues (behaviour, UX, integration) that code review alone misses. It's one of the most valuable CI/CD features for shipping with confidence.

## Preview deploys and the review workflow
The deeper value is how preview deploys fit into a *high-confidence review-and-merge workflow*, which is the modern standard for shipping changes safely. The flow becomes: open a pull request -> CI automatically *tests* the change (W17 tests, lint, types, build) *and* deploys a *preview* -> reviewers read the code *and* test the live preview -> if the tests pass *and* the change works in the preview *and* the code is approved, *merge* -> and (with CD) the change deploys to production. This combines *automated checking* (CI tests catch breakage) with *human review of the real result* (preview deploy lets people verify the actual running change), giving a robust gate before anything reaches production: a change must pass the automated tests *and* be verified working in a real preview *and* be reviewed, before it ships. This is far stronger than either alone (tests catch logic breakage; preview catches "it works but looks/behaves wrong"; review catches code-quality issues), and it's exactly the workflow that lets teams ship frequently *and* confidently, every change is automatically tested, live-previewable, and reviewed before merge. Preview deploys are the piece that adds "verify the real running change" to the automated pipeline, which is invaluable because, as the whole track has stressed, the *real* behaviour can differ from what the code suggests, and *seeing it run* (in an isolated preview, per change) catches what reading doesn't. Adopting preview deploys (which the platforms provide automatically) is a high-leverage way to make your shipping process more confident and your reviews more meaningful, by ensuring every change is verified *running* before it merges.

## Where this fits
You understand preview deploys: an automatic live, isolated deployment of *every* pull request at a unique URL, so you can *see and test the actual running change* before merging, which improves confidence (verify the real result, not just the code), enables richer review (test the running change, involve stakeholders), and fits a robust test-preview-review-merge workflow. Tomorrow you handle *where* to deploy: platforms like Fly.io, Render, Railway.
