items.title: Fly.io / Render / Railway
items.body:
## Deployment platforms: Fly.io, Render, Railway
Your app has to run *somewhere*, and **platform-as-a-service (PaaS)** providers, **Fly.io, Render, Railway** (and Vercel for Next.js, FORGE's), make deploying *easy*: you connect your repository, and they build and run your app, handling the servers, scaling, and infrastructure, so you deploy with minimal ops work. These platforms are the sweet spot for most apps:
```text
connect your repo -> the platform builds and runs your app
   handles: servers, the build, scaling, HTTPS, environment, restarts, logs
   you focus on: your app (not managing servers)
```
They integrate with the CI/CD flow (push to deploy, preview deploys per PR), provide the persistent-server hosting that things like WebSockets need (W16), manage environment variables, and scale your app, all with far less complexity than raw cloud infrastructure (W20's AWS/GCP/Azure). For most apps, a PaaS like these is the right deployment choice.

## Why PaaS is the right default for most apps
Understanding *why* these platforms are the sensible default frames the deployment choice:
- **They handle the ops so you don't have to:** deploying and running an app involves a lot of infrastructure work (provisioning servers, building, configuring HTTPS, scaling, restarts on crash, logging), and a PaaS *handles all of it*, so you deploy by connecting a repo and pushing, without becoming an infrastructure engineer. This is enormous leverage, you get production hosting without the ops burden.
- **They fit the CI/CD workflow:** these platforms integrate naturally with the git-based, push-to-deploy, preview-per-PR workflow (Vercel and Netlify especially, but Railway/Render/Fly too), so they slot into the CI/CD pipeline you're building, push triggers build and deploy, PRs get previews.
- **They suit modern app types:** Vercel is ideal for Next.js (FORGE's stack); Railway and Render are great for full apps (frontend + backend + database); Fly.io gives more control and is cheaper at modest scale and good for persistent connections (W16's real-time). Each fits common app shapes well, with little ops overhead.
- **They scale (to a point) automatically:** they handle scaling your app for typical loads, so you don't manage scaling manually until you're at significant scale.
So a PaaS is the right default for most apps because it gives you easy, integrated, production-grade hosting (handling the ops, fitting CI/CD, suiting modern app types, scaling automatically) with minimal complexity, letting you focus on your app rather than infrastructure. This is the same "use the platform, lean on managed infrastructure" judgement from across the deployment work (the Netlify deploys in W1, the process-management leaning-on-platforms in W9), now for full-stack apps.

## Choosing a platform, and when to go further
The judgement of *which* platform (and *when* a PaaS isn't enough) is the practical skill. Among the PaaS options, you choose based on your stack and needs: **Vercel** for Next.js/frontend-focused apps (best-in-class for that, FORGE's choice); **Railway** or **Render** for full apps with backends and databases (easy all-in-one); **Fly.io** for more control, lower cost at modest scale, edge/global deployment, or persistent-connection needs (W16). They're broadly similar in giving easy git-based deployment; you pick by fit (your framework, whether you need a database/backend hosted too, cost, control, geography). And you stay on a PaaS *until* you have a specific reason to go to raw cloud infrastructure (W20's AWS/GCP/Azure), which is more powerful and flexible but *far* more complex (you manage much more yourself). The guidance, consistent with the track's simplicity discipline, is to *use a PaaS by default* (it covers most apps' needs with minimal ops) and reach for the bigger cloud platforms only when you genuinely need their power/flexibility/scale and have the capacity to manage the complexity, most apps never need to, and starting on raw cloud infrastructure when a PaaS would do is over-engineering (a lot of ops burden for no benefit). So the deployment choice is: a PaaS (Vercel/Railway/Render/Fly) for the great majority of apps, chosen by stack fit, and the major clouds only when specific advanced needs justify their complexity. This keeps your deployment simple and focused on your app, which is exactly right for most projects.

## Where this fits
You understand deployment platforms (PaaS: Vercel, Railway, Render, Fly.io) as the easy, integrated, ops-handling default for most apps, chosen by stack fit (Vercel for Next.js, Railway/Render for full apps, Fly for control/edge/persistent connections), staying on a PaaS until specific advanced needs justify the far-greater complexity of raw cloud. Tomorrow you look at those bigger clouds: AWS, GCP, Azure.

items.title: AWS / GCP / Azure
items.body:
## The big clouds: AWS, GCP, Azure
Beyond the easy PaaS platforms are the **major cloud providers**, **AWS, GCP, Azure**, which offer vastly more *power, flexibility, and services* but at the cost of far *greater complexity*. Where a PaaS gives you "connect repo, it runs," the big clouds give you a huge menu of granular building blocks (compute, storage, databases, networking, queues, and hundreds of services) that you assemble *yourself* into your infrastructure:
```text
PaaS (Vercel/Railway/...):  "connect repo -> it runs"  (easy, opinionated, less control)
Big cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure):  hundreds of granular services you assemble yourself
                            (max power/flexibility/scale, MUCH more complexity)
```
They power the largest applications in the world and offer essentially unlimited scale and capability, but using them well requires significant expertise (you manage networking, security, scaling, the many services, and their interactions), which is why they're the "go further" option, not the default.

## When the big clouds are warranted
Understanding *when* to reach for the big clouds (and when not to) is the key judgement, the same match-the-tool-to-the-need discipline:
- **When you genuinely need their power/flexibility/scale:** very large scale (beyond what a PaaS handles), specific advanced services (specialised databases, ML infrastructure, complex networking), fine-grained control over your infrastructure, or specific compliance/enterprise requirements, these are real reasons that justify the big clouds' complexity. At sufficient scale or with sufficiently specialised needs, the PaaS's simplicity becomes limiting and the big cloud's power is necessary.
- **When you have the expertise/capacity to manage them:** the big clouds require real ops/infrastructure expertise (and often a dedicated team) to use well and securely, so they fit organisations with that capacity, not a solo developer shipping a typical app.
- **Often *via* a PaaS or managed layer anyway:** even teams on the big clouds frequently use *managed* services (managed databases, managed Kubernetes) or PaaS-like layers on top, to reduce the complexity, so "use the big cloud" rarely means using its rawest building blocks directly for everything.
Conversely, for *most* apps, the big clouds are *over-engineering*, you'd take on enormous complexity (managing infrastructure that a PaaS handles for you) for capabilities you don't need, slowing you down and adding risk (misconfigured cloud infrastructure is a common source of security holes and outages) for no benefit. So you reach for AWS/GCP/Azure *only* when you have a *specific, genuine* need for their power/scale/flexibility *and* the capacity to manage them, and otherwise stay on the simpler PaaS that covers most needs with far less burden. This is firmly the "don't over-engineer; use the simplest thing that meets the need" judgement that runs through every track, applied to deployment infrastructure.

## The deeper lesson: match infrastructure to actual needs
The broader lesson is **matching your infrastructure choice to your *actual* needs and capacity, not to what sounds impressive or "scalable"**, which is a recurring and important engineering judgement. There's a temptation (resume-driven, or fear-of-not-scaling) to reach for the big, powerful clouds prematurely, but for most apps this is a mistake: the complexity of raw cloud infrastructure is a real, ongoing cost (in time, expertise, and risk) that's only worth paying when you *genuinely* need the power, and a PaaS gives you production-grade, scalable hosting for the vast majority of apps with a fraction of the complexity. So the mature approach is to *start simple* (a PaaS) and *scale up* (toward the big clouds, or managed services on them) *only when a real need arises and is demonstrated*, rather than over-building infrastructure up front for hypothetical scale you may never reach. This mirrors the simplicity discipline everywhere (the right number of agents is one; the simplest model; the simplest architecture; ship the small complete thing), the right infrastructure is the simplest one that meets your *actual* needs, and you add complexity (bigger clouds) only when the need is real. Knowing *that* the big clouds exist and what they offer (so you can reach for them when genuinely needed, and understand systems built on them) while *defaulting to the simpler PaaS* for most work is the balanced judgement. Most successful apps run on simple platforms for a long time; premature cloud complexity is a common, costly mistake. So you understand the big clouds as the powerful "when you really need it" option, and you choose your deployment infrastructure deliberately by *actual* need and capacity, defaulting to simple.

## Where this fits
You understand the big clouds (AWS/GCP/Azure) as offering maximum power, flexibility, and scale at the cost of far greater complexity, warranted *only* when you genuinely need their capabilities *and* can manage them, with the deeper lesson of matching infrastructure to *actual* needs (defaulting to the simpler PaaS, scaling up only when a real need arises), not over-engineering for hypothetical scale. Tomorrow you handle a critical cross-cutting concern: secrets management.

items.title: Secrets management
items.body:
## Secrets management: handling sensitive configuration safely
Your app uses **secrets**, API keys (Stripe, email, AI providers), database passwords, signing secrets, OAuth credentials, and how you handle these is security-critical, because a leaked secret is a serious breach (someone can charge with your Stripe keys, access your database, impersonate your app). **Secrets management** is the discipline of handling sensitive configuration *safely*, and the foundational rules (which you met in W9) are non-negotiable:
```text
- NEVER hard-code secrets in source code (code goes to git; a secret in git is a leaked secret)
- store secrets in ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES / a secrets manager, read at runtime
- keep a git-ignored .env locally; set real secrets in the platform's secret settings for production
- DIFFERENT secrets per environment (dev/staging/prod), and rotate them periodically
```
So secrets live *outside* your code, in the environment (locally in a git-ignored `.env`, in production in the platform's secure secret storage), read by the app at runtime, never committed, the separation of secrets from code that W9 established, now as a central CI/CD/deployment concern.

## Why secrets management is critical, and the common mistakes
Understanding *why* this matters so much, and the classic failures, drives the discipline home:
- **A leaked secret is a serious, common breach:** secrets grant access to powerful things (your payment account, database, services), so a leaked secret is a *direct* security breach with potentially severe consequences (financial loss via your Stripe keys, data breach via your database password, impersonation via your signing secret). And secret leaks are *common*, the classic mistake is committing a secret to git (especially a public repo), where it's then exposed (and bots actively scan public repos for leaked keys, exploiting them within minutes). So mishandled secrets are a frequent, serious vulnerability.
- **Hard-coding and committing secrets is the cardinal sin:** the most common mistake is putting a secret *in the code* (hard-coded), which then goes into git history (and possibly a public repo), leaking it, and even *deleting* it later doesn't fully help (it's in the git history, and may have been scraped). So the rule is absolute: *never* put a secret in code; always read it from the environment. A committed `.env` file is the same mistake (which is why `.env` is git-ignored).
- **Environment separation and rotation:** you use *different* secrets per environment (a test Stripe key in dev, the live key in production) so a dev leak doesn't compromise production, and you *rotate* secrets periodically (and immediately if one might be leaked) to limit exposure. Using the same secrets everywhere, or never rotating, increases risk.
So secrets management is critical because secrets are high-value and leak easily, the discipline (never in code, in environment/secret-manager, git-ignored locally, secured in the platform for production, separated per environment, rotated) is what prevents the common, serious breaches that mishandled secrets cause. This is foundational security hygiene that every deployed app requires.

## Secrets in the CI/CD pipeline, and the broader posture
In the CI/CD context specifically, secrets management has additional facets worth knowing, and it reflects a broader security posture. The CI/CD *pipeline itself* often needs secrets (to deploy, to run tests against services), so these are stored in the CI/CD platform's *secure secret storage* (e.g. GitHub Actions secrets, the platform's secret settings), *not* in the pipeline config files (which are in git), the same never-in-code rule applied to pipeline configuration. Production secrets are set in the *deployment platform's* secret management (Vercel/Railway/etc. environment variable settings, or a dedicated secrets manager like AWS Secrets Manager / Doppler / Vault for more advanced needs), securely stored and injected into the running app, never in the repo. The broader posture this reflects is *treating secrets as the high-value, dangerous assets they are*, minimising who/what can access them (least privilege, scope each secret to what needs it), keeping them out of code and logs (don't log secrets!), and rotating them, which is the security-mindfulness that runs through the whole track (the W21 security week deepens it). The practical foundation, which every deployed app needs and which this week cements as part of the deployment pipeline, is: secrets *never* in code or git, *always* in environment variables / secure secret storage (locally git-ignored, in production/CI in the platform's secret management), separated per environment, rotated, and treated as sensitive throughout (not logged, scoped tightly). Getting secrets management right is non-negotiable security hygiene for any real, deployed application, and it's woven into the CI/CD pipeline (which handles secrets for deployment and testing) you're building. A single leaked secret can undo all your other security, so this foundational discipline is essential.

## Where this fits
You understand secrets management: handling sensitive configuration (API keys, passwords, signing secrets) safely, never in code/git, always in environment variables / secure secret storage (git-ignored locally, in the platform's secret management for production/CI), separated per environment, rotated, treated as high-value assets, because leaked secrets are common, serious breaches. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship a complete CI/CD pipeline.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a complete CI/CD pipeline
You assemble the week into a working CI/CD pipeline for a real app, demonstrating automated, confident shipping:
- **CI** on every push: install, lint, type-check, run the W17 **tests**, build, blocking broken changes from merging.
- **preview deploys** per pull request (verify the real running change before merging), feeding a test-preview-review-merge workflow.
- **automated deployment** (Continuous Delivery or Deployment, at the right confidence level) to a suitable **platform** (a PaaS like Vercel/Railway, FORGE's Vercel).
- proper **secrets management** (secrets in the platform's secure storage / env vars, never in code).
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "CI/CD pipeline: automated test+build on every push, preview deploys, auto-deploy, secure secrets"
git push   # -> CI runs, deploys if it passes
```

## The deliverable is fast, safe, automated shipping
What makes this project demonstrate real competence is that *shipping a change is now fast, safe, and automated*, the goal the week opened with. The strongest version shows the full pipeline working: you push a change, and *automatically* CI runs (tests, lint, types, build) catching any breakage within minutes, a preview deploy lets you verify the real running change, and on merge the change *automatically* deploys to production, with secrets handled securely throughout, no manual test-running, no manual deploy steps, no leaked secrets. The proof is the *capability*: a change goes from your editor to users in *minutes*, with *confidence* (the tests gated it, you saw it work in preview), via an *automated* pipeline (no manual toil or error). And the pipeline *protects* you, a broken change is caught by CI and *blocked* from reaching production (you can demonstrate this: push a change that breaks a test, watch CI fail and block it). Demonstrating that you can set up a pipeline that ships changes *automatically, quickly, and safely* (automated testing gating every change, preview verification, automated deployment, secure secrets), turning shipping from a manual, risky event into a fast, confident routine, is the deliverable, and it's the practice that makes sustainable, frequent, reliable shipping possible, the way modern software actually ships.

## What CI/CD established
Step back: you have learned to *ship changes fast and safely, automatically*, which is foundational to professional software development. You understand CI/CD's goal (editor to production in minutes, with confidence, no manual steps), CI (auto-test every change, catch breakage in minutes not days, the non-negotiable foundation), the CD stages (Delivery with a manual gate vs full Deployment, chosen by confidence), preview deploys (verify the real running change per PR), deployment platforms (PaaS as the right default, big clouds only when genuinely needed, matching infrastructure to actual need), and secrets management (the critical security hygiene of keeping secrets out of code). The throughline is *velocity with safety*: automation that makes shipping fast *and* confident, by running your tests automatically (so breakage is caught), previewing changes (so the real result is verified), deploying automatically (so there's no manual toil), and handling secrets securely (so you don't leak). This builds on testing (W17, the tests CI runs) and is the pipeline through which every future change flows, enabling the frequent, confident shipping that modern development requires. It's also exactly FORGE's setup (push to Vercel, auto-deploy), so it's directly real-world relevant.

## Where this fits
You shipped a complete CI/CD pipeline, automated testing and deployment on every change, with preview deploys and secure secrets, enabling fast, safe, frequent shipping. One Performance & DX topic remains: next week is **observability, logs, metrics, traces in production**, making your running app's internal state visible so you find out about problems from your monitoring (not from a user's support email two days later), the practice of *seeing* how your app actually behaves in production, which is essential once real users depend on it.

weeks.title: Observability, Logs, Metrics, Traces in Production
weeks.context:
Production is different from your laptop. On your laptop, you know when something breaks because you are watching the terminal. In production, users run into bugs while you are asleep, and unless you have instrumented your application, you find out from a support email two days later. Observability is the practice of making your system's internal state visible from its external outputs.

Three pillars of observability. Logs are timestamped records of events: a user logged in, an order was placed, an error occurred. Structured logs (JSON format) are machine-readable and can be queried. Unstructured logs (plain text sentences) are human-readable but hard to search at scale. Use structured logging. Metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time: requests per second, error rate, database query latency, memory usage. They tell you the system is unhealthy. Logs tell you why. Traces are end-to-end records of a request as it flows through multiple services. They show you which part of a distributed system is slow.

Error tracking is the highest-ROI observability investment for a single-service application. Sentry captures unhandled exceptions, attaches the stack trace, the user's session, the browser/OS, and groups duplicate errors together. Without Sentry, a bug that affects 1000 users generates 1000 separate error reports (or none, if users just leave without reporting). With Sentry, it is one issue with a count of 1000.

Uptime monitoring checks your application from the outside at regular intervals and alerts you if it is down. Services like Better Uptime, UptimeRobot, or Checkly ping your health check endpoint every minute. Your health check endpoint should verify the database connection and any critical dependencies, not just return 200.

Logging in Node.js: use Pino (fast, structured JSON logging) or Winston. In development, pretty-print with human-readable format. In production, output raw JSON so log aggregation services (Datadog, Logtail, Papertrail) can parse it.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Production is different from your laptop
The premise of this week is a hard truth: **production is different from your laptop.** On your laptop, you *know* when something breaks, you're watching the terminal, you see the error. In production, *users* run into bugs *while you're asleep*, and unless you've *instrumented* your application, you find out from a support email *two days later* (if at all), by which time the problem has been hurting users the whole time. **Observability** is the practice of making your system's *internal* state visible from its *external* outputs, so you can *see* what your running app is actually doing, *know* when something goes wrong (immediately, from your monitoring, not days later from a complaint), and *diagnose* it. This week you instrument your app for production, building the ability to see inside it, which is essential once real users depend on it.

## The three pillars: logs, metrics, traces
Observability rests on three kinds of data, the **three pillars**, each answering a different question:
- **Logs:** *timestamped records of events*, a user logged in, an order was placed, an error occurred. Logs tell you *what happened* (the discrete events), and are essential for understanding specific occurrences and debugging. Use **structured logs** (JSON), which are *machine-readable and queryable* (you can search/filter them at scale), rather than unstructured plain-text sentences (human-readable but hard to search across many logs).
- **Metrics:** *numeric measurements aggregated over time*, requests per second, error rate, response time, database query duration. Metrics tell you the *aggregate health and trends* (is the error rate rising? is it slow?), and are how you *monitor* the system's overall state and spot problems.
- **Traces:** the *path of a single request* through your system (the request hit this endpoint, which called this service, which queried the database, with timing for each step). Traces tell you *where time goes* and *what happened* in a specific request across components, essential for diagnosing *where* a slow or failing request went wrong.
```text
LOGS:    what happened (events, for debugging specifics)      -> structured/JSON, queryable
METRICS: aggregate health/trends (rates, latencies, errors)  -> monitor, spot problems
TRACES:  a request's path through the system (where time/failures are)  -> diagnose specifics
```

## Why you need observability, and all three pillars
Understanding *why* observability matters, and why you need all three pillars, frames the week:
- **You can't fix what you can't see:** in production, you have no terminal to watch, so without instrumentation, your app is a *black box*, problems happen *invisibly* (errors users hit, slowdowns, failures) and you only learn of them indirectly and late (a user complains), if at all. Observability makes the black box *transparent*, so you *see* problems (and the system's health) directly and promptly, which is the prerequisite for responding to them. This is the same "you can't manage what you can't measure / silent failures need monitoring" theme from the ML and AI observability lessons, here for web apps.
- **The three pillars answer different questions, together:** metrics tell you *that* something is wrong (the error rate spiked, latency rose) and let you *monitor* health and *alert*; logs tell you *what* happened (the specific events, errors, for *debugging*); traces tell you *where* in a request the problem is (which component/step). You need all three: metrics to *detect* (something's wrong), logs to *understand* (what exactly), traces to *locate* (where in the request flow). Together they let you *detect, understand, and diagnose* production problems, which no single pillar does alone.
- **It enables fast response, not slow discovery:** with observability, you find out about a problem from your *monitoring* (immediately, with the data to diagnose it), not from a user's email two days later, turning slow, blind, after-the-fact firefighting into fast, informed response. This is what makes operating a production app feasible.
So observability is essential because production is a black box without it, and the three pillars (logs, metrics, traces) together make your system's internal state visible so you can detect, understand, and diagnose problems promptly, rather than discovering them late and blindly from user complaints.

## Where this fits
This week completes the Performance & DX phase with observability: logs, metrics, and traces that make your production app's behaviour visible, so you find problems from monitoring, not user emails. It builds on the production-readiness themes (and mirrors the AI/ML observability lessons) and completes the operational toolkit. Today's orientation: production is a black box without instrumentation; observability makes internal state visible via three pillars, logs (what happened, queryable/structured), metrics (aggregate health/trends), and traces (a request's path), which together let you detect, understand, and diagnose problems promptly. Tomorrow you go deeper on the three pillars.

items.title: Logs vs metrics vs traces
items.body:
## The three pillars, in depth
Today you understand each pillar more deeply, including *when to use which*, because using the right observability data for the right question is the skill:
- **Logs** record *discrete events with detail*, and are your tool for *debugging specific occurrences*. When an error happens, the logs (especially the error log with its context, stack trace, the relevant data) tell you *what* went wrong in detail. The key practice (from D1) is *structured logging* (JSON): each log is a structured record with fields (timestamp, level, message, and contextual data like user ID, request ID) that you can *query and filter* at scale ("show me all errors for this user in the last hour"), where unstructured text logs are unsearchable in volume. Logs are detailed and event-specific, for understanding *what happened* in particular cases.
- **Metrics** are *aggregated numbers over time*, and are your tool for *monitoring health and spotting problems*. They answer questions like "what's the error rate? the request rate? the average and p95 latency? the database load?", aggregate measures that show the system's *overall* state and *trends*. Metrics are what you *dashboard* and *alert* on (alert if error rate exceeds X, if latency exceeds Y), because they reveal *that* something is wrong across the system. Metrics are aggregate and trend-focused, for monitoring and detection.
- **Traces** follow *a single request's journey* through the components (endpoint -> service -> database, with timing per step), and are your tool for *diagnosing where* a problem is in a request's flow. When a request is slow or fails, the trace shows *which step* was slow or failed (the database query took 2s; this service call errored), pinpointing the location. Traces are request-scoped and flow-focused, for locating problems within a request.

## Choosing the right pillar for the question
The skill is matching the pillar to the question you're answering, which is what makes observability *useful* rather than just lots of data:
- **"Is something wrong? / How's the system doing?" -> Metrics.** To *monitor* health and *detect* problems (and *alert*), you watch metrics (error rate, latency, throughput), which give the aggregate, real-time picture and trends. Metrics are your detection-and-monitoring layer, the dashboard you watch and the alerts that fire.
- **"What exactly happened (in this error/event)?" -> Logs.** To *debug* a specific failure or understand a particular occurrence, you read the logs (the error details, the events leading up to it, the context), which give the detailed, event-level record. Logs are your debugging layer, the detail you dig into.
- **"Where in the request did it go wrong / why is it slow?" -> Traces.** To *locate* a problem within a request's flow (which component, which step is the bottleneck or the failure point), you examine the trace, which shows the request's path and per-step timing. Traces are your diagnosis-of-location layer, finding *where* in the flow.
The typical workflow uses them together: a *metric* alerts you that error rate spiked (detect) -> you check *traces* to see *where* the failing requests break (locate) -> you read the *logs* for those requests to see *what* exactly went wrong (understand) -> and you fix it. So the three pillars form a *diagnostic flow*: metrics detect, traces locate, logs explain. Knowing which pillar answers which question, metrics for "is something wrong and how's health," logs for "what exactly happened," traces for "where in the request", is what lets you *use* observability effectively to detect, locate, and understand production problems, rather than drowning in undifferentiated data. This complements the AI/ML observability you saw (traces of agent runs, model metrics), here for general web apps, and the *understanding of which data answers which question* is the transferable skill.

## Where this fits
You understand the three pillars in depth and *when to use each*: metrics (aggregate health/trends, for monitoring and detection, the dashboard/alerts), logs (detailed events, for debugging what happened, structured/queryable), and traces (a request's path, for locating where a problem is), forming a diagnostic flow (metrics detect -> traces locate -> logs explain). Tomorrow you implement structured logging with Pino.

items.title: Pino
items.body:
## Structured logging with Pino
You implement the logging pillar with **Pino**, a fast, popular Node logging library that produces **structured (JSON) logs**, the queryable kind. Instead of `console.log` with plain strings, you log structured records with levels and context:
```js
import pino from 'pino';
const log = pino();
log.info({ userId: 42, action: 'login' }, 'user logged in');
log.error({ err, orderId: 7, userId: 42 }, 'order creation failed');
// -> JSON: {"level":"info","time":...,"userId":42,"action":"login","msg":"user logged in"}
```
Each log has a *level* (info, warn, error, debug), a *message*, and *structured context* (relevant data as fields: user ID, order ID, the error). Because the output is JSON with fields, your logging system can *query and filter* it (all errors, all logs for user 42, all order-creation failures), which is what makes logs useful at production scale.

## Why structured logging, and logging well
Understanding *why* structured logging (and logging *well*) matters shows what makes logs valuable:
- **Structured = queryable at scale:** in production you have *enormous* volumes of logs, and *unstructured* text logs ("user 42 logged in at...") are nearly impossible to search/analyse at that scale, while *structured* JSON logs (with fields) are *machine-readable and queryable*, so you can actually *find* the logs you need (filter by user, by error type, by request) among millions. This queryability is the entire point, logs you can't search are nearly useless in production, so structured logging is essential, not stylistic.
- **Levels enable filtering by severity:** log *levels* (debug/info/warn/error) let you control verbosity (log debug detail in development, only info-and-above in production) and *filter* by severity (show me the errors), so you're not drowning in noise when looking for problems. Using levels appropriately (errors at error level, routine events at info, verbose detail at debug) makes logs manageable.
- **Context makes logs actionable:** including the *relevant context* in each log (the user ID, request ID, order ID, the error details) is what makes a log *useful for debugging*, an error log with the user, the request, and the error details lets you understand and reproduce the problem, where a bare "an error occurred" tells you nothing. So you log *with context* (the structured fields), which is what turns a log into a debugging aid.
So structured logging with Pino gives you logs that are *queryable* (JSON fields, searchable at scale), *filterable by severity* (levels), and *actionable* (rich context), which is what makes the logging pillar genuinely useful for understanding and debugging production behaviour, rather than an unsearchable wall of text.

## What and how to log well
The practical discipline of logging *well* (which determines whether your logs help or hinder) involves judgment about *what* to log and *how*:
- **Log the meaningful events and all errors, with context:** log significant events (logins, orders, important state changes) and *especially* all errors (with full context, stack traces, the relevant data), so you have a record of what happened and rich detail for failures. Errors especially must be logged with enough context to diagnose them.
- **Include correlation IDs (request IDs):** attach a *request ID* to all logs from a given request, so you can *correlate* all the logs for one request (and tie them to its trace), which is invaluable for following what happened in a specific request across components. This ties logs together (and to traces) per request.
- **Don't over-log or log sensitive data:** *too much* logging creates noise and cost (and can hurt performance), so you log what's *useful*, not everything, and *crucially*, you *never log secrets or sensitive personal data* (passwords, tokens, full card numbers, PII), logging sensitive data is a security/privacy breach (the logs become a leak), the same PII-redaction discipline from the AI observability lesson, here for app logs. So you log meaningfully and *safely* (no secrets/PII).
- **Use appropriate levels:** errors at error level, warnings at warn, routine events at info, verbose detail at debug, so logs are filterable and production isn't drowned in debug noise.
So logging well means: structured (queryable), with levels (filterable), with rich context and correlation IDs (actionable, correlatable), logging the meaningful events and all errors, but *not* over-logging or logging sensitive data (manageable and safe). Done well, your logs become a powerful tool for understanding and debugging production behaviour; done poorly (unstructured, contextless, or full of noise/secrets), they're useless or even harmful. Implementing structured logging with Pino, following these practices, gives you the logging pillar properly, the queryable, actionable record of what your app does in production.

## Where this fits
You can implement structured logging with Pino: queryable JSON logs with levels, rich context, and correlation (request) IDs, logging meaningful events and all errors but never secrets/PII and without over-logging, which makes the logging pillar genuinely useful for production debugging. Tomorrow you handle getting all this observability data into a system that lets you use it: hosted observability.

items.title: Hosted observability
items.body:
## Hosted observability: where the data lives and is used
You're generating logs, metrics, and traces, but they need to *go somewhere* you can *store, search, visualise, and alert on* them, and **hosted observability platforms**, Datadog, Grafana Cloud, Axiom, Better Stack, Sentry (for errors), and others, provide exactly that, as managed infrastructure. You send your observability data to the platform, and it gives you dashboards, search, and alerting:
```text
your app's logs/metrics/traces  ->  hosted observability platform
   platform provides: storage, search/query, dashboards (visualise metrics),
                      trace viewers, ALERTING (notify you when something's wrong)
   you: instrument your app to send the data, build dashboards/alerts, investigate
```
Rather than building log storage, metric dashboards, trace viewers, and alerting yourself (a large infrastructure effort), you use a hosted platform that provides the whole observability backend, so you focus on *instrumenting* your app and *using* the data (dashboards, alerts, investigation).

## Why a hosted platform, and what it gives you
The reasoning is the familiar build-vs-buy judgement, and observability is a strong case for a platform:
- **Observability infrastructure is substantial:** storing huge volumes of logs/metrics/traces, making them searchable/queryable at scale, rendering dashboards and trace views, and running alerting reliably, is a lot of specialised infrastructure to build and operate, and it's *not* your app's value. A hosted platform provides it all, so you don't rebuild it.
- **It turns raw data into usable insight:** the platform's *dashboards* (visualise metrics, see health and trends at a glance), *search* (query logs/traces to investigate), *trace viewers* (see request flows), and *alerting* (get notified when metrics cross thresholds) are what make the raw observability data *usable*, you don't just have logs/metrics/traces, you have the tools to *monitor, investigate, and be alerted*. The platform is what turns "I'm collecting data" into "I can *see* my system's health and *get told* when it's wrong."
- **Alerting is the key active capability:** crucially, the platform lets you set *alerts* (notify me, via Slack/email/page, when the error rate spikes, latency exceeds X, the app is down), which is what turns observability from *passive* (data you could look at) into *active* (you're *told* when something's wrong, immediately), so you find out from the *alert* (promptly), not the user's email (days later), exactly the week's goal. Alerting is what makes monitoring actually protect you.
So a hosted observability platform gives you the storage, search, dashboards, trace views, and (critically) *alerting* that make your logs/metrics/traces *usable* for monitoring, investigation, and prompt notification, without building the substantial backend yourself. For most apps, using a hosted observability platform (and an error/crash reporter like Sentry, D5) is the right way to get production observability.

## Using observability platforms well: dashboards and alerts that matter
The skill in *using* an observability platform is building dashboards and alerts that are *useful*, not noise, which is a real discipline. **Dashboards** should show the *key health signals* at a glance (error rate, latency, throughput, the metrics that matter for your app), so you can *see* the system's health quickly, a good dashboard answers "is my app healthy?" instantly. **Alerts** are the critical part to get right: you alert on the *conditions that genuinely need attention* (the app is down, error rate spiked, latency is bad, a critical flow is failing), and, crucially, you *tune* alerts so they *mean something*, the recurring discipline from the AI/ML drift and monitoring lessons: an alerting setup that fires *constantly* (on noise, on transient blips) gets *muted/ignored*, and a muted alert protects nothing, so you tune alerts to fire only on *real, actionable* problems, so that an alert reliably means "a human needs to look *now*." Too-sensitive alerts cause alert fatigue (you ignore them, missing the real one); too-lax alerts miss real problems, so you tune for *actionable* signal. So using the platform well means: dashboards that surface the key health signals clearly, and alerts tuned to fire on *genuine, actionable* problems (not noise), so you're *reliably and promptly* notified of *real* issues without being desensitised by false alarms. This is what makes observability *actively protective*, you *see* health (dashboards) and get *told* about real problems (well-tuned alerts) in time to act, which is the entire point. A hosted platform gives you the tools; using them well (meaningful dashboards, well-tuned alerts) is what turns observability into the early-warning, fast-response capability that operating a production app requires.

## Where this fits
You understand hosted observability platforms (Datadog, Grafana Cloud, Sentry, and others) that store, search, visualise, and *alert* on your logs/metrics/traces as managed infrastructure, turning raw data into usable monitoring, used well by building dashboards that surface key health signals and *tuning alerts* to fire only on genuine, actionable problems (avoiding alert fatigue), making observability actively protective. Tomorrow you handle catching errors specifically: crash reporting.

items.title: Crash reporting
items.body:
## Crash reporting: catching errors as they happen
A specific, high-value form of observability is **crash/error reporting**, tools like **Sentry** (the standard) that *automatically capture errors* (exceptions, crashes) as they happen in production, both on the backend *and* in users' browsers (frontend), with the full context needed to fix them:
```text
an error happens (backend exception, or a JS error in a user's browser)
   -> crash reporter automatically captures it WITH context:
      the stack trace, the user, the browser/device, the request, the breadcrumbs (what led up to it)
   -> sends it to you, GROUPED (same error from many users = one issue), with all you need to fix it
```
So instead of errors happening *silently* in production (a user hits a bug, you never know), the crash reporter *automatically* catches every error and tells you about it, with the stack trace and context to diagnose it, and *groups* recurring errors (the same bug hitting 500 users is one issue, not 500 noise), so you see *what's actually breaking* for your users.

## Why crash reporting is so valuable
Understanding *why* dedicated error reporting matters (beyond general logging) shows its high value:
- **It catches errors you'd otherwise never know about:** most production errors happen *silently* from your perspective, a user hits a bug, maybe they leave, maybe they don't report it, and you *never find out* (the "support email two days later", or never). Crash reporting *automatically* captures *every* error the moment it happens, so you *know* about the bugs your users are actually hitting, promptly, even the ones no one reports. This visibility into real, occurring errors is invaluable, you can't fix bugs you don't know exist.
- **It captures frontend errors, which are especially invisible:** errors in users' *browsers* (frontend JS errors) are *particularly* invisible to you (they happen on the user's device, not your server), so without frontend error reporting, you have *no idea* about JS errors breaking the experience for users. Crash reporters capture these (running in the browser, reporting errors back), giving you visibility into frontend failures you'd otherwise be completely blind to. This is a major gap that error reporting fills.
- **It provides the context to actually fix the error:** a crash report includes the *stack trace* (where in the code), the *context* (which user, what browser/device, what request, what they were doing, "breadcrumbs"), so you can *diagnose and reproduce* the error, far more actionable than a vague user report ("it broke"). The rich context turns "something's wrong somewhere" into "this specific error, here, for these users, in this situation."
- **Grouping cuts through the noise:** the same bug hitting many users is *grouped* into one issue (with a count of how many users/times it occurred), so you see the *distinct* problems and their *impact* (this error affects 500 users, that one affects 2), letting you *prioritise* by real impact rather than drowning in duplicate reports.
So crash reporting gives you *automatic, prompt, contextual, grouped* visibility into the errors *actually occurring* for your users (backend *and* frontend), which is exactly what you need to *find and fix* the bugs hitting real users, bugs you'd otherwise never know about. It's one of the highest-value pieces of observability.

## Error reporting in the operational workflow
The deeper value is how crash reporting fits the *operational reality* of running an app for real users, completing the "find out from monitoring, not user emails" goal. With error reporting, your workflow becomes: an error happens for a user -> the reporter *automatically* captures and notifies you (promptly, with context, grouped by issue) -> you *see* the actual bugs hitting users (prioritised by impact) -> you *diagnose* (the stack trace and context) and *fix* them -> ideally before most users even hit them or complain. This is *proactive* (you find bugs from the automatic reports, often before users complain) rather than *reactive* (waiting for support emails), which is exactly the shift the week is about, *seeing* problems from your instrumentation, promptly and actionably, instead of discovering them late and blindly. It also lets you *prioritise* (fix the high-impact errors first, by user count) and *track* (is this error fixed? are new ones appearing?), making bug-fixing data-driven. Combined with the other observability (metrics for health, logs for detail, traces for location), crash reporting is the piece that specifically surfaces the *errors* users hit, with the context to fix them, which is often the most immediately impactful observability for app quality (because user-facing errors directly hurt the experience, and now you *see and fix* them). For any real app with users, a crash reporter (Sentry or similar, covering backend *and* frontend) is essential, it's how you actually know about and fix the bugs your users encounter, rather than letting them suffer silently. This is core to operating an app responsibly, you owe it to your users to *know* when your app breaks for them and fix it, which requires error reporting.

## Where this fits
You understand crash/error reporting (Sentry and similar): automatically capturing every production error (backend *and* the otherwise-invisible frontend) with full context (stack trace, user, situation), grouped by issue and prioritised by impact, so you *know about and can fix* the bugs actually hitting users, promptly and proactively, rather than discovering them late or never. Tomorrow you handle responding to problems: on-call and alerting.

items.title: On-call rotations and alerting
items.body:
## Responding to problems: on-call and alerting
Observability tells you *when* something's wrong; **on-call and alerting** is about *responding* to it, ensuring that when a real problem occurs, *someone is notified and responds*, even at 3am. **Alerting** (from D4) fires notifications when monitored conditions indicate a problem (the app is down, error rate spiked, a critical flow is failing); **on-call** is the practice of having a *designated person responsible* for responding to those alerts at any time:
```text
alert fires (app down / error spike / critical failure)
   -> notifies the ON-CALL person (Slack, email, phone/page)
   -> they acknowledge, investigate (using observability), and respond (fix/mitigate)
   -> the problem is handled PROMPTLY, even at 3am, not left until morning
```
So alerting + on-call closes the loop: a real problem triggers an alert, which reaches a responsible person, who responds promptly, so production issues are *handled* quickly rather than festering until someone happens to notice.

## Why alerting and on-call complete observability
Understanding *why* this matters shows it's the *active* completion of observability:
- **Observability without response is incomplete:** collecting logs/metrics/traces and even having dashboards is *passive*, it only helps if someone *looks* and *acts*. Alerting makes it *active* (you're *notified* of problems, not relying on watching dashboards), and on-call ensures *someone responds* (the notification reaches a responsible person who acts). Without alerting + on-call, a production problem at 3am goes unnoticed and unhandled until someone checks in the morning (hours of impact); with it, the alert wakes the on-call person who fixes it promptly. So alerting + on-call is what turns observability from "data we could look at" into "we're notified of and respond to problems promptly", the actual protection.
- **Real apps fail at any time, and need timely response:** production problems don't wait for business hours, an outage, a spike in errors, a failing payment flow can happen anytime, and the longer it goes unhandled, the more users are hurt, so *timely* response matters. On-call ensures there's *always* someone responsible to respond, so problems are addressed in minutes/hours, not whenever someone notices. For an app real users (and revenue) depend on, this prompt response capability is essential.
- **It enables reliable operation:** alerting + on-call (plus the observability to diagnose) is what makes an app *reliably operated*, you *detect* problems (monitoring/alerts), *respond* promptly (on-call), and *resolve* them (using logs/traces to diagnose, then fix/mitigate), which is the operational discipline that keeps a production app healthy and available for users over time.
So alerting and on-call complete observability by making it *active and responded-to*: alerts notify of real problems, on-call ensures prompt response, turning the visibility observability provides into actual, timely problem-resolution, which is what operating a reliable production app requires.

## Doing it sustainably and well
The discipline in alerting and on-call is making it *sustainable and effective*, because done badly it burns people out and fails. Key practices, several echoing the AI/ML reliability lessons:
- **Alert only on what's actionable (avoid fatigue):** the recurring, critical discipline, alerts must fire only on *real, actionable* problems that *need* a human *now*, not on noise or transient blips, because an on-call person flooded with false alarms gets *fatigued* and *desensitised* (ignoring alerts, including the real one), and burns out. So you tune alerts ruthlessly so that an alert *means* "a real problem needs attention now", which respects the on-call person and keeps alerts trusted. *Actionable* alerts (clear what's wrong and that action is needed), not noisy ones.
- **Sustainable on-call:** on-call should be *humane*, rotated among people (not one person always), with reasonable expectations, good tooling (the observability to diagnose quickly), and runbooks (guidance for common issues), so it's sustainable and not burning anyone out. A solo developer is "always on-call", so for a solo project, the emphasis is on *good alerting* (you're notified of real problems) and *graceful degradation* (the app handles failures well so fewer things are 3am-urgent).
- **Graceful degradation reduces urgency:** the more your app *handles failures gracefully* (degrades cleanly when a dependency fails, rather than fully breaking, the recurring graceful-degradation theme), the *fewer* true emergencies you have, so building resilience *reduces* the on-call burden. Designing for failure (so problems are non-urgent or self-recovering where possible) is part of sustainable operations.
- **Learn from incidents (blameless post-mortems):** after a significant incident, a *blameless* review of what happened and how to prevent it (the post-mortem discipline from across the tracks) turns incidents into improvements, so the same problem doesn't recur. This makes operations *better* over time.
So alerting and on-call, done well, mean: *actionable* alerts (no fatigue), *sustainable* on-call (rotated, humane, well-equipped), *graceful degradation* (fewer emergencies), and *learning from incidents* (continuous improvement), which together make production operations *effective and sustainable*, you're reliably notified of and respond to real problems, without burning out, and you improve over time. This is the operational maturity that keeps a real app reliably available, and it completes the observability picture: see (logs/metrics/traces), be notified (well-tuned alerts), respond (sustainable on-call), and improve (post-mortems).

## Where this fits
You understand alerting and on-call as the *active response* completing observability: alerts notify of real problems, on-call ensures prompt response (even at 3am), done sustainably via *actionable* alerts (no fatigue), humane rotation, graceful degradation (fewer emergencies), and blameless post-mortems (improvement). Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship an observable app.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: an observable, operable app
You assemble the week into a real app instrumented for production observability, demonstrating that you can *operate* an app, not just build it:
- **structured logging** (Pino, JSON, with context and correlation IDs, no secrets) for the events and errors.
- **metrics** (health, error rate, latency) and **traces** (request flows) sent to a **hosted observability platform**, with dashboards surfacing key health signals.
- **crash/error reporting** (Sentry) catching backend *and* frontend errors with context.
- **alerting** tuned to fire on real, actionable problems, with an on-call/response plan.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Observability: structured logs, metrics, traces, crash reporting, tuned alerting"
git push
```

## The deliverable is the ability to operate, not just build
What makes this project demonstrate real competence is that you can *operate* the app in production, *see* its behaviour, *know* promptly when something's wrong, and *diagnose* it, rather than running it blind. The strongest version shows the full observability in place: structured queryable logs (you can investigate what happened), metrics dashboards (you can see health at a glance), traces (you can locate where a request breaks), crash reporting (you automatically know the errors hitting real users, backend and frontend), and *tuned alerting* (you're notified of *real* problems promptly, without fatigue). The proof is the *operational capability*: if something breaks in production, you find out from your *monitoring* (an alert, a crash report) *promptly* and *with the data to diagnose it* (the trace shows where, the logs show what, the error report shows the bug), so you can respond *fast*, instead of finding out from a user's email two days later and debugging blind. Demonstrating that you've made your app's production behaviour *visible* (the three pillars + crash reporting) and *actively monitored* (dashboards + tuned alerts + a response plan), so you can *operate* it reliably (detect, diagnose, respond), is the deliverable, and it's the operational maturity that distinguishes someone who can *run* an app in production from someone who can only *build* one, which is exactly what's needed once real users depend on it.

## What observability, and the Performance & DX phase, established
Step back: you have learned to *operate* an app in production, making its black-box internals *visible* so you can run it reliably for real users. You understand why production needs observability (it's a black box otherwise, problems are silent and discovered late), the three pillars (logs for what happened, metrics for health/detection, traces for location, and which to use when), structured logging (queryable, actionable, safe), hosted observability platforms (the managed backend that makes the data usable, with dashboards and alerting), crash reporting (automatic, contextual visibility into the errors actually hitting users, backend and frontend), and alerting + on-call (the active response, done sustainably with actionable alerts and graceful degradation). The throughline is *making production visible and responded-to*, so you *find out from monitoring, not user emails*, and can *detect, diagnose, and respond* to problems promptly, the operational maturity real apps require. And this *completes the Performance & DX phase*: testing (W17, change without fear), performance (W18, fast for users), CI/CD (W19, ship fast and safe), and observability (W20, operate reliably), the engineering practices and developer experience that make an app reliable, fast, maintainable, and operable, the qualities separating a prototype from a production-grade product.

## Where this fits
You shipped an observable, operable app, instrumented with logs/metrics/traces, crash reporting, and tuned alerting, so you can run it reliably in production, completing the Performance & DX phase. Next comes the **Production phase** (W21-23): security (the threats you haven't thought about), scaling (when 10x more traffic hits), and polish (the last 5% that takes 50% of the time), the final hardening that turns a working, well-engineered app into a robust, secure, scalable, polished product, before the capstone.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Your health check endpoint at /api/health returns 200. An uptime monitor pings it and reports your site is up. But users are getting "Internal Server Error" on checkout. How does this happen and how do you fix it? The health check only checked the HTTP server, not the database connection. If the database is down or out of connections, the health check passes but data operations fail. Fix: the health check must verify all critical dependencies. For the database: await prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT 1`. For Redis: await redis.ping(). If any check fails, return 503 Service Unavailable. Now your uptime monitor detects the real failure.

weeks.title: Security, The Threats You Haven't Thought About
weeks.context:
Security is not a checklist. Every application that handles user data or money has the same set of threats, and most breaches happen because of well-known, well-documented vulnerabilities that were not addressed. This week you learn the OWASP Top 10 and how each applies to Bean Forge.

SQL injection: user-controlled input is included directly in SQL queries, allowing the attacker to modify the query. Parameterised queries (which Prisma uses by default) prevent this entirely, the parameter value is never interpreted as SQL. The vulnerability is using raw string concatenation: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"). Prisma's ORM layer means you are safe if you use the API correctly. Watch for prisma.$queryRaw, use template literal syntax where Prisma escapes the parameters, not string concatenation.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): an attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a page that other users view. In React, JSX automatically escapes text content, {userInput} is safe. The vulnerability is dangerouslySetInnerHTML or using the DOM API to set innerHTML directly. Never use dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user-supplied content unless you run it through a sanitisation library like DOMPurify first.

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF): a malicious website tricks a user's browser into making authenticated requests to your application. Modern defences: SameSite=Strict or SameSite=Lax cookie attribute prevents the browser from including cookies on cross-site requests. The SameSite attribute is now the default in most browsers, making CSRF rare. Still, understand the attack.

Dependency vulnerabilities: your application is only as secure as its dependencies. Run npm audit regularly. Use automated tools (Dependabot, Snyk) to flag known CVEs in your dependency tree. Subscribe to security advisories for your major dependencies.

Security headers: a small middleware call that adds significant protection. Use the helmet package in Express: it sets Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options (prevents clickjacking), Strict-Transport-Security (forces HTTPS), and other headers. In Next.js, configure security headers in next.config.ts.

Rate limiting: prevents brute-force attacks (trying millions of passwords), credential stuffing (using leaked credentials from other breaches), and scraping. Add rate limiting to authentication endpoints and any expensive endpoint.

Environment variables and secrets: never commit secrets to git. Use .env files locally (excluded via .gitignore) and environment variable management in production (Vercel env, Railway env, AWS Secrets Manager).

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Security is not a checklist
This week's framing is important: **security is not a checklist.** It's a *mindset* and an ongoing concern, because *every* application that handles user data or money faces the *same* set of threats, and the sobering reality is that **most breaches happen because of well-known, well-documented vulnerabilities that simply weren't addressed.** Attackers don't usually need exotic, novel exploits, they exploit the *common*, *known* weaknesses (SQL injection, XSS, broken access control) that the developers didn't defend against. So security is largely about *understanding and defending against the well-known threats*, systematically. This week you learn the **OWASP Top 10** (the standard list of the most critical web vulnerabilities) and how each applies to a real app (Bean Forge), building the security awareness that protects real users' data and money, the threats you might not have thought about, made explicit.

## Why "the threats you haven't thought about"
The week's title captures the core problem: the dangerous vulnerabilities are often the ones you *haven't thought about*, because security requires actively considering how your app could be *attacked*, not just whether it *works*. A feature can work perfectly for normal use *and* be wide open to attack, because attackers do things normal users don't (manipulate inputs, forge requests, probe for weaknesses), and if you only think about the *happy path* (does it work for legitimate users?), you miss the *attack paths* (how could someone abuse this?). So security is about *adversarial thinking*, deliberately asking "how could this be exploited?", which surfaces the threats that normal-use thinking misses. The good news, and the week's premise, is that these threats are *well-documented*, the OWASP Top 10 catalogs the most common, critical ones, so you don't have to imagine every attack; you learn the *known* categories of vulnerability and defend against each. This turns security from a vague, scary unknown into a *learnable, systematic* discipline: understand the well-known threats (OWASP Top 10), check your app against each, and apply the known defences. Most breaches are preventable because they exploit *known* vulnerabilities, so learning and defending against those known threats is most of practical security.

## A pattern you've been building: defences throughout the track
Reassuringly, you've already met many of these defences throughout the track, because security has been a recurring theme, and this week *consolidates* and *systematises* that into the OWASP framework:
- **SQL injection** (attacker manipulates your database queries via input): prevented by *parameterised queries*, which Prisma uses by default (W10), the parameter value is never interpreted as SQL, so using Prisma's normal API keeps you safe (the danger is raw string concatenation into queries, which you don't do with Prisma's typed API; watch `$queryRaw`, use its safe template syntax).
- **Broken access control** (users accessing what they shouldn't): defended by *server-side authorisation enforcement* on every protected action (W12), the deny-by-default, check-permission-on-every-request discipline.
- **Input validation** (untrusted input): you've validated forms (W3), file uploads (W15), API input (W11), the "all user input is untrusted" habit.
- **Secrets management** (W9, W19), **secure auth** (W12), **dependency awareness**, all touched.
So you're not starting from zero, you've been building security practices all along (parameterised queries, server-side authz, input validation, secrets management, secure auth), and this week *organises* them into the OWASP Top 10 framework, fills the gaps, and cements the *adversarial mindset* that ties them together. Security isn't a separate add-on; it's been woven through everything, and this week makes it systematic and complete.

## Where this fits
This opens the **Production phase** (W21-23): security (this week), scaling, and polish, the final hardening before the capstone. Security comes first because an insecure app is a liability no matter how good otherwise. It consolidates the security practices from across the track into the OWASP framework. Today's orientation: security is a *mindset* (adversarial, "how could this be attacked?"), not a checklist; most breaches exploit *well-known* vulnerabilities (the OWASP Top 10) that weren't addressed; and you've already been building many defences, now systematised. Tomorrow you learn the OWASP Top 10.

items.title: OWASP Top 10
items.body:
## The OWASP Top 10: the critical vulnerabilities to know
The **OWASP Top 10** is the standard, authoritative list of the *most critical* web application security risks, maintained by the security community, and it's the framework for systematically understanding and defending against the threats that cause most breaches. Knowing it (at least conceptually) is foundational security literacy. The categories (which shift slightly over versions but cover the same ground) include:
```text
- Broken Access Control      (users doing what they shouldn't - the #1 risk, W12)
- Cryptographic Failures     (sensitive data exposed - weak/missing encryption, leaked secrets)
- Injection                  (SQL injection, etc. - untrusted input interpreted as code, W10)
- Insecure Design            (security flaws in the design itself)
- Security Misconfiguration  (insecure defaults, exposed config, e.g. public S3 buckets, W15)
- Vulnerable Components       (using dependencies with known vulnerabilities, D6)
- Auth Failures              (broken authentication/session management, D4)
- Data Integrity Failures    (insecure deserialization, unverified updates/CI-CD)
- Logging/Monitoring Failures (can't detect/respond to breaches - the observability link, W20)
- SSRF                       (server tricked into making requests it shouldn't)
```

## Why the Top 10 is the right framework
Understanding *why* the OWASP Top 10 is so valuable frames how to use it:
- **It focuses you on what actually causes breaches:** security has infinite theoretical attack surface, but the OWASP Top 10 distills it to the *most common, most critical* risks that cause *most real breaches*, so defending against these covers the vast majority of practical risk. Rather than trying to defend against everything (impossible) or guessing (incomplete), you systematically address the *known top threats*, which is where the real risk is. It's a prioritised, evidence-based focus.
- **It's a shared, authoritative standard:** being the community standard, it gives you a *common framework* and *language* (everyone in security knows the OWASP Top 10), a *checklist to verify your app against* (have I addressed each category?), and *documented guidance* for each (how to defend against it). You're not inventing your security approach; you're applying a proven, authoritative one.
- **Each maps to concrete defences:** every category has well-understood *defences* (injection -> parameterised queries; broken access control -> server-side authz; misconfiguration -> secure defaults; vulnerable components -> dependency management), so the Top 10 isn't just a list of fears, it's a list of *threats with known mitigations*, making it actionable, for each, you apply the known defence.
So the OWASP Top 10 is the right framework because it focuses your security effort on the *highest-risk, most-common* vulnerabilities (where breaches actually happen), as an authoritative, shared, actionable standard with known defences for each. Working through it systematically, checking your app against each category and applying the defences, is how you achieve *practical* security that addresses the real risks, rather than either ignoring security or being overwhelmed by infinite theoretical threats.

## Using the Top 10: systematic defence
The practical approach is to *go through the OWASP Top 10 systematically for your app*, which is exactly this week's work (and a recurring professional practice): for *each* category, ask "is my app vulnerable to this, and have I applied the defence?" This turns security from vague anxiety into a *systematic review*: Broken access control, do I enforce authorisation server-side on every protected action (W12)? Injection, am I using parameterised queries / Prisma's safe API (W10)? Misconfiguration, are my defaults secure, no public buckets (W15), no exposed config? Vulnerable components, are my dependencies up to date and free of known vulnerabilities (D6)? Auth failures, is my auth secure (W12)? And so on through each category. This systematic check, against the *known top threats*, with the *known defences*, is how you cover the real risk comprehensively, and it's reassuring because (as W21-D1 noted) you've already implemented many of these defences throughout the track, so much of the review is *verifying* you've done the right thing, plus closing any gaps. The deeper point is that *practical security is systematic, not heroic*, you don't need to be a security genius imagining novel attacks; you need to *systematically address the well-known top vulnerabilities*, which prevents the vast majority of breaches (since most exploit exactly these known weaknesses). Knowing the OWASP Top 10 and methodically applying its defences to your app is the foundation of practical web security, and this week walks through the most important ones (injection/XSS, auth/session attacks, authorisation bugs, vulnerable dependencies) in depth.

## Where this fits
You understand the OWASP Top 10 as the authoritative framework of the most critical, common web vulnerabilities (broken access control, injection, misconfiguration, vulnerable components, auth failures, and more), each with known defences, used by systematically reviewing your app against each category, which focuses security on the real risks and is mostly *verifying* the defences you've built throughout the track. Tomorrow you handle a major one: XSS.

items.title: XSS
items.body:
## XSS: when user input becomes executable code
**Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)** is one of the most common and dangerous web vulnerabilities: it happens when *user-controlled input* is rendered into a page in a way that lets it *execute as code* (JavaScript) in *other users'* browsers. An attacker injects a malicious script (via a comment, a profile field, any user input that gets displayed), and when another user views that content, the script *runs in their browser*, where it can steal their session/cookies, perform actions as them, or deface the page:
```text
attacker submits as a "comment":  <script>steal(document.cookie)</script>
if your app renders that raw into the page -> the script RUNS in every viewer's browser
   -> steals their session, acts as them, etc.  (XSS)
```
The root cause is *treating user input as trusted markup/code* when displaying it, the attacker's input gets *interpreted* (as HTML/JS) rather than *displayed* (as text).

## How to prevent XSS: escape output, and framework defaults
Understanding the defence shows how XSS is prevented, and reassuringly, modern frameworks help a lot:
- **Escape/encode output (the core defence):** the fix is to ensure user input is *displayed as text*, not *interpreted as code*, by *escaping* it when rendering (converting `<script>` into harmless text that *shows* the characters rather than executing). When user content is properly escaped, the attacker's `<script>` is displayed as literal text, not run. *Output encoding* (escaping user data when it's rendered into the page) is the primary XSS defence.
- **Modern frameworks escape by default (a big help):** React (and JSX, W5) *automatically escapes* values you render (`{userInput}` is escaped, displayed as text, not interpreted), so React apps are *protected by default* against the most common XSS, you get the escaping for free by using the framework normally. This is a major reason modern frameworks reduce XSS risk: the safe behaviour (escaping) is the default.
- **The danger is bypassing the escaping:** the vulnerability reappears when you *bypass* the framework's escaping, in React, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (which renders raw HTML, *unescaped*), and similar "render raw HTML" mechanisms. The name *dangerously* is a deliberate warning: using it with *user* content reintroduces XSS, so you *avoid* rendering unescaped user input, and if you *must* render user-provided HTML (e.g. a rich-text field), you *sanitise* it first (with a library like DOMPurify that strips dangerous content). So the rule: rely on the framework's default escaping, and *never* render unescaped user input, sanitise if you genuinely need to render user HTML.
- **Defence in depth, Content Security Policy (CSP):** a *Content Security Policy* (an HTTP header restricting what scripts can run) adds a second layer, even if an XSS slips through, a strict CSP can prevent the injected script from executing, so CSP is a valuable defence-in-depth measure.

## XSS and the broader "untrusted input" principle
The deeper lesson XSS teaches reinforces the pervasive security principle: **all user input is untrusted, and you must handle it safely at *both* input and output.** You've applied "validate input" throughout (forms, files, API), and XSS adds the *output* side: user input must *also* be handled safely when it's *displayed* (escaped/encoded), because input that was stored can become an attack when *rendered* to other users. This is the same root principle as SQL injection (don't let untrusted input be interpreted as SQL) applied to the rendering context (don't let untrusted input be interpreted as HTML/JS), both are *injection* vulnerabilities (untrusted input interpreted as code), defended by keeping the input as *data*, not letting it become *code* (parameterised queries for SQL, output escaping for HTML). So XSS is part of the unifying *injection* threat: never let user input be *interpreted* (as SQL, as HTML/JS, as any code), always treat it as *data* (parameterised, escaped). Modern frameworks (Prisma for SQL, React for HTML) give you the safe defaults (parameterisation, escaping), so the practical guidance is: *use the framework's safe defaults*, *don't bypass them* with user input (no raw SQL concatenation, no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` of user content), *sanitise* if you must render user HTML, and add *defence in depth* (CSP). With these, XSS, one of the most common and serious vulnerabilities, is well-defended. Understanding XSS (and that it's an injection vulnerability defended by output escaping, largely handled by framework defaults) is essential web security knowledge.

## Where this fits
You understand XSS: user input executing as code in other users' browsers (an *injection* vulnerability), prevented by *escaping output* (which React/JSX does by default, so don't bypass it with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` of user content; sanitise if you must render user HTML; add CSP for defence in depth), reinforcing that untrusted input must be handled safely at both input *and* output. Tomorrow you handle authentication and session attacks.
