items.title: Accessibility (a11y)
items.body:
## Accessibility: the app must work for everyone
**Accessibility (a11y)** is both a polish dimension and a *responsibility* (and often a legal *requirement*): your application **must work for users who navigate with a keyboard, use a screen reader, or have colour vision deficiencies**, and many others with diverse abilities. Accessibility isn't optional polish, it's about whether a portion of your users can *use your app at all*. The core areas (some of which you've built throughout the track, here consolidated):
- **Keyboard navigation:** *every* interactive element (buttons, links, form fields, modals) must be *reachable and operable* with the keyboard (Tab to move, Enter to activate, Escape to close), because many users (motor impairments, power users, screen-reader users) navigate *without a mouse*. And *focus indicators* must be *visible* (you must be able to *see* which element is focused as you Tab), critically, *don't remove the focus outline without replacing it* (a common mistake that makes keyboard navigation impossible to follow).
- **Screen reader support:** the app must work with *screen readers* (which read the UI aloud for blind/low-vision users), which requires *semantic HTML* (W1, proper elements that screen readers understand), *labels* (W3, so form fields are announced), proper *ARIA* where needed, and accessible interactive components (W7's Radix). Screen-reader users navigate by the *semantic structure*, so it must be correct.
- **Colour and contrast:** *don't rely on colour alone* to convey information (colour-blind users may not distinguish it, so use text/icons too, not just colour), and ensure sufficient *contrast* (so low-vision users can read text). 
- **Modals and focus management:** modal dialogs must *trap focus* (keyboard focus stays in the modal while open), be *dismissible* (Escape), and *return focus* sensibly when closed, proper focus management so keyboard/screen-reader users can use modals.

## Why accessibility is non-negotiable
Understanding *why* accessibility is essential (not optional) frames it correctly, it's a responsibility, not just polish:
- **Real users depend on it, and excluding them is excluding *people*:** accessibility isn't abstract, *real people* navigate with keyboards, use screen readers, or have colour vision deficiencies, and an *inaccessible* app *excludes* them, they *cannot use it*. A keyboard-only user *can't* use a control that requires a mouse; a screen-reader user *can't* use a UI without semantic structure; a colour-blind user *can't* distinguish colour-only information. So inaccessibility isn't a minor imperfection; it *locks out* a portion of your users entirely, which is both *wrong* (excluding people) and *bad* (losing those users). Accessibility is about *not excluding people*.
- **It's often legally required:** accessibility is frequently a *legal requirement* (the ADA in the US, the European Accessibility Act, and others mandate accessible web apps, especially for businesses/public services), so inaccessibility can be a *legal liability*, not just an ethical/UX issue. Many organisations *must* be accessible by law.
- **It's woven through good development (you've been building it):** accessibility isn't a separate bolt-on; it comes from practices you've used throughout, *semantic HTML* (W1), *labels* (W3), *visible focus states* (W3), *honouring user preferences* (reduced motion W2, colour scheme W7), *accessible components* (Radix, W7), *descriptive link text* (W1). So this week *consolidates* and *verifies* the accessibility you've been building, plus fills gaps (keyboard navigation, screen-reader testing, contrast). Good development *is* largely accessible development.
So accessibility is non-negotiable because it determines whether *real people* (keyboard, screen-reader, colour-vision-impaired users) can use your app *at all* (excluding them is excluding people, both wrong and costly), it's often *legally required*, and it's *woven through* the good practices you've already been building. It's a *responsibility*, not optional polish, though it's also part of what makes an app feel complete and professional.

## Auditing and ensuring accessibility
Practically, you *audit* and *ensure* accessibility, which is both a one-time review and an ongoing practice:
- **Test with the keyboard:** navigate the *entire* app using *only* the keyboard (Tab, Enter, Escape), and verify *every* interactive element is reachable and operable, focus is *visible* throughout, and modals trap/return focus correctly. If you *can't* use a feature by keyboard, neither can keyboard-dependent users, so this test directly finds exclusion. (It's a fast, revealing audit.)
- **Test with a screen reader:** use a screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA) to *experience* the app as a screen-reader user does, verifying the content and structure are announced sensibly (which requires the semantic HTML and labels). This reveals screen-reader problems you'd otherwise miss.
- **Use automated tools:** accessibility checkers (axe, Lighthouse's a11y audit, browser extensions) automatically catch *many* issues (missing labels, low contrast, missing alt text), so you run them to find and fix the detectable problems. (They don't catch *everything*, automated tools find many issues but not all, e.g. they can't fully judge keyboard usability or whether labels are *meaningful*, so you combine automated checks *with* manual keyboard/screen-reader testing.)
- **Check colour contrast and don't-rely-on-colour:** verify text contrast meets standards (tools check this) and that information isn't conveyed by colour alone.
So you ensure accessibility by *auditing* (keyboard testing, screen-reader testing, automated checkers, contrast checks) to *find* the barriers, and *fixing* them (the semantic HTML, labels, focus, contrast, keyboard operability), making the app usable for *all* users. This audit-and-fix process, ideally *ongoing* (accessibility, like security and performance, can regress, so you maintain it), is how you meet the accessibility responsibility. Doing it well, an app that's fully keyboard-navigable, screen-reader-friendly, and not colour-dependent, is both *right* (it includes all users) and part of what makes the app a *complete, professional, legally-compliant* product. Accessibility is the polish dimension that's also a fundamental responsibility, and ensuring it is essential.

## Where this fits
You understand accessibility (a11y) as both polish and a *responsibility* (and often legal requirement): the app must work for keyboard users (everything reachable/operable, focus visible), screen-reader users (semantic HTML, labels), and colour-vision-impaired users (don't rely on colour, ensure contrast), audited via keyboard testing, screen-reader testing, and automated tools, because inaccessibility *excludes real people*, much of which you've built throughout the track and now consolidate and verify. Tomorrow you handle reaching users in their language: internationalisation.

items.title: Internationalisation
items.body:
## Internationalisation: supporting multiple languages and locales
**Internationalisation (i18n)** is building your app to *support multiple languages and locales*, so users in different regions can use it in *their* language and with *their* local conventions (date formats, number formats, currencies). Where relevant, it's a significant polish/reach dimension:
```text
i18n:  structure the app so its text, formats, etc. can be ADAPTED to different locales
   - text in translatable resources (not hard-coded), so it can be translated per language
   - locale-aware formatting: dates, numbers, currencies formatted per the user's locale
   - layout that accommodates different languages (text length varies, some read right-to-left)
   - the user can select / it detects their language and locale
```
i18n is fundamentally about *structuring* the app so it *can* be adapted to different locales (text externalised into translatable resources, formatting done locale-aware, layout flexible), and then *providing* the translations/locale support for the languages you target.

## Why and when internationalisation matters
Understanding *why* and *when* i18n matters helps you judge whether and how to do it:
- **It determines reach, who *can* use your app:** if your app is *only* in one language with one locale's formats, users who *don't* speak that language (or expect their local formats) are *excluded* or poorly served, just as inaccessibility excludes users with disabilities, monolingual design excludes users of other languages. So i18n *expands reach* (more people can use the app in their language) and *improves the experience* for non-native-language users (the app meets them in their language and conventions). For an app with a *global* or *multilingual* audience, i18n is important reach.
- **It's about respect and usability for diverse users:** using the app in one's *own* language, with *familiar* date/number/currency formats, is far more *usable* and *respectful* than forcing a foreign language and conventions. i18n is part of *serving your users well* across linguistic/cultural diversity (related to the respect-for-users theme throughout).
- **But it's *conditional* on your audience (don't over-engineer):** *unlike* accessibility (which is essentially *always* required, you always have users with disabilities), i18n is *conditional*, it matters when you *have* (or want) a *multilingual/international* audience, and may *not* be needed for an app serving a single-language market. So i18n is a *judgement* based on your *actual* audience: invest in it when you serve (or target) multiple languages/locales, and *don't* over-engineer it for a single-locale app that doesn't need it (premature i18n is wasted effort, the don't-over-engineer principle). Match the i18n investment to your *actual* multilingual needs.
So i18n matters for *reach* and *respectful usability* across languages/locales *when you have a multilingual/international audience*, and is a *conditional* investment (do it when your audience needs it, not prematurely for a single-locale app). Judging *whether* your app needs i18n (based on your audience) is part of using it appropriately.

## The key practice: structure for i18n early, even if you don't translate yet
The most valuable i18n lesson, even if you're not translating *now*, is to **structure the app to *support* i18n from the start** (or know how to), because *retrofitting* i18n into an app that hard-coded everything for one locale is *painful*. The key structural practices:
- **Externalise text (don't hard-code UI strings):** put user-facing text in *translatable resources* (i18n message files) rather than hard-coding it in components, so it *can* be translated per language without rewriting the UI. Even if you only have one language now, *externalising* the text means adding a language later is *just adding translations*, not refactoring every component.
- **Use locale-aware formatting:** format dates, numbers, and currencies with *locale-aware* methods (the platform's `Intl` APIs) rather than hard-coding one locale's format, so they *adapt* to the user's locale.
- **Design flexible layouts:** allow for text that's *longer* in other languages (translations vary in length) and consider right-to-left languages, so the layout *accommodates* different languages without breaking.
The point is that *retrofitting* i18n is costly (you have to find and externalise every hard-coded string, fix every hard-coded format, fix layouts), while *structuring for it from the start* (externalised text, locale-aware formatting, flexible layout) makes *adding* a language *easy* (just provide translations) and is *low-cost* to do up front. So even if you don't need multiple languages *yet*, *structuring* the app to support i18n (and knowing how) is wise *if* there's any chance you'll need it, it's cheap as a foundation and expensive as a retrofit. This is the *design-for-future-need-cheaply* judgement: you don't have to *implement* full multilingual support prematurely (over-engineering), but *structuring* so you *could* (externalised text, locale-aware formatting) is a low-cost foundation that saves a painful retrofit *if* you internationalise later. For an app that *does* serve a multilingual audience, you implement the i18n (translations, locale support); for one that *might*, you at least *structure* for it; for one that clearly *won't*, you needn't. Understanding i18n, what it is, when it matters (multilingual audience), and the value of *structuring* for it early (to avoid a costly retrofit), is the polish/reach knowledge to apply appropriately based on your audience.

## Where this fits
You understand internationalisation (i18n): structuring the app to support multiple languages/locales (externalised text, locale-aware formatting, flexible layouts), which expands reach and respectfully serves multilingual users, a *conditional* investment based on your actual audience (do it when needed, not prematurely), with the key practice of *structuring* for i18n early (cheap foundation) to avoid a costly retrofit. Tomorrow you handle guiding new users: onboarding.

items.title: Onboarding
items.body:
## Onboarding: guiding new users to value
**Onboarding** is how you *guide new users* from first arrival to *understanding and using* your app successfully, getting them to *value* quickly. A new user arrives *not knowing* what your app does, how to use it, or why they should care, and *good onboarding* bridges that gap: it *welcomes* them, *shows* them what to do, and *gets them to their first success* (their "aha moment") quickly, while *bad* (or absent) onboarding *abandons* them (a confusing first experience, no guidance), and they *leave*:
```text
no/bad onboarding:  new user arrives -> confused (what is this? what do I do?) -> leaves
good onboarding:    new user arrives -> welcomed, guided to set up / first action
                    -> reaches their first success ("aha, I get it / this is useful") -> stays
```
Onboarding spans the *first-time experience*: a welcome, guidance to the first key action, helpful empty states (D2, often a new user's first screens), maybe a brief tour or setup flow, removing friction so the new user *quickly* understands the value and succeeds.

## Why onboarding is critical
Understanding *why* onboarding matters so much, it's often where users are *won or lost*, shows its importance:
- **First impressions and the first experience are decisive:** new users form a *quick* judgment, and if their *first experience* is confusing (they don't understand the app, don't know what to do, hit friction), they *leave*, often *never to return*. The first few minutes *decide* whether a new user *continues* or *abandons*, so a *good* first experience (clear, guiding, quickly valuable) is *critical* to *retaining* new users. Onboarding *is* that crucial first experience, and getting it right is often the difference between a user who *stays* and one who *bounces*. New-user retention hinges on onboarding.
- **Users need to reach *value* quickly ("time to value"):** users *continue* with an app when they *experience its value*, and the *faster* they reach that "aha, this is useful" moment, the more likely they *stay*. Good onboarding *minimises the time to value*, it *guides* the user *efficiently* to their first success (skipping confusion and friction), so they *quickly* see why the app is worth using. Slow, confusing onboarding *delays* (or *prevents*) reaching value, so users leave before they "get it." So onboarding's job is to get users to value *fast*.
- **It's especially crucial for a product (and the capstone):** for a *real product* (which you're building toward, W24), onboarding directly affects *conversion* and *retention* (whether trial/new users become *active*, *paying* users), making it a *business-critical* aspect, not just polish. A product *lives or dies* partly on how well it onboards new users into active, valuable use.
So onboarding is critical because the *first experience decides* whether new users *stay or leave*, users must reach *value quickly* to continue, and for a real product it directly drives *retention and conversion*. Investing in good onboarding (a clear, guiding, quickly-valuable first experience) is investing in *keeping* the new users you work to attract, which is essential for any product.

## Designing good onboarding: guide to value, reduce friction
The principles of good onboarding (which tie together polish themes) are about *guiding the user to value with minimal friction*:
- **Get them to first value fast:** identify the *core value* / the "aha moment" (the first time the user *gets* the app's usefulness) and *guide* the user *to it quickly*, removing steps and friction in between. Don't make them figure it out alone or wade through setup; *lead* them to the first success efficiently. Minimise *time to value*.
- **Reduce friction and cognitive load:** make the first experience *easy*, minimal required setup (don't demand a lot before they see value), clear next steps (so they're never wondering "what now?"), sensible defaults (so they don't have to configure everything), progressive disclosure (don't overwhelm with everything at once). Every bit of friction or confusion in onboarding loses users, so you *smooth* the path.
- **Use the polished states (it connects):** good onboarding *uses* the polish from this week, *thoughtful empty states* (D2) that guide the new user (whose screens are mostly empty), *clear feedback* and *error handling* (D3) so first actions feel smooth, *accessible* (D4) so all new users can onboard. Onboarding *is* largely the new-user experience of these polished details, so the week's polish *supports* good onboarding.
- **Guide, don't just dump:** *actively guide* the new user (a welcome, prompts to the first action, helpful empty states, maybe a brief tour) rather than dropping them into a complex empty app to fend for themselves. *Lead* them to success.
So good onboarding *guides the new user to value quickly* (identify and lead to the "aha moment"), *reduces friction* (easy first experience, minimal setup, clear steps, sensible defaults), *uses the polished states* (guiding empty states, smooth feedback, accessibility), and *actively guides* rather than abandoning. Done well, onboarding turns confused new arrivals into *engaged, value-realising* users who *stay*, which is critical for retention and (for a product) conversion. It's the polish dimension focused on the *crucial first experience*, and it ties together the week's details (empty states, errors, accessibility) into a smooth, guiding new-user journey. For the capstone product (W24), good onboarding is essential to turning new users into active, paying ones.

## Where this fits
You understand onboarding: guiding new users to value quickly (to their first "aha" success) with minimal friction, which is critical because the *first experience decides* whether users stay or leave and users must reach value fast to continue, especially crucial for a product's retention/conversion, and it ties together the week's polish (guiding empty states, smooth feedback, accessibility) into the new-user journey. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship a polished app.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a polished product
You assemble the week into a thorough polish pass on your app, fixing every rough edge that makes it feel unfinished, demonstrating the difference between a side project and a product:
- thoughtful **empty states** (explain, reassure, guide), graceful **error states** (clear, recoverable, contained), and clear **loading feedback**, all states handled, not just the happy path.
- **accessibility** ensured (keyboard-navigable, screen-reader-friendly, sufficient contrast, audited), and **i18n** structured-for where relevant.
- a smooth **onboarding** flow guiding new users to value, and overall **consistency** (spacing, styling, interactions).
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Polish: empty/error/loading states, accessibility, onboarding, consistency - product, not side project"
git push
```

## The deliverable is an app that *feels* like a product
What makes this project demonstrate real competence is that the app *feels* finished, polished, professional, *like a product, not a side project*, which is what users (and the capstone) need. The strongest version has *all the states handled thoughtfully* (empty states guide, errors are graceful and recoverable, loading gives feedback, no broken-feeling blank screens), is *accessible* (works for keyboard, screen-reader, and colour-vision-impaired users, a responsibility met), *onboards* new users smoothly to value, and is *consistent* (polished spacing, styling, interactions throughout). The proof is the *felt quality*: someone using the app experiences it as *thoughtful*, *robust*, and *finished*, every state is handled, failures are graceful, it works for everyone, new users are guided, the details are consistent, rather than experiencing the rough edges (broken empty states, cryptic errors, inaccessible controls, confusing first use, inconsistent spacing) that make an app feel like an unfinished side project. Demonstrating that you can do the *polish*, the "last 5% that takes 50% of the time", that makes an app *feel* like a quality product (handling all states, accessibility, onboarding, consistency), is the deliverable, and it's exactly what separates a *product* (that users trust, value, and pay for) from a *side project* (that works but feels rough), which is critical for the real-product capstone next.

## What polish established
Step back: you have learned that *polish, the last 5% that takes 50% of the time, is what users notice most and what makes an app feel like a product*. You understand that *users judge quality from the visible details, not the code*, so the polish, *all the states handled* (empty states that guide, error states that recover gracefully, loading feedback, not just the happy path), *accessibility* (the app working for *all* users, a responsibility and often a legal requirement), *internationalisation* (structured-for where the audience needs it), *onboarding* (guiding new users to value, critical for retention), and overall *consistency*, is what determines *perceived* quality and separates a *product* from a *side project*. The throughline is *attending to the details users actually experience*, the unhappy-path states, the diverse users, the first experience, the consistency, with *care*, which is what makes an app feel *finished*, *trustworthy*, and *professional*. And this *completes the Production phase*: security (W21), scaling (W22), and polish (W23), the final hardening that turns a working, well-engineered app into a *robust, secure, scalable, polished product* ready for real users, which is exactly what the capstone delivers.

## Where this fits
You shipped a polished app that *feels* like a product, all states handled, accessible, onboarding new users, consistent, the "last 5%" that determines perceived quality, completing the Production phase. Next is the **Capstone**: **Ship a SaaS, real users, real revenue**, where you stop building features and make everything you've built (Bean Forge, evolved from a static page to a full SaaS) *solid, documented, and ready for real users*, picking a sellable problem, pricing, launching, and handling the compliance and product realities of an actual business, the culmination of the entire track.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a button that opens a dialog modal. When the dialog opens, the user presses Tab. Where should focus go and what should Tab behaviour be inside the modal? When the modal opens, focus must move to the first focusable element inside the modal (or the modal itself if it has tabIndex={0}). While the modal is open, Tab should cycle through focusable elements inside the modal only, focus must not escape to elements behind the modal. When the modal closes (Escape key or close button), focus must return to the button that opened it. This is focus trapping. Use the focus-trap-react library or implement it manually with a ref and a keydown listener.

weeks.title: Capstone, Ship a SaaS, Real Users, Real Revenue
weeks.context:
This is the week you stop building features and start shipping a product. Bean Forge has evolved from a static HTML page to a full-stack SaaS with authentication, payments, real-time updates, file uploads, and email. Week 24 is not about adding anything, it is about making everything you have built solid, documented, and ready for real users.

A real SaaS needs a public landing page, pricing page, and blog. It needs a production monitoring setup (Sentry, uptime monitoring, structured logs). It needs a runbook: a document that describes what to do when something breaks in production. It needs a privacy policy and terms of service (real legal documents, use a template generator like Termly or the EFF's model privacy policy, then have a lawyer review before you have real users). It needs an onboarding flow: what happens between a user signing up and them getting value from the product?

The capstone project: you will ship Bean Forge as a real, publicly accessible SaaS. Set a goal of 10 real users (not test accounts, not friends being polite, users who actually use the product). To get 10 users, you need to distribute it: post in relevant communities (Reddit communities for coffee shop owners, Product Hunt, Twitter/X, local business groups), reach out directly to small coffee shop owners, or write a blog post about building it. The constraint of real users forces every previous lesson into sharp focus: performance matters because users on slow connections will leave; security matters because real data is at stake; reliability matters because users expect the product to be there.

The capstone project for this track is not a toy. It is something you can put in your portfolio, link in job applications, and point to when asked to demonstrate full-stack experience. The code is on GitHub (public, with a clean README), the application is live on a real domain, and it has at least one paying subscriber (even if it is you, to prove the payment flow works end-to-end).

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Stop building features, ship a product
This is the capstone, and its premise is a shift: **you stop building features and start shipping a *product*.** Over 23 weeks, Bean Forge evolved from a static HTML page to a *full-stack SaaS*, with authentication, payments, real-time updates, file uploads, and email, and Week 24 is **not about adding anything**. It's about making *everything you've built* **solid, documented, and ready for real users.** This is the difference between a *project* (a collection of features) and a *product* (something real users can actually sign up for, pay for, and rely on), and it requires more than code: a landing page, monitoring, a runbook, legal documents, onboarding, *and* the *business* thinking (what problem does it solve, how is it priced, how do you launch). This week you make your app a *real, shippable product*.

## A real SaaS is more than features
The orientation is understanding *what a real product needs beyond the features you've built*, which is often *more* than developers expect:
- **A public face:** a landing page (explaining what it is and why to use it), a pricing page, maybe a blog, the *marketing* surface that turns visitors into users (not just the app itself).
- **Production operations:** monitoring (Sentry, uptime monitoring, structured logs, W20) so you *know* when something breaks, and a *runbook* (a document describing *what to do when something breaks in production*) so you can *respond*. The operational readiness to *run* the product reliably.
- **Legal/compliance:** a *privacy policy* and *terms of service* (real legal documents, often required, especially with user data and payments), which you start from a template (Termly, the EFF's model policy) and ideally have a lawyer review before real users.
- **The product experience:** a proper *onboarding* flow (W23) guiding new users to value, the polish (W23) making it feel finished.
- **The business basics:** what problem it solves (is it *sellable*?), pricing, a launch plan.
So a real product = the *features* (which you've built) + the *public face* (landing, pricing) + *operations* (monitoring, runbook) + *legal* (privacy, terms) + *product experience* (onboarding, polish) + *business* (problem, pricing, launch). The capstone is assembling *all* of this into something *real users can actually use and pay for*, which is *more* than the code, and that "more" is what makes it a *product* rather than a *project*.

## Where this fits
This is the **Capstone** of the full-stack-web track: shipping Bean Forge (now a full SaaS) as a *real product, ready for real users and real revenue*, the culmination of everything, making it solid, documented, legal, operational, and business-ready, not adding features. Today's orientation: a real product is *more than features*, it needs a public face (landing, pricing), operations (monitoring, runbook), legal (privacy, terms), product experience (onboarding, polish), and business thinking (problem, pricing, launch), and this week assembles all of that into something real users can sign up for and pay for. Tomorrow you start with the business foundation: picking a sellable problem.

items.title: Picking a sellable problem
items.body:
## Picking a sellable problem
A product exists to *solve a problem people will pay to have solved*, so the foundational business question is whether your product addresses a **sellable problem**, a *real* problem that *real people* have and would *pay* to solve. This is the most important product decision, and it's a *business* judgment, not a technical one:
```text
a sellable problem:  a REAL problem (people actually have it and feel it)
                     that people would PAY to solve (it's valuable enough to pay for)
                     for a SPECIFIC audience (you know who has it)
   -> the product's value rests on solving a problem that's real, painful, and worth paying for
```
The hard truth: a *technically impressive* product that solves a *non-problem* (something no one actually needs or would pay for) has no market, while a *simple* product that solves a *real, painful, paid* problem can succeed. So before launching, you assess: *is the problem real?* (do people actually have it?), *is it painful enough?* (would they pay to solve it?), *who specifically has it?* (your audience).

## Why this is the make-or-break decision
Understanding *why* the sellable-problem question is so decisive frames the business reality:
- **No real problem = no product, regardless of code quality:** a product *succeeds* by *solving a problem people value*, so if there's *no real problem* (or no one will *pay* to solve it), the product *fails* no matter how well-built, the best engineering can't save a product no one needs. This is the most common reason products fail: they're built *well* but solve a problem that's *not real, not painful, or not paid*. So the *problem* (not the technology) determines viability, you can build anything, but it only *succeeds* if it solves something people will pay for.
- **It's a *validation* question, answered by talking to people, not building:** whether a problem is *real and sellable* is validated by *understanding the people* who'd have it, ideally *talking* to potential users/customers, *before* over-investing, not by *assuming* (the developer's trap of building what *seems* cool without checking if anyone needs it). This echoes the user-research-before-code discipline (from the AI/ML capstones): *validate* that the problem is real and the audience exists, rather than building on an *assumption*. (For Bean Forge, you've built it; the capstone-as-product framing asks you to *think* about its sellable-problem framing, who would *pay* for this, and *why*, which is the product thinking even for a learning project.)
- **It defines everything downstream:** the *problem* and *audience* define the product's *positioning* (how you describe it), *pricing* (what it's worth to them, D3), *marketing* (how you reach them), and *launch* (where they are). So *clarifying the sellable problem* is the foundation the rest of the product/business decisions build on, get it clear, and pricing/marketing/launch follow; leave it vague, and everything downstream is unfocused.
So picking (or clarifying) a sellable problem is make-or-break because *the problem, not the technology, determines viability* (a great product solving a non-problem fails), it's a *validation* question (understand/talk to the people, don't assume), and it *defines* the downstream product/business decisions. It's the most important product judgment, and it's *business* thinking that's essential to shipping a real product (not just code).

## The shift: from "can I build it?" to "should I, for whom, why?"
The deeper lesson, fitting the capstone's product framing, is the *shift in thinking* from *engineering* ("can I build this?") to *product/business* ("*should* I build this, *for whom*, and *why would they pay*?"), which is the mindset a real product requires. As an engineer, you've focused on *building* (can I make this work?); as a *product* person (which shipping a real product requires), you must *also* think about *value* (does this solve a real problem people will pay for?), *audience* (who specifically?), and *viability* (is there a market?). This is a genuinely *different* and *essential* lens, the best engineering serves a *product* that solves a *real problem* for a *real audience*, and without that product/business validation, even brilliant engineering builds something no one wants. So the capstone asks you to apply *both* lenses: the *engineering* (which you've mastered, build it well) *and* the *product/business* (which this week introduces, is it solving a sellable problem for a real audience?). For your capstone product, *clarifying the sellable problem*, articulating the *real problem*, the *specific audience*, and *why they'd pay*, is the foundational product thinking that turns "I built an app" into "I built a *product* that solves *X* for *Y* who'll pay *because Z*." This product/business thinking is what separates *shipping a product* from *building an app*, and it's a valuable skill (especially for anyone who'll build their own products or work on product teams) that the capstone deliberately introduces alongside the technical culmination. Understanding that a product's success rests on solving a *sellable problem* (real, painful, paid, for a specific audience), validated by understanding the people, is the foundation of the product thinking the capstone is about.

## Where this fits
You understand picking a sellable problem: the make-or-break product judgment that the product must solve a *real* problem people would *pay* to solve for a *specific* audience (the problem, not the technology, determines viability), validated by understanding/talking to the people, which defines all downstream decisions and reflects the essential shift from "can I build it?" to "*should* I, for *whom*, and *why would they pay*?" Tomorrow you handle how to charge: pricing.

items.title: Pricing
items.body:
## Pricing: how to charge for your product
If your product solves a sellable problem, you need to *charge* for it, and **pricing**, how much, and in what structure, is a crucial, surprisingly hard product decision (you built the payments mechanics in W13; now the *pricing strategy*). Pricing has *structure* and *level*:
```text
pricing STRUCTURE (the model):  subscription (monthly/annual), one-time, usage-based, freemium, tiers
pricing LEVEL (the amount):     what to actually charge (based on VALUE to the customer, not cost)
common SaaS pattern:            tiered subscriptions (e.g. Free / Pro / Business),
                                often with a free tier or trial to let users experience value first
```
You decide the *model* (subscriptions are standard for SaaS, often *tiered*, sometimes with a free tier/trial) and the *level* (how much each tier costs), which together form your pricing.

## Why pricing is hard, and how to think about it
Understanding *why* pricing is hard and the key principles helps you approach it sensibly:
- **Price on *value*, not *cost*:** the most important pricing principle is to price based on the *value* the product delivers to the customer (what it's *worth* to them, the problem-solving value), *not* on what it *costs* you to build/run. A product that saves a business thousands is worth far more than its hosting cost, so you price by *value to the customer*, not your costs. (Cost sets a *floor*, you must cover costs, but *value* sets the *price*.) Pricing too low (by costs) *leaves money on the table* and can *signal low value*; pricing by *value* captures the product's worth. This value-based thinking is central and counterintuitive (engineers often think in costs).
- **It's a balance with real trade-offs:** pricing balances *capturing value* (charge enough to reflect worth and sustain the business) against *accessibility/adoption* (too high a price limits who buys; too low undervalues and undercharges). Tiers help (Free/cheap tiers for accessibility and adoption; higher tiers to capture value from those who'll pay more), and a *free tier or trial* lets users *experience the value* before paying (which drives conversion, you've seen the product's value, now you'll pay), connecting to the subscription/trial mechanics from W13. Finding the *right* level and structure is genuinely hard (it requires understanding what customers value and will pay), and it's often *iterated* (you adjust pricing based on what you learn).
- **Pricing communicates and positions:** your price *signals* your product's value and *positions* it (a higher price signals premium/serious; a very low price can signal cheap/unserious), so pricing is also a *positioning* decision, it tells the market what the product *is*. So you price to *position* the product appropriately for its value and audience.
So pricing is hard because you must price on *value* (not cost, the key, counterintuitive principle), *balance* value-capture against accessibility (via tiers, free trials), and use price to *position* the product, all of which require understanding what your customers *value* and will *pay*. Approaching pricing thoughtfully (value-based, tiered, with a trial, positioned right), rather than just picking a number, is the product-business skill the capstone introduces here.

## Pricing as part of product/business thinking
The deeper point is that *pricing is a core product decision* (not an afterthought), and thinking about it, even for a learning capstone, builds the *product/business* judgment that complements your engineering. Pricing *directly* determines whether the product is a *viable business* (it must capture enough value to sustain itself) *and* how *accessible* it is (who can afford it), so it's *central* to the product's success, not a detail to slap on at the end. And it requires the *value-based*, *customer-understanding* thinking that's the heart of product judgment (what's this *worth* to the customer? what will they *pay*?), which is the same audience-and-value lens as picking the sellable problem (D2). For your capstone product, *thinking through the pricing*, the *model* (likely tiered subscriptions, leveraging the W13 payment infrastructure), the *level* (value-based, what your audience would pay for the problem solved), and the *structure* (free tier/trial to let users experience value, paid tiers to capture it), is the product-business exercise that, combined with the sellable-problem thinking (D2), turns your *built app* into a *priced product* with a *plausible business model*. Even if you don't actually charge real money for a learning capstone, *reasoning about* pricing (how *would* you price this, *why*, for *whom*) develops the product/business judgment that real products require and that's valuable for anyone building or working on products. Pricing, like the sellable-problem question, is part of the *product thinking* that the capstone adds to your *engineering*, the recognition that shipping a *product* (vs building an app) means thinking about *value*, *audience*, and *how to capture value* (pricing), not just *building*. Understanding pricing, value-based, tiered, positioning, balancing capture and accessibility, is a core piece of that product thinking.

## Where this fits
You understand pricing: the product decision of *structure* (model, often tiered subscriptions with a free trial, using the W13 payment mechanics) and *level* (the amount), with the key principle of pricing on *value to the customer* (not your cost), balancing value-capture against accessibility, and using price to position the product, a core product/business decision (not an afterthought) that, with the sellable-problem thinking, turns your built app into a priced product with a business model. Tomorrow you handle getting it in front of users: launch strategy.

items.title: Launch strategy
items.body:
## Launch strategy: getting the product in front of users
Building a product nobody *sees* helps no one, so **launch strategy**, how you get your product *in front of* potential users, is essential. Launching isn't just "flip it live"; it's *deliberately reaching the audience* who has the problem you solve:
```text
launch = getting the product to the PEOPLE WHO HAVE THE PROBLEM (your audience, D2)
   - go where your audience IS (the communities, platforms, channels they use)
   - communicate the VALUE clearly (the problem you solve, why it matters to them)
   - common channels: relevant communities, Product Hunt, social media, content/SEO,
     direct outreach, word of mouth - WHERE YOUR SPECIFIC AUDIENCE is
   - start small, learn, iterate (D5) - a launch is a beginning, not a one-shot event
```
A launch is about *connecting your product to your audience*, reaching the people who have the problem (D2), where they *are*, with a clear message about the *value* you provide.

## Why launch strategy matters, and how to think about it
Understanding *why* launching deliberately matters (rather than "build it and they'll come") shows the product reality:
- **"Build it and they will come" is false, you must *reach* people:** a common, fatal assumption is that a good product *automatically* attracts users, it doesn't. Users won't find your product unless you *get it in front of them*, so *deliberately reaching your audience* (launch/marketing/distribution) is *essential*, a great product *no one knows about* fails just as surely as a bad one. So you must *actively* connect the product to its audience, which is what launch strategy is. *Distribution* (getting to users) is as important as the product itself.
- **Go where your *specific* audience is:** effective launching means reaching *your* audience (the specific people with the problem, D2) where *they* are, the communities, platforms, and channels *they* use, with a message about *their* problem. This follows directly from knowing your audience (D2): you reach *them*, specifically, not "everyone" generically. A targeted launch (to the right people, with the right message) is far more effective than a broad, unfocused one. So launch strategy *depends on* understanding your audience (the D2 foundation).
- **Communicate the *value* clearly:** when you reach people, you must *clearly communicate the value*, what *problem* you solve and *why it matters to them* (the landing page, the pitch, D1's public face), so they *understand* why to use it. A clear value message (tied to their problem) converts reached people into users; a vague one doesn't. So launching includes *communicating value clearly* to the audience you reach.
- **A launch is a *beginning*, learn and iterate:** a launch isn't a one-shot make-or-break event; it's the *start* of getting users, learning from them, and iterating (D5). You launch, *see* how users respond, and *iterate* (improve the product, the message, the targeting), so launching is the *beginning* of a learning loop, not a finale. (Many products launch small, learn, and grow, rather than "big bang" launching.)
So launch strategy matters because *distribution is essential* (build-it-and-they-come is false, you must *reach* people), you reach *your specific audience* where they are (depending on the D2 audience understanding), you *communicate value clearly* (so reached people convert), and a launch is a *beginning* (launch, learn, iterate). Thinking about *how you'd reach and convince your audience* is the product/business skill that complements building the product.

## Launch thinking as part of shipping a product
The deeper point, continuing the product/business theme, is that *getting users (distribution/launch) is a core part of shipping a product*, as essential as building it, and *thinking about it* (even for a learning capstone) builds crucial product judgment. Developers often *under*-value distribution (focusing on *building*, assuming users will come), but for a *real product*, *reaching users* is *half the battle* (or more), a brilliant product no one finds fails. So shipping a *product* (vs building an app) requires *also* thinking about *how to get it to users* (launch/marketing/distribution), which is the product/business lens applied to *reach*. For your capstone, *thinking through the launch*, *who* your audience is (D2), *where* they are, *how* you'd reach them, *what* value message you'd communicate, *how* you'd start small and iterate, is the exercise that develops this distribution judgment, completing the product picture: you've *built* it (engineering), framed the *sellable problem* and *pricing* (D2-D3), and now think about *getting it to users* (launch). Even without a real launch, *reasoning about* it (how *would* I reach my audience and communicate value?) builds the distribution/marketing judgment that real products require and that engineers often lack. Launch strategy is the piece that turns "I built and priced a product" into "I have a plan to *get it to the people who need it*", which is essential to a product *succeeding* (vs just *existing*). Understanding that *distribution is essential* (not automatic), reaching *your specific audience* where they are with a clear *value* message, as the *start* of a learning loop, is the launch thinking that's a core part of the product/business judgment the capstone develops.

## Where this fits
You understand launch strategy: deliberately getting the product in front of your *specific* audience (where they are, with a clear value message), because *distribution is essential* (build-it-and-they-come is false) and a launch is the *beginning* of a learn-and-iterate loop, a core part of shipping a product that complements building it, developing the distribution judgment engineers often lack. Tomorrow you handle learning from real users: first-week iteration.

items.title: First-week iteration
items.body:
## First-week iteration: learning from real users
Once you launch and *real users* start using your product, the crucial activity is **first-week iteration**, *learning* from how real users actually behave and *rapidly improving* based on what you learn. The launch is the *beginning* (D4): real users *reveal* what *assumptions* were wrong, what's *confusing*, what's *missing*, what they *actually* value, and the first week (and beyond) is about *observing*, *learning*, and *iterating*:
```text
launch -> real users use it -> OBSERVE (analytics, behaviour, feedback, errors)
   -> LEARN (what's confusing? where do they drop off? what do they value? what's broken?)
   -> ITERATE (fix the friction, improve onboarding, address feedback) -> repeat
   -> the product IMPROVES based on REAL usage, not assumptions
```
You *watch* how real users behave (via the analytics, observability, and error monitoring you built, W20), *gather* their feedback, *learn* what's working and what isn't, and *iterate quickly* to improve, especially the onboarding and friction points that determine whether new users *stick*.

## Why first-week (and ongoing) iteration matters
Understanding *why* learning from real users is so important shows a fundamental product truth:
- **Real users reveal what assumptions got wrong:** *no matter how carefully* you built and designed, *real users* behave in ways you *didn't fully anticipate*, they get confused where you thought it was clear, value things you didn't expect, ignore features you thought were key, hit problems you didn't foresee. *Real usage* is the *only* way to *truly* learn what works, your assumptions (however good) are *hypotheses* that real users *test*, and they're *often wrong* in surprising ways. So *observing real users* reveals the *truth* about your product (vs your assumptions), which is invaluable and unavailable any other way. The first contact with real users is hugely informative *because* it tests your assumptions against reality.
- **Iterating *fast* on early learning is high-leverage:** the *early* learning (first users, first week) is especially valuable because *fixing* the problems it reveals (the confusing onboarding, the friction, the missing thing) *quickly* improves the product *for all subsequent users*, and *early* users are where you learn the *most* (the biggest, most fundamental issues surface first). So *rapid* iteration on early feedback is *high-leverage*, you learn the most important things early and fixing them fast benefits everyone after. The first-week iteration *compounds* (each fix improves the product for all future users).
- **It's the *measure-learn-improve* loop, for the product:** this is the empirical, *measure-then-improve* discipline (pervasive across the tracks, performance, ML, everything) applied to the *product*: you *measure* (real user behaviour, feedback), *learn* (what's working/not), and *improve* (iterate), rather than assuming you got it right. The product, like a model or a system, is *improved* by *observing reality* and *iterating*, not by assuming the initial version is perfect. So first-week iteration is the *product* version of the measure-learn-improve loop that's central to good engineering throughout the track.
So first-week iteration matters because *real users reveal the truth* (your assumptions are hypotheses they test, often wrongly), *early* learning is *high-leverage* (you learn the most and fixes benefit everyone after), and it's the *measure-learn-improve* loop applied to the product. *Learning from real users and iterating* is how a product *actually* gets good (vs how you *imagined* it would be good), which is essential to a successful product.

## The mindset: launch is the start, the product is never "done"
The deeper lesson, fitting the capstone's culmination, is the *mindset* that **launching is the *start*, not the end, and a product is *never* "done", it's continuously improved based on real users**, which is the product version of the "it's not done at launch, you maintain/improve it" theme that's recurred throughout (performance, security, ML models, everything). The developer's instinct is to treat *launch* as the *finish line* (built it, shipped it, done); the *product* reality is that launch is the *starting line* of the *real* work, *learning from users and continuously improving*. A successful product is *never* finished; it *evolves* based on *real* user needs and behaviour, iteration is *perpetual* (first-week, and ongoing). This mindset, *ship, learn, iterate, repeat*, is what makes products *succeed* (they get better and better at serving real users) vs *stagnate* (a launched-and-abandoned product that never improves past its initial, assumption-based version). For your capstone, *understanding* this (launch is the beginning; you'd observe real users and iterate, especially on the early friction) is the product mindset that completes the picture: you've *built*, *framed* (sellable problem), *priced*, *planned the launch*, and now understand that *post-launch* you'd *learn and iterate* perpetually. Even for a learning capstone, internalising that *a product is shipped to be learned-from and improved, not finished*, is the crucial product mindset, it's the same *empirical, never-done, continuously-improving* discipline as the rest of your engineering, now applied to the *product* as a whole. Understanding first-week (and ongoing) iteration, *learning from real users and rapidly improving*, as the start of a perpetual improvement loop (not the end), is the product mindset that the capstone instills, and it's how real products actually succeed.

## Where this fits
You understand first-week iteration: learning from *real users* (who reveal where your assumptions were wrong) and rapidly improving, which is high-leverage (early learning matters most, fixes benefit all later users) and is the measure-learn-improve loop applied to the product, embodying the mindset that *launch is the start, not the end, and a product is never "done"* but continuously improved from real usage. Tomorrow you handle the legal realities: compliance basics.

items.title: Compliance basics
items.body:
## Compliance basics: the legal realities of a real product
A *real* product with *real users* (and their *data* and *money*) has *legal obligations*, and **compliance basics**, the essential legal/regulatory realities, are part of shipping responsibly. The key ones:
- **Privacy policy and terms of service:** real products *need* these legal documents, a *privacy policy* (how you collect, use, and protect user data, often *legally required*, especially under GDPR/CCPA) and *terms of service* (the rules/agreement for using your product). You *start* from a *template* (Termly, the EFF's model privacy policy, or similar generators) and, *before* you have real users, ideally *have a lawyer review* them (templates are a starting point, not a substitute for legal advice for a real business).
- **Data protection / privacy law (GDPR, CCPA, etc.):** if you handle *personal data* (you do, users' info), privacy regulations *apply* (GDPR for EU users, CCPA for California, and others), requiring things like a lawful basis for processing, user rights (access, deletion), data protection, and consent where needed (the W12/data-handling themes). You *comply* with the regulations relevant to your users.
- **Payment/financial compliance:** handling *payments* (W13) involves compliance (PCI, which Stripe handles for you, the reason you use it), and *charging* customers involves tax and financial obligations.
- **Other relevant rules:** depending on your product/audience, there may be sector-specific or regional rules (accessibility laws, W23; email/marketing laws, W14; etc.) that apply.

## Why compliance matters and how to approach it
Understanding *why* compliance matters and the *sensible* approach (without becoming a lawyer) frames it correctly:
- **Real products have real legal obligations, and ignoring them is a real risk:** once you have *real* users, *real* data, and *real* money, you have *legal responsibilities* (privacy law, terms, payment compliance), and *ignoring* them is a *real risk*, legal liability, fines (GDPR fines are substantial), and loss of user trust. Compliance *isn't* optional for a real product; it's a *requirement* of operating legally and responsibly. So a *real* product (vs a hobby project) *must* address its compliance obligations, it's part of being a legitimate business.
- **It's mostly about *known*, *standard* obligations (handle the basics):** the *good news* is that for most products, the compliance basics are *known* and *standard*, you need a privacy policy and terms (start from templates), comply with the *standard* privacy laws (GDPR/CCPA basics, which have well-understood requirements), use a compliant payment processor (Stripe, handling PCI), and address the standard obligations for your situation. You don't have to be a legal expert; you need to *address the known basics* responsibly. So compliance, like security (W21), is largely about *systematically handling the known, standard obligations*, not navigating infinite legal complexity.
- **Use templates *and* (for real launch) get legal review:** the *practical* approach is to *start* from *templates/generators* (Termly, the EFF model policy) for the documents (a good, cheap starting point), *and*, *before* real users/revenue, *have a lawyer review* (because templates aren't tailored to your specifics, and the stakes, legal liability, warrant professional review for a real business). So you *bootstrap* with templates (accessible, cheap) but *don't* treat them as a *substitute* for legal advice for a *real* product, get a professional review before real launch. This balances *practicality* (templates to start) with *responsibility* (legal review before real stakes).
So compliance matters because *real products have real legal obligations* (ignoring them is a real risk), it's mostly about *handling the known, standard basics* responsibly (privacy policy, terms, privacy law, payment compliance), and the *approach* is *templates to start* plus *legal review before real launch*. Addressing compliance is part of shipping a *real, responsible* product (vs a hobby project that ignores legal realities).

## Compliance as part of responsible, real-product shipping
The deeper point is that *compliance is part of shipping a product *responsibly* and *legitimately**, and *awareness* of it (even for a learning capstone) is part of the product maturity the capstone develops. Shipping a *real* product to *real* users isn't just a *technical* act; it's *operating a business* that has *responsibilities*, to users (protecting their data, the privacy/responsibility themes from across the tracks), and *legally* (the regulations). *Ignoring* compliance (no privacy policy, ignoring GDPR, etc.) isn't just risky; it's *irresponsible* (failing your users and the law). So a *responsible* product *addresses* its compliance obligations, which is part of the *maturity* of shipping a *real* product (vs a careless hobby project). This connects to the *responsibility* themes throughout the track (responsible ML, security, privacy, accessibility), shipping responsibly means *meeting your obligations to users and the law*, of which compliance (privacy, terms, data protection) is a key part. For your capstone, *being aware* of the compliance basics (you'd need a privacy policy and terms, you'd comply with privacy law, you'd use compliant payments) and *how to approach* them (templates plus legal review) is the product-maturity awareness that completes the responsible-shipping picture: a real product is *built well*, *solves a real problem*, is *priced* and *launched* thoughtfully, *learns and iterates*, *and* meets its *legal/compliance obligations* (responsibly, legitimately). Even for a learning capstone, *understanding* that real products have real compliance obligations, and how to responsibly address the basics, is essential product maturity, it's the recognition that *shipping a real product is operating a responsible business*, with obligations to users and the law, not just deploying code. Compliance basics are the legal/responsibility piece of shipping a real product, and awareness of them is part of the product maturity the capstone instills.

## Where this fits
You understand compliance basics: real products have real legal obligations (privacy policy, terms of service, data protection law like GDPR/CCPA, payment compliance) that you address responsibly via templates-plus-legal-review, because ignoring them is a real legal and trust risk, part of shipping a product *responsibly and legitimately* (the responsibility theme), and essential product maturity. Tomorrow you assemble everything and ship the real product, completing the track.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a real product, and the track
You assemble everything into a *real, shippable SaaS product*, completing the full-stack-web track. Bean Forge (or your app) is now not just built but *product-ready*:
- the *full-stack SaaS* (auth, payments, real-time, files, email, all the features) made *solid* (secure, scaled-aware, polished, tested, observable, the W17-23 hardening).
- a *public face* (landing page, pricing page), *operations* (monitoring, a *runbook* for when things break), *legal* (privacy policy, terms), and a *product experience* (onboarding, polish).
- the *business thinking*: a clear *sellable problem*, *pricing*, a *launch plan*, an *iteration* mindset, and *compliance* awareness.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Capstone: Bean Forge shipped as a real, solid, documented, product-ready SaaS"
git push   # live, monitored, ready for real users
```

## The deliverable is a real product, ready for real users
What makes this capstone the culmination is that you've produced a *real product, ready for real users and real revenue*, not just a working app, but a *solid, documented, operational, legal, polished, business-framed product* that real users could actually sign up for, pay for, and rely on. The strongest version is *genuinely product-ready*: the full SaaS *works* and is *hardened* (secure, tested, observable, polished, the production-grade quality from the whole track), it has the *public face* and *product experience* (landing, pricing, onboarding) that turn visitors into users, the *operations* (monitoring, runbook) to *run* it reliably, the *legal* basis (privacy, terms) to operate responsibly, *and* the *business framing* (sellable problem, pricing, launch, iteration mindset, compliance) that makes it a *product/business*, not just code. The proof is that it's *ready for real users*: a real person could find it (landing page), understand it (clear value), sign up and pay (auth + payments), use it (the polished, accessible features), and rely on it (it's monitored, secure, solid), and you could *operate* it responsibly (runbook, compliance) and *improve* it (iteration mindset). Demonstrating that you can take an app *all the way* to a *real, shippable, product-ready SaaS*, technically solid *and* product-and-business-ready, is the deliverable, and it's the ultimate proof of full-stack capability: you can build *and ship a real product*, end to end, which is exactly what the track was for.

## What the full-stack-web track delivered
Step back across all 24 weeks. You began with "a website is a set of files" and finish able to *build and ship a real, full-stack SaaS product*. You can build the *frontend* (HTML/CSS/JS fundamentals, React, Next.js, Tailwind, state management), the *backend* (Node/Express, PostgreSQL/Prisma, REST APIs, auth), the *real-world features* (payments, email, files, real-time), with *production quality* (testing, performance, CI/CD, observability) and *production hardening* (security, scaling, polish), and finally *ship it as a product* (with the business and product thinking). More than any single skill, you've internalised what *full-stack product development* is: not just building features, but *building them well* (engineered, tested, secure, performant, observable) *and shipping them* as a *real, polished, operational, responsible product* that solves a real problem for real users. You evolved *one project* (Bean Forge) from a static page to a full SaaS, learning *each layer* deeply and *from first principles* (so you understand what the tools do for you), and you finish as a *full-stack developer who can ship real products*, the rare and valuable combination of *building* and *shipping*, *engineering* and *product*. You started learning what a website is; you finish able to ship a SaaS.

## Where this fits in the track
You shipped a real, product-ready SaaS, the culmination of the full-stack-web track: the full-stack engineering (frontend, backend, features), the production quality and hardening (testing, performance, CI/CD, observability, security, scaling, polish), and the product/business thinking (sellable problem, pricing, launch, iteration, compliance), all integrated into something real users can use and pay for. This is the end of the track, and the beginning of your work as a full-stack developer who can *ship real products*. You can build the whole stack, and, rarer and more valuable, you can take a product all the way from idea to a real, shippable, solid SaaS, end to end.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have 10 users. One of them emails you at 2am saying "I can't log in." What is your process? Step 1: check your uptime monitor, is the site down? Step 2: check Sentry, is there an unhandled exception in the auth flow? Step 3: check your structured logs for login attempts from that user's email, did the attempt reach the server? What was the response? Step 4: try logging in yourself, does it work for you? Step 5: if you cannot reproduce it, ask the user for their browser, device, and any error message they saw. Step 6: if the site is down, follow your runbook for the incident type. If you can reproduce the bug, write a failing test first, then fix it.
